The brain reads melatonin through two receptors, MT1 and MT2; in mice, losing MT1 removed melatonin's quieting of the brain's clock, while losing MT2 caused no obvious change in daily rhythms.
In 2019, X-ray laser structures of human MT1 showed a binding pocket sealed from outside, and a 2012 gene study linked rare broken forms of MT2 to type 2 diabetes.
start_here.how_sure_note: That light lowers melatonin and that melatonin acts through MT1 and MT2 is well established; which receptor does which job rests on a few small mouse studies, and the diabetes link is an association with very rare gene variants.

could_be_wrong.point: Most inbred lab mouse strains make no melatonin, so knockout studies test the receptors in animals that may not use the hormone the way people do.
The MT2 clock-slice test used only 6 knockout mice against 11 normal mice, and the paper finds limited overlap in the two receptors' jobs, so the split between MT1 and MT2 is not clean.
The 2019 structures hold man-made compounds that switch the receptors on, not melatonin itself, so the shape with the natural hormone may differ.
How melatonin gets into its pocket is still open: both receptors show a channel from the membrane, and the MT2 team suggests a second way in from outside that they did not prove.
The diabetes link rests on very rare gene variants and shows association, not cause.

summary: A 2024 study of about 61,000 UK adults scored how steady their sleep and wake times were from about one week of activity tracker data.

Over about six years, the more regular sleepers had a 20% to 30% lower risk of death than the least regular, after full adjustment, and regularity predicted death from any cause better than sleep length.
The study shows a link and cannot show that changing your sleep timing would change your risk; a small student study links irregular sleep to a later body clock.
start_here.how_sure_note: Two large analyses of the same UK cohort agree, but both are observational, older and mostly white, with one week of tracker data per person.

Limits the authors list: one week of data, an older, mostly white sample, covariates measured years earlier, and correlational design.
annotations.funding: not stated in the article (full text read Nov 20, 2026)
annotations.conflicts: AJKP and SWC have received research funding from Delos and Versalux and are co-founders and co-directors of Circadian Health Innovations PTY LTD; SWC has also received research funding from Beacon Lighting and has consulted for Dyson. Nonfinancial disclosure: none.

annotations.source: Phillips AJK, Clerx WM, O'Brien CS, Sano A, Barger LK, Picard RW, Lockley SW, Klerman EB, Czeisler CA (2017), Irregular sleep/wake patterns are associated with poorer academic performance and delayed circadian and sleep/wake timing, Scientific Reports 7:3216, doi 10.1038/s41598-017-03171-4 (full text read Oct 17, 2026, Europe PMC PMC5468315, CC BY)
annotations.note: Followed 61 undergraduates for 30 days; the 12 least regular sleepers had melatonin onset more than 2 hours later than the 12 most regular, and regularity tracked grades. Small, one campus, melatonin measured on one day, and the authors say they cannot determine causality.
annotations.conflicts: Extensive, as disclosed in the paper's Competing Interests statement (summarised): several authors report consulting, equity, patents or research support from companies in wearables, lighting, sleep medicine and sport; for example RWP co-founded and holds shares in Empatica and Affectiva, AJKP holds a patent on estimating physiological states from sleep and circadian measurements, and CAC received royalties from Philips Respironics for Actiwatch devices.

could_be_wrong.point: An independent analysis of 88,975 people in the same UK Biobank found the link was not a straight line: risk was highest for the most irregular sleepers and levelled off above the median, and the cancer link may partly reflect illness causing irregular sleep.

The authors list one week of tracker data per person, an older and mostly white sample, covariates measured years before the trackers, and a correlational design; regularity may be both a cause and a marker of risk.
Regularity was not a significant predictor of cardiometabolic death once sleep duration was in the same model, so the 'better than duration' result does not hold for every cause of death.
An editorial on the study notes that no study had directly tested the health effect of experimentally changing sleep regularity, and that findings need checking in more diverse groups.
The student study cannot say whether irregular sleep delays the body clock or a late body clock drives irregular sleep; the authors name at least two competing explanations.

The paper gives two sample sizes: 60,977 (abstract, introduction and discussion) and 60,997 (results, 'participants with valid SRI scores'), so the post says about 61,000. The 20% to 48% in the abstract comes from the minimally adjusted model; fully adjusted, it is 20% to 30%, and the authors say the true size likely lies between the two.
The melatonin delay: the abstract's group means (00:08 vs 21:32) differ by about 2.6 hours, while the results text gives an actual average delay of 2.2 hours, so the post says 'more than 2 hours'.

summary: Overload, a film shown at Dutch Design Week 2026, imagines cloud storage as a fantasy memory world where saved files grow into creatures.
In lab tests across three experiments, people remembered art they photographed or screenshotted worse than art they only looked at, and screenshots hurt memory most.
Surveys and interviews link keeping too many files to stress and emotional security, and brain research shows that forgetting is an active process, mostly studied in flies.
start_here.how_sure_note: The photo and screenshot cost is repeated across several labs, but other studies find no cost or a gain under some conditions, and the hoarding studies are single surveys and interviews.

claims.claim: Overload, a film shown at DDW 2026, turned cloud storage into a fantasy memory world where files grow into creatures.
Across three experiments, artworks people photographed or screenshotted were remembered worse than ones they only looked at.
claims.study: three lab experiments, 31 to 42 students each

claims.claim: Screenshots hurt memory most. Harder tasks did not make it worse, so divided attention is unlikely to be the main cause.
claims.where: Study 2 results (76, 63 and 54 percent); General discussion

claims.claim: In 344 students, stress was the strongest of the six cognitive and emotional factors tested for digital hoarding, but the links were small.
claims.study: one survey, 344 university students in Chile

claims.claim: It was one survey at one time, so we cannot tell if stress drives hoarding or the reverse.
In interviews, Gen Z participants kept files for two kinds of reasons: competitive pressure, and emotional security.
Forgetting is a brain function too. Active forgetting pathways clear what no longer matters, mostly shown in flies.
claims.where: Section on the neurobiology of active forgetting

claims.claim: 21 of 35 Gen Z interviewees said deleting content caused anxiety or a sense of loss.

annotations.source: Lurie et al. 2025
annotations.note: Students viewed art and either just looked, photographed it or screenshotted it; memory was worse for saved images, worst for screenshots, and did not track how hard the saving task was. Limits: undergraduate samples, art on screens, and no objective measure of task difficulty in the main studies, which the authors list as a limitation.
annotations.funding: Funding: not applicable (as stated in the paper).
annotations.conflicts: The authors have no conflicts of interest or competing interests to disclose.

annotations.source: Bravo-Adasme et al. 2026
annotations.note: A survey of 344 university students modelled how memory, attention, decision making, stress, enjoyment and anxiety relate to hoarding disorder symptoms and digital hoarding. Stress was the strongest factor for both, and the model explained 37.6 percent of the variance in digital hoarding. Limits: students on one campus in Chile, self-report, one time point.
annotations.funding: Supported by ANID Fondecyt Regular Folio 1230187.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

annotations.source: Zhang, Li and Hao 2025
annotations.note: In-depth interviews with 35 Chinese Generation Z participants, analysed with fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, found two routes to accepting digital hoarding: competitive pressure and emotional security. Limits: a small purposive and snowball sample from one country, which the authors acknowledge.
annotations.funding: Funded by the Research and Practice Program on Higher Education Teaching Reform in Henan Province (No. 2023SJGLX250Y).
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

annotations.source: Berry et al. 2024
annotations.note: A review of active forgetting, the brain processes that weaken or hide memory traces, and how they may go wrong in neuropsychiatric conditions. Most of the mechanisms come from fruit fly studies. Limits: the authors say research into forgetting in model animals is still in its early stages.
annotations.funding: Supported by Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council grant RGPIN-2021-02545 (J. A. Berry) and NIH grant R35NS097224 (R. L. Davis).
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests.

could_be_wrong.point: Freely chosen photo taking can help some memory: across one field and three lab studies, people allowed to take photos recognised more of what they saw, though less of what they heard.
The screenshot studies used undergraduates viewing art on screens, and the authors note they did not objectively measure how hard each saving task was in the main studies.
The hoarding survey was one time point with self-report measures and possible unmeasured confounders such as personality, so it cannot show that stress causes digital hoarding.
The interview study had 35 people from one country chosen through personal and online networks, so its two routes may not hold elsewhere.
Active forgetting pathways are mapped mostly in fruit flies; the review says this research is still at an early stage, so links to human digital habits are a step beyond the evidence.

glossary.plain: Remembering something worse because you photographed it instead of only looking.
Letting a device, such as a phone, hold information so your memory does not have to.
Splitting focus between two tasks at once, which can weaken memory for each.
Saving large amounts of digital files and finding it hard to delete them, even when they are rarely used.
A recognised mental health condition in which people have persistent difficulty discarding possessions.
A survey taken at one time point, which can show links but not what causes what.
A number from a statistical model showing how strongly one measure predicts another.
Brain processes that weaken or hide memories that are no longer useful.
Fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, a method for finding combinations of conditions that lead to an outcome.

A brain structure in the limbic system that is essential for learning and for forming new memories of facts and events. People with damage to the hippocampus have great difficulty forming new memories of this kind.
A cell that receives and sends messages through the nervous system using small electrical signals and chemical messengers.
The front part of the cortex, involved in mood, thinking and perception. The strongest psychedelic effects are linked to activity here.

lines: 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (US): call or text 988
safety.note: Education, not medical advice. Saving lots of files is common and is not a diagnosis. If clutter, digital or physical, is causing distress, a doctor or licensed therapist can help, and anyone in crisis in the US can call or text 988.

summary: Electric Grand, by Antoon Versteegde and Bart van Dongen at Dutch Design Week 2026, sent each of a Yamaha CP-70's 72 keys to its own loudspeaker in a terracotta pot hung in bamboo.
In one lab study, a sound's frequency often set how high people heard it, and in another, moving rival tones away in space helped a low tone stand out far more than a high one.
Both studies used noise or tones in quiet lab rooms with small groups, so no study has tested what listeners hear while walking inside this work.
start_here.how_sure_note: The lab findings are careful but come from 8 to 13 people each, with noise and tones, not music or a walk-through room.

summary: Your body makes its own cannabinoids, and two receptors, CB1 and CB2, pick up their signals.
Lab work found them step by step: CB1 cloned from rat brain in 1990, anandamide from pig brain in 1992, CB2 in 1993 and 2-AG in 1995.
Enzymes such as FAAH and MAGL end the signal, and since 2016 labs have mapped the receptors atom by atom.
start_here.how_sure_note: The discovery history and the receptors are well established and repeated across many labs; ideas about what the system does in health and disease are far less settled.

claims.claim: 1990: a receptor gene cloned from rat brain turned out to carry the effects of THC; it is now called CB1.
1992: a molecule in pig brain was found to bind the cannabinoid receptor and was named anandamide, from Sanskrit ananda, bliss.
1993: a second receptor, CB2, was found first in the spleen and immune cells, so it was called peripheral.
1995: a second body-made cannabinoid, 2-AG, was isolated from dog gut; it acts on both CB1 and CB2.

could_be_wrong.point: The central and peripheral labels are out of date. CB1 is also found outside the brain and CB2 inside it, so the 1993 name tells you where CB2 was first found, not where it works.
The founding papers of 1988 to 1995 are behind paywalls and were not read for this post; the history comes from open reviews that report them.
Atom-level maps are made under artificial conditions. The 2023 CB1 structure used a stable analog and an engineered complex, so it shows where a molecule can sit, not what happens in a living brain.

The popular idea of an 'endocannabinoid deficiency' is not well supported. A 2022 meta-analysis found no difference in blood anandamide or 2-AG between people with fibromyalgia and controls, contrary to the theory.

The paper gives two different control counts for the pooled fibromyalgia comparison: its Results text says 230 patients and 285 controls, but its own Table 3 says 185 controls. We use 185: the three pooled studies in its Table 2 have 36, 116 and 33 controls (185), and Table 3's plasma total (233 controls) is 185 plus 48 from the widespread-pain studies. The 285 in the Results text looks like a typo.

Blood levels of endocannabinoids are a poor window on the brain: they shift with time of day, exercise, food, stress and how blood is handled, and they are not related to brain levels in a straightforward way.
Small studies point different ways. In PTSD, one study of 46 people found lower blood 2-AG, while another of 48 found higher anandamide and 2-AG.
could_be_wrong.source: Hill et al. 2013; Hauer et al. 2013

glossary.plain: A fatty signalling molecule the body makes itself that acts on cannabinoid receptors.
A protein on a cell that a specific molecule binds to, which changes what the cell does.
The cannabinoid receptor most common in the brain, which carries the effects of THC.
The second cannabinoid receptor, found mostly on immune cells and less in the brain.
A body-made cannabinoid found in 1992, named from the Sanskrit word for bliss.
The most plentiful body-made cannabinoid in the brain; it acts on both CB1 and CB2.
Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, the main intoxicating compound in cannabis.
Finding and copying the gene that codes for the receptor so scientists can study it.
Fatty acid amide hydrolase, the enzyme that mainly breaks down anandamide.
Monoacylglycerol lipase, the enzyme that mainly breaks down 2-AG.
A 3D map of a protein's atoms made from crystals or frozen samples.
Chemicals that act on the body's cannabinoid system. Plant cannabinoids (phytocannabinoids) such as THC and CBD come mostly from the resin in the female flowers of the cannabis plant.

The plant species that includes both hemp and marijuana. Names such as indica and ruderalis describe forms of this plant; botanists disagree on whether they are separate subspecies, varieties or species.
The most common cannabinoid receptor in the brain and THC's main target.
A non-intoxicating cannabis compound that acts on several targets, including the 5-HT1A receptor.
The brain and spinal cord.
Ethan Russo's unproven theory that some pain conditions, including migraine, involve too little endocannabinoid activity.
The body's cannabis-like signaling network of endocannabinoids, receptors and enzymes.
A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction in the body, such as building or breaking down a messenger.
A long-term condition that causes pain all over the body, tiredness and other symptoms. Its cause is unknown, and people with it seem to process pain differently.
A disorder of the intestines marked by belly pain, bloating and changes in bowel habits.
A recurring type of headache with moderate to severe throbbing pain, often on one side of the head, that can come with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound.
A cell that receives and sends messages through the nervous system using small electrical signals and chemical messengers.
A mental health disorder that can follow a frightening event, with symptoms such as flashbacks, nightmares and frightening thoughts.
Describes a substance that changes mood, thinking or perception. Antidepressants, hallucinogens and anti-anxiety drugs are examples.
The calm, good feeling that can follow long exercise. In mice it depends on cannabinoid receptors, which points to the endocannabinoid system rather than endorphins alone.
The tiny gap between the end of one nerve cell and the next cell, where neurotransmitters carry the signal across.

summary: A big trade show floor asks a lot: choosing among many options, listening through noise and standing for hours.
Two famous findings are weaker than they look: the jam study's choice overload averages near zero across studies, and the hungry judge effect is likely overstated.
Listening in noise takes measurable effort, and long standing raises leg and back discomfort in lab and workplace studies.
start_here.how_sure_note: The listening-effort and standing findings are steady across studies; choice overload and decision fatigue are contested: a 2010 meta-analysis and a 2022 test found little or no choice overload effect, and a 2016 simulation suggests the hungry judge effect is overstated.

claims.claim: In a 2000 grocery study, a table of 24 jams drew more shoppers to stop than a table of 6 (60 percent against 40 percent).
claims.source: Iyengar, S. S., & Lepper, M. R. (2000)
claims.study: one field experiment in a grocery store, 502 passersby

claims.claim: Of shoppers who stopped, about 30 percent bought from the 6 jams, against about 3 percent from the 24.
claims.source: Iyengar, S. S., & Lepper, M. R. (2000)

claims.claim: A 2010 meta-analysis found an average choice overload effect of virtually zero; a 2022 test with 2 to 80 charities found no meaningful difference in giving.
claims.where: Introduction (reporting Scheibehenne et al. 2010); Results; Fig. 1

claims.claim: Listening through background sound takes effort, which hearing researchers track by how wide the pupil opens; hearing loss can change that response.
claims.source: Zekveld, A. A., Koelewijn, T., & Kramer, S. E. (2018)
claims.where: Review sections on speech in noise and on hearing status

claims.claim: Favorable parole rulings fell from about 65 percent to near zero within each session, then rebounded after a food break.
claims.source: Danziger, S., Levav, J., & Avnaim-Pesso, L. (2011)

claims.claim: A 2016 simulation: if favorable rulings simply take longer, a drop appears without any fatigue; the effect is likely overestimated.

annotations.source: Iyengar, S. S., & Lepper, M. R. (2000). When choice is demotivating. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 995-1006
annotations.note: Three studies; the famous one set out 6 or 24 jams at a tasting booth in a Menlo Park grocery on two Saturdays, rotating the displays hourly. More shoppers stopped at the big display, but far more bought from the small one. Limits: one store, and shoppers chose whether to stop, so the two displays may have drawn different shoppers.

annotations.note: Simulations show that a fully rational judge who avoids starting long cases late in a session would produce an effect of similar size. The author says this does not rule out fatigue, only that its size is overestimated. CC BY 3.0.

could_be_wrong.point: Choice overload is not reliable. A 2010 meta-analysis found an average effect of virtually zero, and a 2022 preregistered test with up to 80 charities found no meaningful change in giving.
The parole drop may come from case order: prisoners without lawyers were usually heard last in a session and won parole less often.
A simulation shows the hungry judge pattern can arise without any fatigue if favorable rulings take longer; the effect is likely overestimated.

The idea that willpower runs down like fuel has failed large tests: a 36-lab replication found an effect close to zero (d = 0.06), and a registered study of 231,076 nurse calls found no evidence of decision fatigue.
could_be_wrong.source: Vohs et al. 2021; Andersson et al. 2025

could_be_wrong.point: Listening effort has no gold-standard measure. In 116 older adults, pupil size, brain waves, skin conductance and self-report did not agree with each other.
The standing figures come from lab studies of people standing still: most volunteers were young and healthy, and standing broken up by walking or sitting, as on a show floor, was not studied.

glossary.plain: The idea that too many options make people less likely to choose or less happy with the choice.
A study that pools the results of many earlier studies to estimate an average effect.
A study whose plan and analysis were posted publicly before the data were collected.
The mental work it takes to follow speech, which rises with background noise or hearing loss.
Measuring how wide the pupil opens, which grows with mental effort as well as with darkness.
The idea that making many decisions in a row wears down the quality of later ones.
The idea that self-control draws on a limited store that runs down with use; large replications have not supported it.
A computer model that shows what results a set of assumptions would produce.
How many times more often something happens in one condition than in another.
Information that comes straight from the person, such as how they rate their own pain or sleep, rather than from a lab test or device.
A review that uses clear, planned methods to find, select and combine the results of all the studies on a clearly stated question. A meta-analysis is often part of one.

summary: One prescription CBD medicine is approved by the FDA, for seizures in three rare conditions: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex.
Four randomized, placebo-controlled trials back it: seizures fell more on CBD than on placebo, and side effects such as sleepiness, lower appetite and diarrhea were more common.
How it stops seizures is unknown, and for other uses the FDA says it lacks adequate evidence on how much CBD can be consumed and for how long.
start_here.how_sure_note: For the three seizure conditions, four placebo-controlled trials agree; for anxiety, sleep, pain and everyday use, the evidence is thin or mixed.

claims.claim: CBD purified from cannabis is the active ingredient in one FDA-approved medicine (2018), for seizures in three rare conditions, from age 1.
Four randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials back the label: two in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, one in Dravet syndrome, one in tuberous sclerosis complex.
claims.study: four randomized controlled trials, 120 to 225 patients each

claims.claim: Dravet trial, 120 children and young adults: median convulsive seizures fell from 12.4 to 5.9 a month on CBD, and from 14.9 to 14.1 on placebo.
claims.source: Devinsky, O., Cross, J. H., Laux, L., et al. (2017), New England Journal of Medicine

claims.claim: Lennox-Gastaut Study 1, 171 patients aged 2 to 55: drop seizures fell by a median 44 percent on CBD and 22 percent on placebo.
Pooled over 9 trials, sleepiness, lower appetite and diarrhea were each about twice as frequent on CBD.
claims.source: Fazlollahi et al. (2023), JAMA Network Open

claims.claim: The precise mechanisms are unknown, and CBD does not appear to act through cannabinoid receptors.
Outside the label, the FDA says it lacks adequate evidence on how much CBD can be consumed, and for how long; it flags liver harm, drug interactions and possible male reproductive harm.
claims.source: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (Jan 26, 2023), statement by Janet Woodcock

annotations.note: The Dravet trial: 120 children and young adults at 23 centers, CBD or placebo added to usual treatment for 14 weeks. Convulsive seizures fell more on CBD; the share whose seizures halved (43 against 27 percent) and the share seizure-free (5 against 0 percent) did not differ significantly (P = 0.08 each). Limits: short, and funded by the drug's maker.

annotations.note: A meta-analysis of 9 randomized trials of CBD in Dravet, Lennox-Gastaut and tuberous sclerosis. Any side effect was slightly more common on CBD (risk ratio 1.12), serious ones more so (2.67), and liver enzyme rises much more (12.29). Limits: varied ages, doses and co-medications, and side effects reported in fewer than 3 trials were left out.

could_be_wrong.point: In the Dravet trial, the clearer outcomes were not statistically clear: 43 percent on CBD against 27 percent on placebo had their seizures halved, and 5 against 0 percent became seizure-free, each with P = 0.08.
The trials were funded by the drug's maker, and they ran for about 14 weeks, so they say little about years of use.
could_be_wrong.source: Devinsky et al. 2017; FDA prescribing information

could_be_wrong.point: Liver signals extend beyond epilepsy patients. In an FDA-run trial of 201 healthy adults over 28 days, 8 of 151 on CBD and none of 50 on placebo had liver enzymes above 3 times normal; levels returned to baseline within 1 to 2 weeks.
For anxiety, a review of 15 randomized trials found conflicting results, and few trials had a low risk of bias.
The pooled side-effect numbers mix trials with different ages, doses and co-medications; sleepiness was tied in part to clobazam taken alongside CBD.

glossary.plain: A compound from the cannabis plant that does not cause a high.
A study that assigns people by chance to a treatment or a comparison, such as a placebo.
Neither the patients nor the researchers know who got the real treatment until the end.
A dummy treatment that looks the same as the real one but has no active ingredient.
A severe childhood-onset epilepsy with several seizure types, including drop seizures.
A rare genetic epilepsy that starts in infancy, with seizures that resist many medicines.
A genetic condition that causes benign growths in the brain and other organs and often seizures.
A seizure that makes a person suddenly fall or slump.
The middle value when results are put in order.
How many times more likely an event is in one group than in another; 2 means twice as likely.
Liver enzymes measured in blood; high levels can signal liver stress or injury.
Conditions in which worry, fear and dread are strong and lasting enough to disrupt daily life. They include generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder and PTSD.
Chemicals that act on the body's cannabinoid system. Plant cannabinoids (phytocannabinoids) such as THC and CBD come mostly from the resin in the female flowers of the cannabis plant.

The plant species that includes both hemp and marijuana. Names such as indica and ruderalis describe forms of this plant; botanists disagree on whether they are separate subspecies, varieties or species.
The outcome a clinical trial measures to judge whether a treatment works. The primary endpoint is the main one, chosen before the trial starts.
A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction in the body, such as building or breaking down a messenger.
Metals such as lead and cadmium. Cannabis plants can soak them up and store them throughout the plant, so labs test for them.
Ongoing trouble falling asleep or getting enough sleep.
A method that pools data from many studies on the same question to get a stronger overall answer.
A study that watches and measures what happens without assigning a treatment. It can show links but not prove cause.
Taken by mouth and swallowed. Swallowed cannabis acts slowly and unevenly, because it is absorbed through the gut and processed by the liver first.
A molecule, usually a protein, on or inside a cell that a specific chemical messenger binds to, which sets off an effect in the cell. It is often pictured as a lock that only certain keys fit.
A review that uses clear, planned methods to find, select and combine the results of all the studies on a clearly stated question. A meta-analysis is often part of one.
The main intoxicating compound in cannabis.

Under federal law, cannabis with no more than 0.3 percent THC. A 2025 law changes the test to total THC, including THCA, and excludes some intoxicating products. Part took effect November 12, 2026; the rest starts December 11, 2026.

A product taken by mouth to add to the diet, usually containing one or more dietary ingredients such as vitamins, minerals, herbs, amino acids or enzymes. Some can cause side effects or interact with medicines. RN's article quotes an exhibitor describing a psilocybin product as a microdosing supplement; psilocybin is a Schedule I substance under federal law.

A written directive from the President to federal agencies. Executive Order 14370 of December 18, 2025 told the Attorney General to finish rescheduling marijuana to Schedule III; it states that it creates no enforceable rights.

summary: Terpenes are smell molecules made by many plants: limonene in citrus peel, linalool in lavender and pinenes in pine resin.
The nose reads them with about 400 kinds of odorant receptor, and each odor molecule fits several of them.
In mice, linalool odor eased anxiety-like behavior only when the mice could smell; for people, NIH says little rigorous research shows whether aromatherapy helps sleep.
start_here.how_sure_note: The chemistry and the receptor biology are well established; the calming effects rest on mouse studies, and claims about scent and mood in people have little rigorous testing.

could_be_wrong.point: The calming effect comes from mice. Harada et al. tested only adult male mice; a 2024 study reported effects in female mice too, but its terpenes were gifted by a terpene company that employs one author.

could_be_wrong.point: Terpene profiles do not predict how a product smells to people very well: in 91 samples rated by a 24-person panel, terpene profiles alone poorly predicted sensory character.
Two reviews conclude that claims of terpenes boosting cannabinoids are unproven, with no clinical trials designed to test the idea.
could_be_wrong.source: Christensen et al. 2023; André et al. 2024

could_be_wrong.point: People smell the same molecule differently: 63 percent of odorant receptors tested had common gene variants that changed how they worked, and two people differ at over 30 percent of their receptor alleles.
Strain labels do not match chemistry: across 89,923 samples from six states, terpene groups did not consistently align with the labels on the product.

glossary.plain: A large family of plant-made molecules, many of them strong-smelling.
A small terpene built from 10 carbon atoms, such as limonene, linalool or pinene.
The main smell molecule of citrus peel.
A floral-smelling terpene alcohol found in lavender and many other plants.
A piney-smelling terpene found in conifer resin.
A plant enzyme that folds a building-block molecule into a particular terpene.
A nerve cell high inside the nose that carries one type of odor receptor and signals the brain.
A protein on smell neurons that binds certain odor molecules; humans have about 400 kinds.
Unable to smell.
Reducing anxiety.
Using essential oils from plants, by smelling them or on the skin, to try to improve health or mood.
Chemicals that act on the body's cannabinoid system. Plant cannabinoids (phytocannabinoids) such as THC and CBD come mostly from the resin in the female flowers of the cannabis plant.
The most common cannabinoid receptor in the brain and THC's main target.
The hypothesis that cannabis compounds work together to change THC's effects. It is still being tested.
A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction in the body, such as building or breaking down a messenger.
The offspring of two genetically different parents. Breeders make hybrids by crossing plants, for example a sativa type with an indica type.
A cell that receives and sends messages through the nervous system using small electrical signals and chemical messengers.
A molecule, usually a protein, on or inside a cell that a specific chemical messenger binds to, which sets off an effect in the cell. It is often pictured as a lock that only certain keys fit.
When two or more drugs act together so that their combined effect is greater than the sum of their separate effects.
Strong-smelling plant compounds, such as myrcene, limonene, linalool and pinene, behind each cannabis variety's aroma.
The main intoxicating compound in cannabis.
Tiny hair-like glands on cannabis flowers and leaves. The glandular ones make and store most of the plant's cannabinoids and terpenes.

summary: In 2017 a National Academies committee screened more than 10,000 study abstracts on cannabis and health and graded nearly 100 conclusions, from conclusive to no or insufficient evidence.

The best-supported treatment uses were chronic pain in adults, and oral cannabinoids for chemotherapy nausea and for MS spasticity as patients report it; the strongest harm findings were statistical links, which alone do not prove cause.

For many conditions the evidence was too thin to call, and the committee tied the gaps to Schedule I rules and a single federal research supply; growing rules eased in 2020 and the scheduling story is still moving.
start_here.how_sure_note: The grades come from a large, formal National Academies review, but they reflect evidence up to 2016; newer reviews still rate much of the evidence low.

could_be_wrong.point: The grades describe evidence up to 2016. A 2026 overview of 102 systematic reviews rated 70 of them critically low in quality and found only low to moderate certainty of benefit for uses such as chronic non-cancer pain, MS and chemotherapy nausea.
Most harm conclusions are statistical associations. The committee itself graded them as links, so they do not show that cannabis caused the outcome.

The chronic pain grade is for cannabis in adults in general; a later review of 39 studies with 12,143 adults rated the certainty of its evidence very low and found adverse events in about a quarter of people, though serious ones were under 1 in 20.
The nearly 100 count and the grade tallies on the slides are our own hand count of the report's annex (94 entries), not a number the report prints.
could_be_wrong.source: NASEM 2017 report (summary annex, counted Nov 7 and Nov 13, 2026)

could_be_wrong.point: The scheduling line can go out of date: as of Nov 20, 2026 no final rule on moving all marijuana appears in the Federal Register and no judge's recommendation on the 2026 hearing was found.

glossary.plain: A private, nonprofit body of US science, engineering and medicine academies that writes expert reports for the government and public.
The report's top grade: strong evidence from randomized trials with no credible opposing findings.
The second grade: strong evidence with very few or no credible opposing findings.
The bottom grade: not enough good research to reach any conclusion.
Two things that tend to occur together; it does not show that one causes the other.
A chemical that acts on the body's cannabinoid receptors, such as THC or CBD from the plant, or a lab-made version.
Cannabinoid medicines taken by mouth, such as capsules, tested in clinical trials.
Stiff, tight muscles that are hard to relax, common in multiple sclerosis.
The federal drug category for substances judged to have no accepted medical use and a high potential for misuse, which brings the tightest research rules.
A federal drug category for substances with an accepted medical use and lower potential for misuse than Schedules I and II.
Moving a drug from one federal schedule to another through a formal rule.
The National Institute on Drug Abuse, the NIH institute that funds most US research on drugs.
A study that gathers and appraises all research on a question using a set method.
A checklist used to rate how well a systematic review was done.
Conditions in which worry, fear and dread are strong and lasting enough to disrupt daily life. They include generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder and PTSD.

The plant species that includes both hemp and marijuana. Names such as indica and ruderalis describe forms of this plant; botanists disagree on whether they are separate subspecies, varieties or species.
A medical diagnosis for a pattern of cannabis use that causes real problems or distress, such as being unable to cut down. It is a type of substance use disorder.
A non-intoxicating cannabis compound that acts on several targets, including the 5-HT1A receptor.
A weaker cannabinoid that forms as THC breaks down with age. Evidence that it helps sleep is thin.
Treatment that uses drugs to stop the growth of cancer cells, by killing them or stopping them from dividing.

A mental health condition with ongoing sadness, loss of energy and loss of pleasure that makes daily life hard. It can also bring feelings of worthlessness, changes in sleep or eating, and thoughts of death.
A state-licensed store that sells cannabis. Oregon law, for example, registers medical marijuana dispensaries for patients and licenses marijuana retailers to sell to adult consumers.
A method that pools data from many studies on the same question to get a stronger overall answer.
Taken by mouth and swallowed. Swallowed cannabis acts slowly and unevenly, because it is absorbed through the gut and processed by the liver first.
A mental health disorder that can follow a frightening event, with symptoms such as flashbacks, nightmares and frightening thoughts.

A severe mental state in which a person loses touch with reality. In people prone to psychotic illness, heavier use, stronger cannabis and starting young can bring on a first psychotic episode earlier.

summary: In a 2024 blind test, 20 students and 5 textile professors felt 22 fabrics with one fingertip and rated how rough, scratchy, hairy and even each one felt.
Mesh felt roughest and scratchiest and laminates smoothest, and experts and students agreed in all but 9 of 176 comparisons.
Wool science adds that prickle comes mostly from fibers wider than about 30 microns, and nerve recordings show that hairy skin has slow nerves tuned to gentle stroking.
start_here.how_sure_note: The fabric results come from one small study of 25 raters that has not been repeated; the wool and nerve points come from two reviews of older work.

claims.where: Methods: Participants and Experimental setup; Fig. 3

claims.claim: The swatches were knits, wovens, meshes and laminates; each got 20 seconds of one index finger, then 8 ratings.
claims.where: Methods: Textile swatches and Experimental setup; Fig. 1

Wool prickle comes mostly from coarse fibers over about 30 microns, whose stiff ends push on the skin; next-to-skin wool is finer than 18 microns.
claims.where: Section on garment comfort and skin health
claims.study: review reporting earlier wearer and nerve studies

claims.claim: Hairy skin has C-tactile nerves that fire most for slow stroking, about 1 to 10 cm per second, the speeds people rate most pleasant.
claims.where: Section on CT afferents; Fig. 3A to C

annotations.source: Mehta et al. 2024
annotations.note: Twenty students and five textile professors felt 22 fabrics through a screen and rated eight touch qualities from 1 to 5. Ratings followed how each fabric was built, and the two groups mostly agreed. Limits: one finger, 20 seconds, flat swatches, and an expert panel of five, which the authors say may limit how far the results apply.
annotations.funding: Partially supported by USDA NIFA grant WVA00742; the paper states the funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, the decision to publish, or preparing the manuscript.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declared that no competing interests exist.

annotations.source: Doyle et al. 2021
annotations.note: A review of sheep and wool production by wool scientists. It names mean fiber diameter as the most important property of wool and reports earlier work linking prickle to coarse fibers over 30 microns. Limits: a broad review that summarises the prickle studies rather than testing them, and it presents wool's comfort and health benefits favourably.
annotations.funding: not stated
annotations.conflicts: none declared (the paper has no conflict statement; its author notes say Phil Hynd chairs the Expert Panel for Meat and Livestock Australia and works as a private consultant)

annotations.source: Liljencrantz and Olausson 2014
annotations.note: A review of C-tactile nerve fibers in human hairy skin. Recordings show they fire most for slow, gentle strokes, at the same speeds people rate most pleasant, and they have never been found in the palm. Limits: the figure's data come from one earlier study of 16 nerve fibers and 10 raters, and the role of these fibers in touch pain is still debated.
annotations.funding: not stated
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.

could_be_wrong.point: The expert panel had only five people. The authors say this small group may limit how far the findings can be generalized.
Agreement was not even across fabrics. Eight of the nine expert and student differences were in woven fabrics, so the groups agreed less on wovens than the overall count suggests.

The test used a fingertip, but clothes rest on hairy skin. The slow nerves tuned to gentle stroking have never been found in the palm, so a fingertip test cannot capture what they add when a garment is worn.

Nerve firing does not tell the whole story of pleasant touch. In a later recording study, C-tactile firing tracked pleasantness only when the probe was at skin temperature, and the authors concluded that pleasantness is built from many sensory inputs and from the person's state.
The 30 micron prickle figure comes from 1980s work that the wool review reports but that this post could not read in full, and the review is written by wool scientists who present wool favourably.

Feel is not the only way clothes bother skin. A review of a century of reports found no good evidence that wool fiber itself is an allergen, and named disperse dyes used on synthetic fibers as the most common textile dye sensitizers.

glossary.plain: A sensor in the skin that responds to pressure, stretch or vibration and sends a signal along a nerve.

summary: In a 2024 study, 36 university students in Norway wrote words in cursive with a digital pen or typed them with one finger while a 256-sensor EEG net recorded their brain rhythms.
Writing by hand showed more theta and alpha coherence, brain rhythms in step, between parietal and central regions than typing.

A published commentary points out that no learning was tested, typing used one finger with no letters on screen, and no behaviour was reported, so the study shows a rhythm difference, not a learning benefit.
start_here.how_sure_note: One lab EEG study of 36 adults with no learning test; a published commentary disputes the leap to learning, though other studies do support handwriting for learning letters.

This read grew out of a postcard workshop at Dutch Design Week 2026.

annotations.note: Forty students at NTNU in Trondheim were tested and 36 gave usable 256-channel EEG while writing 15 words in cursive with a digital pen or typing them with one finger. Handwriting showed more theta and alpha coherence between parietal and central regions, and the authors read this as evidence that handwriting promotes learning. Limits: adults only, one-finger typing with no letters shown, and no learning or behaviour measured.
annotations.funding: The article processing charge was covered under one of NTNU's open publication agreements; no other funding is stated.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.

annotations.note: A commentary by two handwriting researchers. It argues that the protocol included no learning, the statistics only compared the two tasks, the typing was unlike skilled typing, and no behaviour was reported, so the classroom conclusions do not follow; it notes other studies that do support handwriting for letters and word recall.
annotations.funding: French National Research Agency grant ANR-23-CE28-0025, the Basque Government BERC 2022-2025 program, the Spanish State Research Agency (CEX2020-001010 and PID2020-113926GB-I00) and AMPIRIC France 2030.

annotations.source: Dutch Design Week 2026 programme page
annotations.note: The DDW 2026 programme page for the postcard workshop where this read began. It makes no claim about handwriting or the brain.
annotations.funding: not stated
annotations.conflicts: not stated

could_be_wrong.point: The study tested no learning: students wrote well-known words over and over with no need to remember them, so it cannot show that handwriting helps learning.
Typing used only the right index finger and the typed words did not appear on screen, which is quite unlike everyday typing, so the comparison may favour the pen.
The statistics were run only on the difference between writing and typing, and no behavioural measures were reported, so it is unclear what the extra coherence reflects.

For learning new letters, handwriting practice did help adults learn faster and generalize better than typing or looking, in a training study of 42 adults, so the learning question has evidence elsewhere, just not from this EEG study.

In a 2026 study, people taking notes with an ink pen, a digital pen or a laptop showed different brain rhythms, but no significant difference on the immediate test, so brain differences do not always mean learning differences.

But in resting brain scans of 1,011 people aged 7 to 29, lateralization worked region by region, and people did not split into left-brained or right-brained types.
A 2014 essay concludes that the popular left-brain, right-brain split owes more to myth than to evidence.
start_here.how_sure_note: A large brain-scan study and decades of research agree that there is no whole-brain left or right type, though the 2013 study had no personality or behaviour data.

claims.claim: 1,011 brain scans showed no whole-brain left or right type.
claims.study: one resting-state fMRI study, 1,011 people aged 7 to 29

claims.claim: The brain's two sides do specialize; language hubs such as Broca's and Wernicke's areas leaned left.
The study measured how lateralized each connection was between 7,266 brain regions, in resting scans of 1,011 people aged 7 to 29.
Lateralization worked region by region; people did not split into stronger left-brain or right-brain networks overall.
There were small increases in lateralization with age (r = 0.08 and 0.09), and no differences by gender.
The largest site's scans matched all the others closely (r = 0.85).
Left-right asymmetries are widespread among animals, and left-brain and right-brain polarities owe more to the power of myth than to the scientific evidence.

annotations.source: Nielsen et al. 2013
annotations.note: Resting scans of 1,011 people aged 7 to 29 from public datasets were split into 7,266 regions. Language and attention hubs were lateralized, but a person's left and right networks were not stronger as a whole, so there was no left-brained or right-brained type. Limits: no behaviour or personality data, and handedness data were lacking, as the authors note.

annotations.source: Corballis 2014
annotations.note: An essay on the history and evolution of brain asymmetry, from the 1860s discovery of left-side speech to Sperry's split-brain work, arguing that popular left-brain, right-brain claims go far beyond the facts. Limits: an expert essay, not new data.
annotations.funding: Some of the research summarised was funded by the Marsden Fund of the Royal Society of New Zealand; the funders had no role.
annotations.conflicts: The author has declared that no competing interests exist.

could_be_wrong.point: The 2013 study had no behaviour or personality data, so it shows no whole-brain left or right type in brain networks, not directly that personality is unrelated to the brain's sides.
Handedness data were lacking for much of the 2013 sample, so the authors could not fully test links with left-handedness.
Language is not left-sided in everyone. In 297 healthy adults, about 7 percent of left-handers had strongly right-sided language, and some people were ambilateral.
The study used resting scans, not people doing tasks, so it says how networks are wired at rest rather than how each side works during reading or drawing.

summary: Zachtzicht by Natrufied Architecture, a planted screen of fibre crops and timber, was shown at Dutch Design Week in Eindhoven (Oct 17 to 25, 2026).
In a 2018 lab study of 68 people, most groups were slightly less annoyed by highway sound when the window view showed green, but the sound level mattered most.
In a second lab study of 30 students, a tree belt that blocked no sound was rated about as helpful as real noise barriers in most scenes.

could_be_wrong.point: The 68-person study is small, and its authors say the scenes may not have suited everyone equally and that larger groups may show other effects.
In the 30-student study, the cases where barriers beat the tree belt in loud scenes were close to significant but not quite, so the tree belt result may not hold when traffic is heavy.
Green does not always help. In a Hong Kong lab study of 246 people, more mountain greenery in the view raised the chance of feeling highly annoyed.
In a Ghent virtual reality study, about 30 percent greenery worked best, the gain was only half a point on an 11-point scale, and a very dense tree belt made annoyance worse.
An earlier Sheffield lab study of 23 people found the opposite ranking for barriers: concrete was judged most effective, and planted and see-through screens least, though they looked best.
In a randomized trial of 354 adults in Zurich, forest walks were less annoying than street walks only when traffic was quiet; at high noise both scored near the top of the scale.

summary: A 1930 police album in the Rijksmuseum shows a thermos and a pot of fake flowers that hid smuggled opium in the Dutch East Indies.
Police chased smugglers because the colonial state ran its own opium monopoly, the opium regie, which handled import, refining and retail until 1942.
In the brain, opioids such as morphine act at the mu-opioid receptor; mice bred without it got neither pain relief nor reward from morphine.
start_here.how_sure_note: The album is a museum record and the receptor finding has been repeated in several mouse lines; how much the regie's rules cut smoking is still argued by historians.

could_be_wrong.point: Historians disagree on whether the regie cut opium use. Chandra argues that the Great Depression explains much of the fall in sales.
Strict regimes were placed where local opium use was already low, so lower use under strict rules may reflect where the rules were put rather than what they did.

The regie was sold as a health measure, but one historian concludes that humanitarian arguments did not dominate in practice; the debate was more about limiting Chinese tax farmers and fighting smuggling.
Sources differ on dates: one gives Java and Madura under the regie by 1903, another Jan 1, 1904, which is why the post says 1903 to 1904.
The receptor evidence comes from mice. No study shows the same from gene loss in people, and one knockout line is harder to interpret than the others.
How tolerance works inside cells is still not settled; the main review says large gaps remain.
No published record says who used the thermos or flowerpot, when they were seized, or how common the trick was.

summary: SOW HEMP, by textile and photography students from UMPRUM in Prague, was shown at Dutch Design Week (Oct 17 to 25, 2026), using yarn from a Czech farm that built its own scutching mill.
A hemp stem gives two kinds of fibre: long bast fibres from the outer phloem, rich in cellulose, and short fibres of the woody core, full of lignin.
In six hemp lines grown in the Netherlands, glucose made up 76% of the bast fibre wall but 54% of the whole stem, and lignin about 2% against 14%.
start_here.how_sure_note: The two fibre types are textbook plant biology; the exact percentages come from one Dutch field season and vary between hemp lines.

claims.claim: SOW HEMP by students of UMPRUM in Prague was shown at Dutch Design Week (Oct 17 to 25) at the Klokgebouw, Eindhoven.

Students felted, spun, wove pictorial wall weavings, embroidered by machine and dissolved fibre into bioplastic; a hemp and wool yarn tested with weaving mill Kubak met the bar for interiors.

could_be_wrong.point: The two-fibre picture comes from seedlings 6 to 20 days old, not the mature stems used for yarn.
The 76% and 2% figures are averages of six hemp lines from one Dutch season, and the lines differed significantly in cell wall make-up.
Cellulose content in hemp fibre ranges from about 55% to 80% depending on variety, maturity and fibre type, so no single number fits all hemp.
How well bast and core separate depends on retting, a controlled rot in the field: under-retted stalks stay stiff and over-retted fibre turns weak.

The woody tissue in a stem that carries water; it forms hemp's core.

Letting cut stalks partly rot so the fibre loosens from the woody core.
Machine separation of the outer fibre from the woody core.
The long sugar chains that make plant fibres strong; glucose is its building block.
A stiff, glue-like material that hardens wood and makes fibres coarse.
An extra inner wall layer in some fibres, rich in tightly packed cellulose.
Cellulose broken into fibrils a few millionths of a millimetre wide, used in new materials.
A plastic made from plant material rather than oil.

could_be_wrong.point: Across 13 randomised trials that changed how clinicians relate to patients, the pooled effect on health outcomes was small (d = 0.11).
The empathy study is a cohort: patients chose and rated their own doctors, so better outcomes may partly reflect how they already felt.
The AI scribe survey had no control group, and several authors had ties to the scribe's maker, Abridge.
In a randomised trial of 238 physicians, one AI scribe cut note time by 9.5% and another made no significant difference; well-being gains needed confirmation in larger trials.
In a stepped-wedge trial of 66 practitioners, an AI scribe lowered work exhaustion, but professional fulfilment did not change significantly; staff were volunteers who knew they had the tool.
AI chatbot replies beat clinicians on rated empathy in 13 of 15 text studies, but raters were proxies, and in one study the advantage vanished when readers knew the reply was from AI.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, visitors to a basement parliament at the Van Abbemuseum chose a museum object or animal and spoke for it, an idea the programme traces to Bruno Latour's Parliament of Things.
In a 2023 lab game, 48 Japanese adults played with a person, a small robot and a computer that all chose at random, and rated the robot and computer far lower than the person on the ability to feel.
Even so, the more feeling people saw in the robot, the more responsibility they gave it when their reward came up short.

annotations.source: Kawai et al. 2023
annotations.note: Forty-eight Japanese adults played a repeated money game with a human, a small robot and a computer, each choosing at random, and then said who caused and who was responsible for a disappointing reward. Mind perception shaped blame differently for each partner. Limits: one small sample from one culture, small sums of money, a simple game, and correlations rather than experiments on mind perception itself.
annotations.funding: Supported by JST RISTEX (grants JPMJRX17H4 and JPMJRX19H5) and the JSPS Topic-Setting Program to Advance Cutting-Edge Humanities and Social Sciences Research (JSPS00118070707), Japan.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests.

could_be_wrong.point: All participants were Japanese. The authors note that Japanese people tend to blame themselves for failures, so people elsewhere might blame a robot more.
The stakes were small. The authors say that with serious outcomes, such as larger losses or harm, people might attribute cause and responsibility to a machine differently.

Overall, the type of partner made no significant difference to how much cause people assigned to it. The link between feeling and blame appeared only inside the robot condition, and only in after-game ratings.
The game was simple and the partners were scripted. The authors call for tests in more realistic settings, such as bargaining with a shopkeeper robot.
Responsibility was measured with one question. The authors note that responsibility covers blame, apology, punishment and more, which this study did not separate.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2025, ENSEMBLE served a dinner in Eindhoven with five food designers, five short films and five courses.

Researchers call pairing sound with taste sonic seasoning: in lab tests, matched music lifted wine enjoyment a little, and different soundscapes shifted how bitter, sour and likeable the same chocolate seemed.
The effects are real but small, come from lab tastings, and no study measured this dinner.
start_here.how_sure_note: Several lab studies agree that sound shifts taste ratings by small amounts; most use students or volunteers in one setting, and some are tied to commercial work.

annotations.note: Social drinkers matched classical music to fine wines, and 26 tasters then rated three wines in silence and with the matched music; enjoyment rose from 5.19 to 5.65 of 10. Limits: silence was always rated first, and a wine merchant provided the venue and wines.
annotations.funding: not stated; the acknowledgments thank The Antique Wine Company for the testing facilities and wine, and the London Symphony Orchestra for the music.

could_be_wrong.point: In the wine study, tasters always rated the wines in silence first, so part of the rise with music could come from tasting the wine a second time.

The chocolate study used young university students, four tastings of the same chocolate in one session, and did not ask whether tasters guessed the samples were the same; the authors list these as limits.

The chocolate study reports 120 participants, each tasting under all four sounds (a within-subjects design, 30 per order), but its statistics fit 60 people: the contrasts give 59 degrees of freedom, and the ANOVA degrees of freedom (for example 165.61 at a correction of 0.936, which is 3 times 59) point the same way. The paper does not explain the gap.
In a large study of 1,611 tasters, the music's emotional tone mattered more than whether its sound matched the taste, so the effect may run through mood rather than a direct sound to taste link.
Much sonic seasoning work is tied to brands and paid events, which the 2021 review discloses; independent tests in real restaurants are rare.
No study measured ENSEMBLE's films or dishes, so whether its pairings changed taste is unknown.

summary: Small studies find grief in the body as well as the mind: a 2008 scan of 23 bereaved women found pain-related activity in all of them and reward-area activity only in complicated grief, tied to yearning.

could_be_wrong.point: The 2008 reward finding came from 23 women scanned once while one photo was shown repeatedly, and the authors call for larger samples.

When the same lab scanned 25 older adults, the groups did not differ, and the yearning link appeared in a different brain area in a post hoc test the authors call preliminary and in need of replication.
The inflammation result is from one blood draw and shows an association; depression scores overlapped with grief by about a third.
The endocannabinoid result rests on small groups in one study; one author holds equity in cannabinoid companies.

Two small trials testing the opioid blocker naltrexone for prolonged grief, an idea that grew from the reward finding, both stopped early: one for low enrolment (9 people), one when funding was withdrawn (7 people).

glossary.plain: The response to losing someone close, felt in thoughts, emotions and the body.
Intense grief that lasts and disrupts daily life long after a loss.
A strong longing for the person who died.
A small area deep in the brain tied to reward and wanting.
A brain area folded inside the side of the brain that tracks body feelings, including pain.
A front brain area below the knee of the corpus callosum, linked to mood.
A brain scan that tracks blood oxygen changes as a stand-in for brain activity.
A molecule in the blood, such as IL-6, that rises when the immune system is active.
A cannabinoid the body makes itself, such as anandamide.
One of the body's own cannabinoids, a signaling molecule made from fats.
The wear and tear on the body from stress responses that run too long.
Two things that occur together; it does not prove that one causes the other.
One of the body's two best-studied endocannabinoids; it tends to rise during stress and helps end the stress response.
A region of the cortex that works with the insula in reading signals from inside the body and in emotional responses such as fear.
A drug used to treat depression. Trazodone is one example.
Chemicals that act on the body's cannabinoid system. Plant cannabinoids (phytocannabinoids) such as THC and CBD come mostly from the resin in the female flowers of the cannabis plant.
A hormone made by the adrenal glands and released in larger amounts during stress. It helps the body use sugar, protein and fat.

A mental health condition with ongoing sadness, loss of energy and loss of pleasure that makes daily life hard. It can also bring feelings of worthlessness, changes in sleep or eating, and thoughts of death.
The body's protective response to injury or infection, which brings redness, swelling, heat and pain.
A method that pools data from many studies on the same question to get a stronger overall answer.
A hormone and brain messenger made in the hypothalamus that is released during touch and closeness and is linked to social bonding and calm.
Information that comes straight from the person, such as how they rate their own pain or sleep, rather than from a lab test or device.

Care that improves quality of life by preventing or treating symptoms of a disease and side effects of its treatment, as early as possible. It includes physical, emotional, social and spiritual support.
A review that uses clear, planned methods to find, select and combine the results of all the studies on a clearly stated question. A meta-analysis is often part of one.

summary: In a 2006 study, students who reread a passage did better on a test 5 minutes later, but students who practiced recalling it remembered much more 2 days or a week later.

A week on, students who read a passage once and recalled it three times kept 61 percent of it, against 40 percent for students who read it four times, and rereading made students feel more sure they would remember.
Recall practice also beat making concept maps in a 2011 study, and across 86 studies, producing an answer beat reading one by about 0.4 standard deviations.
start_here.how_sure_note: The testing effect has been repeated in hundreds of studies; the exact numbers here come from single lab experiments with US college students and prose or science passages.

could_be_wrong.point: Recall practice helps only for what you manage to recall. Roediger and Karpicke later wrote that testing cannot help with material that is not retrieved unless feedback is given, and their own passages were recalled at about 70 percent.
The effect has limits in time. In the 2006 study, rereading beat recall on the test 5 minutes later, and the authors later pointed to that immediate test as a boundary condition.

Not every kind of generating helps. In the meta-analysis, anagrams gave a small negative effect across 18 studies, and free-recall experiments that compared separate groups of people showed only a small average gain of about 4 percent.

The generation effect was smaller for free recall (0.32) than for recognition (0.46) or cued recall (0.55), so it does not show that recall beats recognition, and the authors ask for more studies because some groups were small.
These are lab studies with US college students and short texts or word lists, so the size of the gain in a real course, at other ages or with other material may differ.

summary: In a 2007 brain scan study of 19 women, money going to a food bank lit up reward areas even when the transfer was required, like a tax.
Women whose reward areas responded more to the food bank's gains gave more often, and choosing to give added extra reward activity, a sign of a warm glow.
A 2022 survey of 15,545 Americans found that people who had donated in the past month reported more well-being at every age and income, but a survey cannot show cause.
start_here.how_sure_note: The scan study was small and reward activity is not a direct readout of feelings; giving and happiness go together in surveys, but experiments give mixed results.

could_be_wrong.point: Seeing activity in a reward area does not prove a person feels rewarded; the same areas do many jobs, a problem called reverse inference.
Brain scan results replicate only modestly at typical sample sizes, and studies far larger than 19 people still fall short.
A model of generous choices explained them without any reward value for generosity itself.
When the original team repeated its giving-and-happiness experiment at scale, one study found a clear effect, one found none and one a very small effect.
An independent close replication with 133 students found no effect on the original happiness measure.
A registered trial of 1,234 adults asked to do kind acts three times a week for three weeks found no difference from the comparison groups in the main analysis.
In a lottery experiment, choosing to save a life gave a small short-term lift that reversed after four weeks.

A deep brain area that responds to rewards like money and food.

How happy and satisfied people say they are with their lives.
A measure of how big a difference between two groups is; 0.2 is usually called small.
A number showing how likely a result this large would be by chance alone; below 0.05 is the usual cutoff.
Two things going together, which does not show that one causes the other.
In a study, the group that does not get the treatment being tested, so its results can be compared with the group that does. In a placebo-controlled study, the control group gets a placebo.

A mental health condition with ongoing sadness, loss of energy and loss of pleasure that makes daily life hard. It can also bring feelings of worthlessness, changes in sleep or eating, and thoughts of death.
How big a difference or link is, not just whether it exists. It is one of the main things that decide whether a result matters in practice.
A method that pools data from many studies on the same question to get a stronger overall answer.
A reward area deep in the brain that is part of the dopamine reward pathway.

summary: Phygital Seasoning, by sensory food designer Laila Snevele (SENSOVERSE), was shown at Sprout Coffee Roasters during Dutch Design Week 2026: diners eat one base food while a headset switches between sweet and sour worlds.
The maker reports that about 80% of tasters at DDW 2025 noticed a flavour shift, but no control group is described.
Lab studies show expectation and smell shape flavour: people who could not taste the difference between sugar and sweetener told them apart mostly by what they expected.
start_here.how_sure_note: The two brain studies are careful but small (27 and 25 adults), and the maker's 80% figure has no control; a VR lighting study found that expectations barely changed taste.

could_be_wrong.point: The 80% figure is the maker's own count from visitors who knew what to expect; with no blind or control condition, it cannot separate the headset's effect from expectation.

In a VR study of 34 people, red light made samples taste a little sweeter, but neither red nor green light changed sourness or fruit flavour, even though people linked the colours to those tastes. The study was funded by and partly run at Sony.
The sugar study scanned only 27 people chosen because they could not tell sugar from sweetener; the authors say it is unclear whether the result holds for everyone.
The smell study used 25 people and two learned flavours, so it shows a shared code in a lab, not what happens with a full meal.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2025, designer Jillian de Bie presented Towards Inclusive Gastronomy, a TU/e project that aims to let people with food allergies dine out without the stress of a reaction.
Ten food experts met over a workshop dinner and built quick, rough prototypes the team calls magical elements.
A 2025 Canadian survey of 1,500 people shows why: most allergic diners felt restaurants underestimate allergies, and most restaurant reactions happened even though staff had been told.
start_here.how_sure_note: One large survey of 1,500 people in Canada, with self-reported answers; the patient-group sample was drawn from a patient organization and is not representative of all allergic diners.

claims.claim: 82 percent of food-allergic respondents in the patient-group sample felt restaurants underestimate how serious food allergies are (71 percent in the general allergic sample).
Most restaurant reactions happened even though staff had been told about the allergy: 78 percent in the patient group, 67 percent in the general sample.
43 percent of the patient group and 27 percent of the general allergic sample had had a severe reaction while dining out or ordering food.
Allergies shaped where people ate for 88 and 74 percent of the allergic samples, and for 44 percent of people without allergies.
Most allergic respondents still felt safe dining out: 60 percent of the patient group and 85 percent of the general sample.
91 percent of the patient group were fairly or very loyal to restaurants, which the authors read as a way of managing risk.
Reactions in restaurants often come from miscommunication between diners and staff, or from staff who know too little about allergies.

could_be_wrong.point: The patient-group sample came from members of Food Allergy Canada, a patient organization that co-funded and co-wrote the study, so its answers may reflect people with more severe allergies or more concern.
All figures are self-reported in an online survey, so reactions and whether staff were told rest on people's memory, not records.
The survey was in Canada; diners and restaurant rules in the Netherlands, where the design project took place, may differ.
People's sense of how common food allergies are can run far above clinical rates, about 30 against 7.5 percent in one Canadian survey, so perceived risk and real risk are not the same.
The design project's prototypes are early workshop probes; no study has tested whether they reduce reactions or stress.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, TU/e showed Making the Invisible Visible, Stefanie Gillmeier's wind tunnel work on how air and pollution move through city streets.
In one public TU/e dataset, a 1:350 model of central Sofia was tested with a tracer gas released at two points and measured at 76 points.
A 2026 review of 54 systematic reviews found that fine particle pollution (PM2.5) was linked to poorer brain health in 10 of 11 outcomes.
start_here.how_sure_note: The exhibit and dataset facts come from DDW, TU/e and the dataset itself; the brain link rests on a large review of observational studies, which shows a steady direction but not an exact size, and the tunnel tests measured no health outcome.

annotations.note: An umbrella review of 54 systematic reviews on city environments and brain health. Air pollution had the strongest evidence (PM2.5 10 of 11 outcomes, NO2 and NOx 5 of 10); social ties and green and blue spaces were linked to benefit. Limits: high heterogeneity, uneven review quality and wide prediction intervals, so the authors say the estimates show direction, not exact size.

could_be_wrong.point: The review's authors say its numbers show direction and consistency, not precise size: heterogeneity was high, some reviews may have overstated effects, and wide prediction intervals mean the true effect in a new population may not be significant.

A BMJ review of 51 studies judged most at high risk of bias, and its overall estimate for PM2.5 and dementia (hazard ratio 1.04 per 2 micrograms per cubic metre, 0.99 to 1.09) did not reach significance; the link was larger in studies that actively checked every participant for dementia.
A review of 66 papers found methodological problems common and only a few dementia findings that met its quality criteria.

The tunnel tests measure gas in a scale model, not what people breathe. They used one wind direction and neutral air, and as of Nov 13, 2026 no paper had reported the Sofia model against computer simulations; the project team says that will come in future work.
could_be_wrong.source: Gillmeier et al. 2026 (ERIES database); Pantusheva et al. 2025

could_be_wrong.point: No randomised trial has tested whether cleaner outdoor air or air filtration lowers dementia risk; the evidence comes from observational studies (Europe PMC and ClinicalTrials.gov searches, Nov 13, 2026).

A group of conditions in which memory and thinking decline enough to affect daily life.
A plant hormone that helps steer flower sex in cannabis. Silver compounds that block it push female plants to make male flowers.
A method that pools data from many studies on the same question to get a stronger overall answer.
A review that uses clear, planned methods to find, select and combine the results of all the studies on a clearly stated question. A meta-analysis is often part of one.

summary: Short-day plants such as chrysanthemums and poinsettias flower once the night grows longer than a set length, the critical night length.
A few minutes of light in the middle of the night, a night break, can stop them from flowering; in Japanese morning glory, 5 minutes of red light was enough.
The light sensor is phytochrome, the plant's response to a night break rises and falls on a daily rhythm, and temperature shifts the timing in poinsettias.
start_here.how_sure_note: Night length and the night break have been shown in many plants for about a century; how plants actually keep the count is still debated, as the 2025 review says.

claims.claim: In short-day plants the night is what counts: once nights grow longer than the critical night length, flowering can begin.
claims.where: Section on classical physiology of photoperiodism

claims.claim: In Japanese morning glory, 5 minutes of red light in the middle of the night held back flowering.
A short night break, often only a few minutes, inhibits flowering in many short-day plants.

could_be_wrong.point: The neat textbook result, a single night break of a few minutes fully blocking flowering, comes mainly from short-day plants. In rice, a short-day crop, repeated 10-minute pulses each day were needed to change flowering time, and some long-day plants such as carnation need hours of light.

No single model explains how plants count the night. The review finds that molecular results often fit more than one classic model, and that detailed knowledge is still limited to a few species such as Arabidopsis and rice.

Light color and the light that came before matter, not only length. Blue light added after LED short days still let chrysanthemums flower, but the same blue extension after sunlight in a greenhouse did not.

Varieties differ. In the 1970 bulletin, at cool temperatures 'Paul Mikkelsen' poinsettias started flowers even with a 4-hour light break, while 'Barbara Ecke Supreme' stayed leafy with a 2-hour break, so one variety's numbers do not fit every poinsettia.

summary: In Vietnam, 29% of US Army enlisted men used narcotics regularly and 20% said they were addicted, while only 1% had used one more than a few times before service.
Lee Robins's team followed the men home: only about 5% of those classed as addicted in Vietnam were addicted again in the first year, though nearly half tried opiates again.
Later reviews use this as evidence that setting matters, but they also warn that these men differ from people who seek treatment, where relapse is far more common.
start_here.how_sure_note: The 1970s follow-up was large and careful, but some figures here come through later reviews, and whether the result applies beyond these men is debated.

could_be_wrong.point: Remission in community surveys may look higher than it is: diagnoses in community samples are unstable, the national NESARC remission analysis left out opioids, and in treatment samples stable abstinence from opioid addiction is under 30% after 10 to 30 years.

Some of the figures on the slides (nearly half tried again, 6% re-addicted, 12% relapsed briefly) come from a 1993 Robins paper that is closed, and are reported here through two reviews rather than read in the original.

The veterans were young men whose use began in an unusual setting; most had no addiction before service, and the main predictor of re-addiction was addiction before service, so the result may not carry over to people whose addiction began at home.
Early clinical samples over-represent people who do not quit, which is one reason treatment-based and population-based pictures of addiction differ.
