summary: A popular garden claim says soil microbes, even the dirt under your nails, help make serotonin; it traces to a 2007 study that injected killed soil bacteria into mice.

In those mice a small group of their own serotonin neurons became more active and serotonin turnover rose in one front brain area; treated mice were less still in a swim test at 12 hours, but not at 36.
No human study shows soil microbes lift mood over time; small single-session soil studies exist, and gardening itself is linked to better mood in a 2017 review.
start_here.how_sure_note: The serotonin finding comes from mice given injected killed bacteria; human evidence is limited to single sessions, and the gardening review cannot separate microbes from the activity.

claims.claim: Mycobacterium vaccae is described as a harmless bacterium that feeds on dead matter; microbes of its kind live in soil, water and air.

claims.claim: In 2007, adult male mice got shots of heat-killed, lab-grown M. vaccae; within hours a small group of serotonin neurons in the brainstem became more active.
Serotonin turnover rose in one front area of the mouse brain, measured 12 hours after the last injection.
The bacteria did not make serotonin; the mice's own neurons responded, and the authors propose immune signals carried the message.
Treated mice were less still in a forced swim test 12 hours later, 8 per group; by 36 hours the effect was gone.
In a 2013 study, mice fed live M. vaccae ran a maze faster with fewer anxious behaviors.

glossary.plain: A harmless soil bacterium related to the germs behind tuberculosis, studied for its effects on the immune system.

A chemical messenger made by some nerve cells, involved in mood, sleep and many body functions.
How fast serotonin is released and broken down, measured from serotonin and its breakdown product.
A cluster of serotonin-making nerve cells in the brainstem.
A front part of the brain involved in planning and handling emotion.
A mouse test that times how long an animal stays still in water; it is used to screen antidepressant drugs, not to measure human mood.
A small protein immune cells use to signal each other.
A common group of soil bacteria, the source of soil's earthy smell.
A study that pools the results of many studies to get one overall estimate.
A standard measure of how big a difference is; around 0.2 is small and 0.5 is medium.
When studies with positive results are more likely to be published, making an effect look bigger than it is.

Tools for watching the working brain. Functional MRI (fMRI) tracks blood flow, PET scans use a small radioactive tracer, and EEG records electrical activity through the scalp.
The stalk at the base of the brain that connects to the spinal cord and runs vital functions such as breathing and heart rate. The medulla is its lowest part.
Treatment that uses drugs to stop the growth of cancer cells, by killing them or stopping them from dividing.

A mental health condition with ongoing sadness, loss of energy and loss of pleasure that makes daily life hard. It can also bring feelings of worthlessness, changes in sleep or eating, and thoughts of death.

A brain structure in the limbic system that is essential for learning and for forming new memories of facts and events. People with damage to the hippocampus have great difficulty forming new memories of this kind.
The body's protective response to injury or infection, which brings redness, swelling, heat and pain.
A cell that receives and sends messages through the nervous system using small electrical signals and chemical messengers.
A mental health disorder that can follow a frightening event, with symptoms such as flashbacks, nightmares and frightening thoughts.
The front part of the cortex, involved in mood, thinking and perception. The strongest psychedelic effects are linked to activity here.
A person's overall enjoyment of life, including well-being and the ability to carry out daily activities. Many trials measure it as an outcome.

summary: In 1969 the Supreme Court said a State has no business telling a man at home what books he may read, but a footnote kept drug possession laws; RN's column asks whether protection for thought reaches altered states.

On the brain side, a 2012 psilocybin scan study found only drops in blood flow and signal, largest in hub regions, and a 2019 model called REBUS offers an explanation that its authors say still needs testing.
A slow brain signal builds before self-paced movements, but scans and recordings show where and when activity changes; none of these studies reads what a person is thinking.
start_here.how_sure_note: The scan findings come from small studies, REBUS is an untested hypothesis, and the meaning of the readiness potential is still argued over.

A 2012 study scanned 30 healthy people after placebo and psilocybin: 15 had blood flow scans and 15 had BOLD scans, and all had used psychedelics before.

claims.claim: Psilocybin brought only decreases, largest in hubs such as the thalamus and the cingulate cortex.
Bigger drops in anterior cingulate blood flow went with more intense effects (r = -0.55).
The authors proposed that the drop in hubs may allow unconstrained cognition; that is their reading, not something the scans showed.
REBUS, a 2019 model, proposes that psychedelics relax the weight the brain gives top-level beliefs, so more information flows up from below; its authors say it needs testing.
The default mode network, described in 2001, is a set of brain areas active at rest that quiet during goal-directed tasks.
A slow signal, the readiness potential, appears over motor areas hundreds of milliseconds before the conscious decision to move.
In Libet's classic results, the readiness potential of spontaneous moves begins about 500 ms before movement and people report deciding about 200 ms before.
claims.where: Text on Libet et al. 1983 (type II RPs; average W-time)

claims.claim: A 2012 model reads the build-up as random noise plus a steady push crossing a threshold; a 2023 reanalysis found the steady push is the dominant input.
A 2023 decoder recovered the gist of heard or imagined speech, but only with the person's cooperation.

could_be_wrong.point: The 2012 study scanned two separate groups of 15 experienced psychedelic users, and earlier PET studies of glucose use found increases rather than drops, so the all-decreases picture may depend on method and sample.
REBUS is a proposal. Its authors write that further work is needed to test these hypotheses.
The 2012 reading that random noise largely sets the moment of moving was challenged: a 2023 reanalysis found the steady push is the bigger input.
The readiness potential's timing does not show that conscious will is an illusion; a 2021 review argues that conclusion cannot be drawn from it.

For deliberate choices that mattered, donating $1000 to one of two nonprofits, the readiness potential was strikingly absent, so arbitrary finger moves may not stand for real decisions (read in full in the package's long form research).
Decoding is advancing: the 2023 decoder needed each person's cooperation, but its authors call for policies that protect mental privacy, so today's limits may not hold.
On the legal side, a legal scholar argues that the proposed new neurorights are poorly drafted and not good candidates to adopt as new rights (read in full in the package's long form research).

summary: The Smelling Brain, by olfactory designer Andrea Mammarella with glass artist Serim Kwack, paired glass vessels with natural perfumes at Dutch Design Week 2026.
A 2026 review of 18 studies found memories cued by smell slightly more emotional and older than memories cued by sights, sounds or words, but not clearly more vivid.
Single studies disagree on how far back smells reach, and no study pooled in the review tested whether smell memories are more accurate.
start_here.how_sure_note: The pooled effects are small, the studies are mostly small with some quality concerns, and two studies in this post disagree on the age of smell memories.

claims.claim: A 2026 review of 18 studies found smell-cued memories slightly more emotional, not clearly more vivid; none tested accuracy.
claims.where: Tables 2 and 6 (emotional intensity g 0.23; vividness g 0.14, interval crosses zero); outcomes analysed (seven features, accuracy not among them)
claims.study: systematic review and meta-analysis, 18 studies, 1,330 people

claims.claim: The Smelling Brain, by olfactory designer Andrea Mammarella with glass artist Serim Kwack, was shown at Dutch Design Week, Oct 17 to 25.
Glass vessels on supports form 'a small anatomy of unfamiliar instruments', each paired with a natural perfume tuned to memory, attraction or flavour.
A 2014 perspective article sums up smell memories as LOVER: Limbic, Old, Vivid, Emotional, Rare; people often feel 'brought back in time'.
In a small study of 62 students, smell cues brought up memories that peaked around age 6; sight and sound peaked later; only 13 were in the smell group.
At a public science event, about 400 visitors tried cues for all five senses; smell and taste brought up fewer, less detailed memories.
claims.study: one public-event study, about 400 adults, 2,627 responses

claims.claim: Smell and taste leaned toward memories never recalled before; for taste that lean passed the authors' strict statistical test, for smell it did not.

annotations.source: Bobei, Cirneci and Podina 2026
annotations.note: Pools 18 studies (1,330 people) comparing memories cued by smell with memories cued by pictures, sounds or words. Smell cues gave slightly more emotional, pleasant and 'brought back' memories and older ones; vividness, specificity and rarity showed no clear edge. Limits stated: few studies, small ones may inflate effects, and only one study blinded its assessors. CC BY, open in PMC13710685.

Limits: a summary of the authors' own and others' work, not a new test; the 2026 meta-analysis supports old and emotional but not clearly vivid or rare. CC BY.

Limits: small groups (13 in the smell group), and the authors note weaker effects than earlier work, possibly from sample size or age. CC BY.

Smell and taste cues brought fewer and less detailed memories; the age of memories did not differ by sense. could_be_wrong.point: The effects are small. The pooled edge for emotional intensity is g 0.23, and the age result rests on only 8 contrasts, which the authors say should be read with caution.
Study quality is uneven: only 1 of 18 studies blinded the people scoring the memories, and only 4 measured outcomes in a clearly reliable way.
The two single studies disagree on age. Willander's smell group peaked near age 6, but in Ernst's 400 visitors the age of memories did not differ by sense.
The age-6 peak comes from a smell group of only 13 students, and the authors suggest sample size may explain why their effects were weaker than in earlier work.
Feeling sure is not being right. A review of the field notes that counting details measures how specific a memory is, not whether it is accurate, and the pooled studies did not test accuracy.
could_be_wrong.source: Hacklander, Janssen and Bermeitinger 2019 (read in full for the long form; not in set.json)

could_be_wrong.point: Lab tests may miss the real thing: the Proust effect is an unexpected, involuntary memory, which an experiment that asks people to recall on cue cannot easily capture.

summary: Meditation and THC have both been linked to the default mode network, the brain areas tied to thinking about yourself and a wandering mind.
In a 2011 scan study, 12 long-time meditators reported less mind wandering than 12 newcomers and showed less activity in the network's hubs while meditating.
In a 2013 study of 20 men, the network quieted less than usual after THC during a focus task, and scores fell; no study has tested meditation and THC together.
start_here.how_sure_note: Both key studies are small, the meditation study compared two groups once, and later THC studies at rest disagree with each other.

claims.claim: In 2011, 12 people with over 10 years of meditation and 12 newcomers were scanned; meditators reported less mind wandering and the network's hubs were less active.
claims.where: Results; mind-wandering ratings and default mode hub results
claims.study: cross-sectional scan study, 12 meditators and 12 controls

claims.claim: Focused attention works as a trained loop: notice a distraction, let it go, and return to the chosen object.
In a 2013 placebo-controlled study, 20 healthy men did a focus task; after THC they caught fewer targets (74.7% against 83.7%) and made more false alarms (5.7% against 3.5%).
During a focus task this network normally quiets; after THC it quieted less than after placebo (F(1,19) = 13.20, p = 0.002), while the working network did not change.
Across the 20 men, less quieting went with lower accuracy.
In a 2008 study of 16 people who used cannabis now and then, THC dulled the amygdala's response to threatening faces; the authors called it preliminary.

could_be_wrong.point: The meditation study compared two groups once, so it cannot show that practice caused the difference; people who stick with meditation for 10 years may differ to begin with.

A review of 78 meditation imaging studies found that agreement across studies is the exception rather than the rule and raised concerns about publication bias (read in full as the arXiv accepted manuscript in the package's long form research).
A meta-analysis of 12 mindfulness training studies found only a small effect on posterior cingulate connectivity, and its authors say their hypothesis was only partially supported.

At rest, THC studies split: several small studies report weaker default mode measures, but the largest, a pooled re-analysis of 87 people, found no default mode change (read in full in the package's long form research).
The THC focus-task study tested only men, with one task, and its authors say the result cannot be generalized to other aspects of executive function.

glossary.plain: A set of brain areas more active at rest and during self-focused thought, which quiet during demanding tasks.
A hub of the default mode network near the middle back of the brain.
A hub of the default mode network at the front middle of the brain.
When attention drifts from the task at hand to other thoughts.
Holding attention on one object, such as the breath, and bringing it back when it drifts.
Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, the main intoxicating compound in cannabis.
Each person gets both the drug and a placebo on different days, without knowing which is which.
A drop in a brain area's activity below its resting level during a task.
Responding to something that was not a target.
A small brain region that responds to threat and emotion.
A study that compares different groups at one time point, so it cannot show cause.

The plant species that includes both hemp and marijuana. Names such as indica and ruderalis describe forms of this plant; botanists disagree on whether they are separate subspecies, varieties or species.
A medical diagnosis for a pattern of cannabis use that causes real problems or distress, such as being unable to cut down. It is a type of substance use disorder.
In a study, the group that does not get the treatment being tested, so its results can be compared with the group that does. In a placebo-controlled study, the control group gets a placebo.

A family of top-down mental skills used to concentrate and stay in control rather than run on autopilot. The three core ones are self-control (inhibition), working memory and cognitive flexibility. The prefrontal cortex is central to them.
The parts of the brain and spinal cord that are rich in nerve cell bodies, such as the cortex. They look darker than white matter, which is mostly insulated nerve fibers (axons).
A method that pools data from many studies on the same question to get a stronger overall answer.
Awareness of present-moment experience with a kind, non-judging attitude. Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) is an eight-week course built on it.
A cell that receives and sends messages through the nervous system using small electrical signals and chemical messengers.
The front part of the cortex, involved in mood, thinking and perception. The strongest psychedelic effects are linked to activity here.
The main psychedelic compound in "magic" mushrooms. The body turns it into psilocin, the active form. It is being studied for depression and for distress in people with cancer.

How much something stands out from everything else and draws attention. Emotional salience is standing out because of emotional weight. A brain network centered on the insula and the anterior cingulate cortex picks out salient signals from inside and outside the body.

summary: Wool prickle comes mostly from coarse fibres wider than about 30 micrometres whose stiff ends press into the skin; wool worn next to the skin needs fibres finer than 18.
Earlier work reported in a 2021 wool review put the threshold at fibre ends that push with about 0.74 millinewtons, and found that moist skin makes the nerve response stronger.
At DDW 2026, Lilian Marie Furrer felted discarded Austrian wool straight into objects with a CNC machine and a robot; no one has measured whether felting changes prickle.
start_here.how_sure_note: The prickle science is decades old and well replicated in wool research, but it reaches this post through one review written by wool scientists, and felted objects were never tested.

annotations.source: Doyle et al. 2021
annotations.note: A review of sheep and wool production by wool scientists. It names mean fibre diameter as the most important property of wool and reports earlier work linking prickle to coarse fibres over 30 micrometres and to fibre ends pressing with about 0.74 millinewtons. Limits: it summarises the prickle studies rather than testing them, and it presents wool's comfort and health benefits favourably.
annotations.funding: not stated
annotations.conflicts: none declared (the paper has no conflict statement; its author notes say Phil Hynd chairs the Expert Panel for Meat and Livestock Australia and works as a private consultant)

could_be_wrong.point: The 30 micrometre and 0.74 millinewton figures come from 1980s work that the review reports but that this post could not read in full.
The review is written by wool scientists and presents wool's comfort favourably; it is not a neutral test of prickle.

Itch is not always prickle. A review of a century of reports found no good evidence that wool fibre itself is an allergen, and named disperse dyes on synthetic fibres as the most common textile dye sensitizers.

Clothing trials in eczema are mixed: a trial of 300 children found no evidence that special silk garments improved eczema severity over standard care alone, so fibre choice alone may matter less than people expect.

summary: Sunflowers can take up metals and radioactive elements through their roots: in greenhouse tests they pulled lead, zinc, cadmium and uranium out of polluted water, and on a raft near Chernobyl they took up cesium and strontium from a pond.
Soil is harder: the EPA says plant cleanup may take several years and mostly reaches the top foot, and the pollution leaves only when the plants are harvested and handled as waste.
Results vary by plant and place; in a 12-hour test with local soil and well water on the Navajo Nation, 13 sunflower seedlings did not lower arsenic or uranium.
start_here.how_sure_note: Uptake is well documented in lab and pilot tests, but field cleanup of soil is slow and site-specific, and the EPA called the Chernobyl method pilot scale.

summary: Harim Lee's PRISMA1.0, shown at DDW 2026, uses clear and reflective materials so its colours appear, disappear and change as it is turned, with no digital parts.
Part of that colour is made by you: three cone types in the eye send signals that are compared in pairs, and in monkey visual cortex those pairs combine in patches that prefer particular hues.
Moving helps too: in a study of 9 students, image motion made surfaces look glossier, and motion matched to their own head movement more so.
start_here.how_sure_note: Cones and opponent signals are textbook science; the cortex finding comes from one imaging study in seven monkeys, and the gloss result from one small study.

claims.claim: A clear lamp, full of colour: part of that colour is made in your eyes and brain.
claims.study: imaging study in monkeys, framed by human colour research

claims.claim: PRISMA1.0 by Harim Lee combines transparent and reflective materials; turned, its colours appear, disappear and transform without digital parts.
Your eye has three cone types, tuned to long, middle and short wavelengths of light.
Their signals are compared in pairs: long against middle cones, and short against the other two together.
In monkey visual cortex, those paired signals combine in patches that prefer particular hues, following rules from human colour studies.
claims.study: imaging and recording study, seven macaque monkeys

claims.claim: In 9 students, image motion made surfaces look glossier, and motion matched to their own head more so.
Turn it and look again: the object changes the light, and your eyes and brain make the colour.

annotations.source: Li et al. 2022
annotations.note: Using optical imaging and two-photon calcium imaging in the primary visual cortex of seven macaque monkeys, the authors found patches that combine the two kinds of cone-opponent signals in the ways human colour studies predict, along with hue pinwheels. Limits: anaesthetised monkeys, not people, and the authors did not test single neurons across the full colour space.
annotations.funding: Supported by NIH grants EY022577, NS105129 and MH063912 (E. M. Callaway), EY028084 (A. K. Garg), the Gatsby Charitable Trust (E. M. Callaway) and the Pioneer Fund (P. Li).
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests.

annotations.source: Tani et al. 2013
annotations.note: Nine students compared computer-rendered surfaces that were still, moving on the screen, or moving with their own head. Surfaces looked glossier with image motion, and glossier again with head-matched motion. Limits: nine people, rendered images rather than real objects, and the authors note that the effect varied between people.
annotations.funding: Supported by a Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research on Innovative Areas (#22135005, for S. Nakauchi); the funders had no role in the study.
annotations.conflicts: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.

could_be_wrong.point: The hue patches were found in anaesthetised macaque monkeys. The study did not record from people.
The authors say they have not explored how single neurons respond across the full three-dimensional colour space, and call for future studies of how other cortex patches interact with these ones.
The gloss study had nine participants viewing computer-rendered surfaces; the authors note the size of the effect differed between people and plan to set specular levels for each person.
Neither study tested PRISMA1.0 or any physical object, so how much of the lamp's colour change comes from optics and how much from perception was not measured.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Philips Design showed Soul & Science across three sites; its basement piece, Care Felt, used light and sound to explore how a frightening moment can become bearable.
The sound side has deep evidence: a 2018 review pooled 81 randomized trials and found music lowered anxiety and pain around surgery, though many trials had a moderate to high risk of bias.

The light side is thinner: in one MRI study, patients in a room with colored light, a screen and slow music reported less anxiety than two of three other groups, but it changed several things at once.
start_here.how_sure_note: Music around surgery rests on many trials of mixed quality; the light finding comes from one non-randomized study that cannot separate light from screen and music.

could_be_wrong.point: The music trials were rated at moderate to high risk of bias, and the trials disagreed a lot (I squared 87 percent for anxiety).
The MRI rooms were in different centres and patients were not assigned at random, so differences between rooms could reflect the hospitals or the patients.
The MRI study found no significant difference between several pairs of rooms, including the light-and-screen room against a room with no light but fast music.
In children, a review of 3 trials (196 children) found music lowered pain and distress after surgery, but with moderate risk of bias, so the evidence for younger patients is thin.
The installation shows design ideas, not a tested treatment; the listing does not name the frightening moment it addresses.

summary: In a 2012 lab study, most of 90 children aged 9, 12 and 15 who played with a humanoid robot believed it had feelings and could be a friend, though the 15-year-olds less so.

annotations.note: Ninety children, 30 each aged 9, 12 and 15, spent 15 minutes with the humanoid robot Robovie, watched it put in a closet against its objections, and were interviewed for about 50 minutes. could_be_wrong.point: Robovie looked autonomous but was secretly operated by a person, so its talk and timing came from a hidden person rather than from the robot itself.
There was no adult group, so the authors say it is unclear whether teenagers are simply the most skeptical age, and children's views varied: 28 percent scored moderate to low on all three scales.
Children gave the robot some moral standing but not liberty or civil rights, so they did not treat it as equal to a person.
In a robot trust study, children's choices depended on the kind of mind described, and the authors caution that one of the three studies lacked comprehension checks.
The 2026 review's findings are known here only from its abstract; its methods, quality ratings and which studies support each line could not be checked.

summary: A Dutch Design Week installation by Maria Mombers styled a short film like slot-machine reels and social media Reels, and its listing speaks of a "dopamine hit" from our phones.

In two monkeys, dopamine neurons gave a quick signal that tracked the odds of a reward and a slower one that grew with uncertainty, and a study of over one million posts found that posting fits reward learning.
Neither study measured dopamine in people using a feed, so the feed as a dopamine slot machine is still an untested idea.
start_here.how_sure_note: The monkey dopamine signals and the posting patterns are well measured, but no study has linked the two in people scrolling a feed.

could_be_wrong.point: The slow ramp in the monkey study may not be an uncertainty signal at all. A modelling critique showed that averaging many small prediction errors across trials can produce a ramp of the same shape.
The original team replied with further analyses that they say fit uncertainty better, so the meaning of the ramp is still argued over twenty years on.

The posting study measured behaviour only. Its authors write that their findings "cannot speak to the neurobiological basis of reward learning on social media" and that the big data are correlational.

A larger 2026 study of Twitter users found that models mixing reward learning with habit fit posting better than reward learning alone, and frequent posters looked more habitual. A habit can run on cues with little reward.

Dopamine may drive wanting more than pleasure. Rats with nearly all brain dopamine removed still showed normal liking of sweet tastes, which cuts against the idea of a dopamine hit as a burst of pleasure.
In rats, brief dopamine pulses did not make cues rewarding in themselves; the rats learned which event follows which. A burst does not simply stamp value onto whatever came before it.

The only study found that measured dopamine and real phone use in the same people had 22 adults, compared PET scans with phone logs from other days, and cannot say which came first. The authors call for replication.
The slot machine's best known trick, the near miss, failed to keep pigeons or students playing longer once wins stopped, and no study has tested a near miss inside a social media feed.
Calling heavy use an addiction is disputed. Reviewers warn that applying addiction checklists to common habits risks "overpathologizing everyday life".

A systematic review of 28 brain imaging studies of social media use judged that conclusions "should remain tentative" and that comparisons with substance addiction are premature without long-term data.

glossary.plain: A chemical messenger made by a small group of neurons deep in the midbrain that send it to wide areas of the brain.
The gap between the reward an animal expected and the reward it got, which dopamine neurons signal with a burst or a dip.
A brief burst of firing by dopamine neurons right after a cue or a reward.
A slower rise in dopamine neuron firing that builds while an animal waits to find out whether a reward will come.
How unsure the outcome is; it is highest when a reward has a 50/50 chance and zero when the reward is certain or impossible.
Changing what you do, and how fast you do it, based on the rewards past actions brought.
The time a person waits between one social media post and the next.
Data that show two things go together without showing that one causes the other.
Heavy phone or social media use that causes trouble in daily life, a term some researchers prefer to addiction.
Privately published Japanese woodblock prints, often commissioned by poets as New Year's greeting cards.

summary: Ghrelin is a stomach hormone found in 1999; GHSR is the receptor on cells that hears it, including in brain areas that regulate eating.
In people, ghrelin rises nearly twofold just before meals, and in a 2001 study a ghrelin drip made all nine volunteers eat more, 28% on average.
Structures from 2020 to 2025 show the receptor in detail, but studies of mice without ghrelin suggest it is not essential for starting a meal.
start_here.how_sure_note: The appetite effect of given ghrelin is consistent across many small human studies; whether the body's own ghrelin drives everyday hunger is debated.

could_be_wrong.point: In mice bred without ghrelin, studies do not support a role for ghrelin as an essential meal-starting or hunger hormone, according to the main review.
A review of appetite hormones notes that 72 hours of fasting does not raise ghrelin, and the before-meal pattern may partly reflect the fall after meals.
Across 121 studies of given ghrelin, appetite rose consistently, but most studies were small and short and many lacked a placebo or randomisation.
The drip study had nine people and gave ghrelin from outside the body, so it shows what added ghrelin can do, not what the body's own ghrelin does day to day.
The short stature families had few carriers, some of normal height, and the authors call the receptor's role in the body an open question.

glossary.plain: A hormone made mostly in the stomach that rises before meals and can increase appetite.
The growth hormone secretagogue receptor, the protein that ghrelin binds to.
A protein that a messenger molecule fits into, setting off a signal inside the cell.
A large family of receptors that pass signals through partner proteins called G proteins.
Adding a short fatty acid to a protein; ghrelin needs one to switch its receptor on.
Ghrelin O-acyltransferase, the enzyme that attaches ghrelin's fatty acid tag.
A small brain region that helps control hunger, body temperature and hormones.
A receptor's built-in signalling even when nothing is bound to it.
Imaging frozen molecules with electrons to see their shape in near-atomic detail.
Neither the volunteers nor the researchers know who got which treatment.

An almond-shaped structure in the temporal lobe, part of the limbic system, that is important for emotional memory, such as learning to fear something. THC reduced its response to threatening faces in one study.
A neurotransmitter tied to reward and motivation. It drives the brain's reward pathway and helps make music pleasurable.
A trial in which neither the participants nor the researchers know who got which treatment until the end.
A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction in the body, such as building or breaking down a messenger.

A brain structure in the limbic system that is essential for learning and for forming new memories of facts and events. People with damage to the hippocampus have great difficulty forming new memories of this kind.
A substance made by a gland that travels in the blood and changes how certain cells or organs work. Cortisol and melatonin are hormones.
A method that pools data from many studies on the same question to get a stronger overall answer.
The chemical changes in cells and the body that make energy and the materials cells need, and that help clear toxic substances.
A reward area deep in the brain that is part of the dopamine reward pathway.
A pea-sized gland at the base of the brain, attached to the hypothalamus, that releases hormones controlling other glands.

summary: RN wrote about her own migraines and reached a limit every scientist knows: one person's relief cannot show what caused it.
Migraine days rise and fall with stress, sleep, hormones and chance, and these confounders can make a treatment look like it worked when it did not.
Studies add blinding, a comparison group and random assignment; a small 2021 Yale psilocybin study and a 2020 cannabis app study show what each design can and cannot tell us.
start_here.how_sure_note: The psilocybin result comes from 10 people in an exploratory study with a fixed order; the cannabis app data had no placebo group.

claims.claim: A confounder is a variable that distorts a result so it does not reflect the real relationship; random assignment breaks links between a treatment and its confounders.

claims.claim: A 2021 Yale study of psilocybin for migraine was exploratory, double-blind and placebo-controlled, and each person was their own control.
Ten people were analyzed; weekly migraine days fell by 1.65 on average after psilocybin and by 0.15 after placebo.
Placebo always came first, by design, so a lasting drug effect could not leak into the placebo session, and the authors flagged possible unblinding.
A 2020 app study logged headache ratings 47.3% lower after cannabis, with no placebo group, and its lead author suspected slight overestimates.

could_be_wrong.point: The psilocybin study analyzed only 10 people, gave placebo first every time, and the authors say the drug's noticeable effects may have revealed which session was which.
The app data had no placebo group and came from people who chose to log their use and may have expected relief; the lead author suspected slight overestimates.
Trigger data are self-reported in a single clinic sample, so what people blame for an attack may not be what caused it.

Placebo responses in migraine prevention trials grew from 1990 to 2021, so improvement without an active drug is common and can be large (a meta-analysis of 83 trials, funded by Biohaven; read in full in the package's long form research).

glossary.plain: A brain disorder with repeated attacks of moderate to severe, often one-sided, throbbing headache, sometimes with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound.
Something a person links with the start of an attack, such as stress, a missed meal or poor sleep.
A third factor that affects both the treatment and the outcome and so distorts the apparent link between them.
An inactive look-alike treatment used so that a study can tell drug effects apart from expectation and chance.
Neither the participants nor the staff running the sessions know who got the drug and who got the placebo.
When people can guess which treatment they got, for example from a drug's noticeable effects, which weakens the blind.
A study in which each person receives both the treatment and the comparison at different times and acts as their own control.
Using chance to decide who gets which treatment or in which order, so confounders are spread evenly.
A small early study meant to see if an effect is worth testing properly, not to prove it.
The psychedelic compound made by some mushrooms.

A comparison drug that causes some noticeable effects, so trial participants have a harder time guessing whether they got the real treatment. One psilocybin trial for alcohol use disorder used the antihistamine diphenhydramine this way.
Inserting thin needles through the skin at specific points on the body to ease pain and other symptoms. It is a type of complementary medicine.
A non-intoxicating cannabis compound that acts on several targets, including the 5-HT1A receptor.
In a study, the group that does not get the treatment being tested, so its results can be compared with the group that does. In a placebo-controlled study, the control group gets a placebo.
A substance made by a gland that travels in the blood and changes how certain cells or organs work. Cortisol and melatonin are hormones.
A method that pools data from many studies on the same question to get a stronger overall answer.
A person's overall enjoyment of life, including well-being and the ability to carry out daily activities. Many trials measure it as an outcome.
A study that assigns people by chance to different treatments, such as a drug or a placebo, so the groups can be compared fairly.
The main intoxicating compound in cannabis.

summary: Designer Ori Orisun Merhav won a 2026 Dutch Design Awards Emerging Talent Award and showed Woven Landscapes at Dutch Design Week: woven palm textiles fused with lac, a resin made by tiny insects.
Lac is secreted by lac insects, mainly Kerria lacca in India, as a covering for their young; growers cut the coated branches, and industry mostly uses it as the coating called shellac.
Her programme text asks how a material remembers. In the brain, learning leaves lasting changes in a small group of cells, though scientists still debate exactly where a memory is stored.
start_here.how_sure_note: The award, the work and the lac facts come from official pages and a full review; the memory science is a 2016 expert forum that says the question is still open.

claims.claim: The adult female stays in one place, bound in her own resin; growers harvest lac by cutting the coated branches.
Lac coats pills and food and turns up in paint and electronics insulation; in one review's sample, shellac patents rose from 2 to 12 by 2019 to 2022.
Inspired by insects building cocoons, Merhav began shaping lac in three dimensions.
In the brain, learning leaves lasting physical and chemical changes in a small group of cells; in mice, reactivating those cells brought a memory back.
On 17 October 2026 she won a Dutch Design Awards Emerging Talent Award, one of three, each with EUR 10,000 from the Keep an Eye Foundation.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Cubcho Lab ran free workshops where children pressed recycled paper pulp into blocks and learned how much pressure makes a solid block.
In an EEG study of 88 people aged 8 to 30, children aged 8 to 10 held a light pinch least precisely and adults most precisely, and better grip went with coupling in a grasping network in the brain.
Across 11 studies, young children's hand skills went with maths and reading, but only as correlations; no study here tested a workshop or a toy.

summary: Migraine aura is tied to a slow wave of silenced brain activity, spreading depression, which in animals can switch on the trigeminal pain nerve that releases CGRP, now a major drug target.
The brain makes its own cannabinoids, and in rats switching on CB1 receptors in a brainstem pain hub cut migraine-type pain signals by up to 19%.
In people, app data showed ratings falling after cannabis with no placebo group, a clinic review linked cannabis use to rebound headache, and the first placebo-controlled trial was small.
start_here.how_sure_note: The brain circuit is well studied, but the cannabis evidence in people is mostly observational, and the one randomized trial is small and short.

Limits: animals, not people. doi 10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0943-13.2013; read in full by the package (PMC3771033).

annotations.source: Okusanya et al. 2022
annotations.note: A review of 12 studies (1,980 people) of medical cannabis for migraine, mostly retrospective records and app data, five of them conference abstracts. It reports the app study and the rebound headache link and concludes it is impossible to recommend cannabis for migraine with confidence. Open copy PMC9197380, CC BY 4.0.
annotations.funding: Arizona Department of Health Services (contract ADHS12-017291), which played no role in the review.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no commercial or financial relationships that could be a potential conflict of interest.

annotations.note: App data from 653 people and 7,441 migraine sessions; ratings fell 49.6% after cannabis. Read through Okusanya et al. 2022 and Hooper et al. 2026, which note biased sampling, no placebo group and no control of dose; the paper itself was not read in full.
annotations.funding: not read (paper not read in full)
annotations.conflicts: not read (paper not read in full)

annotations.source: Schuster et al. 2026
annotations.note: The first randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of vaporized cannabis for acute migraine: 92 enrolled, 234 attacks analysed. Pain relief at 2 hours was 67% with THC plus CBD and 69% with THC-dominant flower against 47% with placebo; CBD-dominant flower did not beat placebo. Limits: prior users, single potencies, no long-term risks. Open copy PMC12872409, CC BY-NC.
annotations.funding: Migraine Research Foundation; UC San Diego Academic Senate; NIH CTSA grant UL1TR001442; Leonard and Marilyn Berger.
annotations.conflicts: The first author has advised or consulted for Lundbeck, Rapport, Vertex, Averitas, Delphian, Eli Lilly, Lohocla, Salvia and Syqe; a co-author has consulted for Abbvie, Amgen, Biohaven, Lilly, Lundbeck, Teva and Theranica; the others report none.

could_be_wrong.point: The CGRP part of the story is less settled than it sounds: a review states there is little evidence unambiguously connecting CGRP and spreading depression, and no evidence that CGRP can trigger it.
The app study had no placebo group and likely over-represents people who find cannabis helpful; reviewers note biased sampling and no control of dose.
could_be_wrong.source: Okusanya et al. 2022; Hooper et al. 2026

could_be_wrong.point: The rebound headache link comes from one retrospective chart review; it cannot show whether cannabis causes overuse headache or whether people with worse headaches use more cannabis.
The 19% cut in pain signals was measured in anesthetized rats, not in people with migraine.
The registry that reported improving scores is run by a cannabis clinic company, most authors work for it, there was no control group and up to 60% of data were missing by two years.

glossary.plain: Visual or other sensory changes, such as zigzag lines, that can come before or with a migraine headache.
A slow wave of strong activity followed by silence that moves across the brain's surface.
The main nerve carrying pain and touch from the face and head coverings to the brain.
Calcitonin gene-related peptide, a messenger released by pain nerves that widens blood vessels; several migraine drugs block it.
A cannabinoid the body makes itself, such as anandamide or 2-AG.
Cannabinoid receptors on cells; CB1 is common in the brain and is where THC acts to cause its effects.
A migraine drug that acts on serotonin 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D receptors.
Headache that gets more frequent when pain or migraine medicines are used too often.
A study where some people get a dummy treatment, so researchers can tell what the real treatment adds.
A study that looks back through existing medical records rather than testing a treatment.
A six-question score of how much headaches affect daily life; higher means more impact.
One of the body's two best-studied endocannabinoids; it tends to rise during stress and helps end the stress response.
One of the body's two best-studied endocannabinoids. It tends to fall during stress and is broken down by the enzyme FAAH.
The stalk at the base of the brain that connects to the spinal cord and runs vital functions such as breathing and heart rate. The medulla is its lowest part.
Chemicals that act on the body's cannabinoid system. Plant cannabinoids (phytocannabinoids) such as THC and CBD come mostly from the resin in the female flowers of the cannabis plant.
A medical diagnosis for a pattern of cannabis use that causes real problems or distress, such as being unable to cut down. It is a type of substance use disorder.
The most common cannabinoid receptor in the brain and THC's main target.
A cannabinoid receptor found mainly on immune cells that helps regulate inflammation.
A non-intoxicating cannabis compound that acts on several targets, including the 5-HT1A receptor.
The brain and spinal cord.
Ethan Russo's unproven theory that some pain conditions, including migraine, involve too little endocannabinoid activity.

A range of values, worked out from study data, that is likely to hold the true value. A 95% confidence interval comes from a method that would capture the true value 95% of the time if the study were repeated many times. The interval also shows how uncertain the estimate is.
In a study, the group that does not get the treatment being tested, so its results can be compared with the group that does. In a placebo-controlled study, the control group gets a placebo.
A slow wave of electrical disruption across the brain's surface that is thought to cause migraine aura.

A mental health condition with ongoing sadness, loss of energy and loss of pleasure that makes daily life hard. It can also bring feelings of worthlessness, changes in sleep or eating, and thoughts of death.
The overall level of activity in the body's endocannabinoid system. It reflects how much anandamide and 2-AG the body makes and breaks down and how many cannabinoid receptors are present.
Newer migraine medicines that block the CGRP receptor.

A brain area that controls body temperature, hunger and thirst and links the nervous system to the hormone system. It holds the body's main clock for sleep and wake cycles (the suprachiasmatic nucleus) and starts the hormonal stress response.
The three thin layers of tissue that cover and protect the brain and spinal cord.
A method that pools data from many studies on the same question to get a stronger overall answer.
A recurring type of headache with moderate to severe throbbing pain, often on one side of the head, that can come with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound.
A cell that receives and sends messages through the nervous system using small electrical signals and chemical messengers.

A way of comparing how likely something is in one group with how likely it is in another. An odds ratio of 1 means no difference; above 1 means higher odds in the first group. It is often used in backward-looking (case-control) studies and shows a link, not a cause.
A class of pain-relieving drugs, made from the opium poppy or in a lab, that block pain signals by binding to opioid receptors. They can be highly addictive.
An area in the midbrain that helps control pain, defensive behavior and anxiety. It is part of the brain's own pain-control system.
A molecule, usually a protein, on or inside a cell that a specific chemical messenger binds to, which sets off an effect in the cell. It is often pictured as a lock that only certain keys fit.
A review that uses clear, planned methods to find, select and combine the results of all the studies on a clearly stated question. A meta-analysis is often part of one.
A relay station deep in the brain that passes information from the senses on to other brain areas.
The main intoxicating compound in cannabis.
The part of the cortex in the occipital lobe, at the back of the brain, that processes what the eyes see.

summary: Huis is a play installation on wheels by Studio Kars en Boom and RAUM, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026, built with more than fifty children with and without disabilities and meant to offer space for both movement and rest.
In one school study, 27 autistic children used a multisensory room programme; sensory and adaptation scores improved, but repetitive behaviour did not change significantly.
That study had no control group and a small sample, and its authors call the evidence on these rooms limited and sometimes controversial.
start_here.how_sure_note: The rest-space evidence comes from one small before-and-after school study without a control group; reviews of inclusive play are mostly descriptive.

could_be_wrong.point: The school study had no control group and 27 pupils, so the gains could come from time, maturing or other school changes rather than the room; the authors say these limits affect how far the results can be generalized.
Earlier studies of multisensory rooms share the same problems: pre and post designs without control groups, small samples, reliance on caregiver reports and inconsistent measures.

Calmer bodies are not the same as better regulation: in the hand-held robot study, children moved less and had lower heart rates, but the authors note that less movement is not necessarily better self-regulation.
The idea that crossing a threshold resets the mind did not hold up well: across four experiments, doorways had no significant effect on forgetting.
No study measured Huis itself; the evidence on these pages concerns other rooms, playgrounds and settings.

summary: When researchers measured the forces between partner dancers' hands during a lead and follow stepping task, the forces were small, about 10 to 30 newtons, roughly the weight of a 1 to 3 kilogram bag.
Expert pairs used larger forces than novices, and the authors suggest these small forces act as guiding cues that carry the movement goal more than they push.
In linked-hand lab tasks, both the weaker and stronger partner tracked a target better, and groups of up to four coordinated within seconds.
start_here.how_sure_note: Three lab studies from two research groups agree that touch carries information, but samples were small and the step from lab handles to the ballroom is an inference.

summary: A Dutch Design Week talk listing said 92% of people check their phone on waking and only 5% sleep with it outside the bedroom, without naming a source.
In a small pilot trial, 19 students with poor sleep who stopped phone use 30 minutes before bed for four weeks fell asleep faster, slept longer and did better on a memory task than 19 controls.
A large tracking study found phone app habits are stronger in the places and routes people use most, which suggests where the phone sleeps may matter.
start_here.how_sure_note: The sleep result comes from one small pilot trial with self-reported sleep; the listing's figures have no named source.

could_be_wrong.point: The sleep trial was small, used self-reported sleep rather than objective measures, and included only students who already believed phones hurt their sleep and wanted to cut back.
A popular claim that a phone's mere presence drains thinking power has not held up: two replications of the 2017 brain drain study failed.
The famous finding that people would rather shock themselves than sit and think is disputed: critics note participants rated thinking time as somewhat enjoyable and most never shocked themselves.

glossary.plain: Thoughts drifting away from the task at hand to something else.
Brain areas that are more active when a person is not focused on an outside task.
How long it takes to fall asleep.
Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, a questionnaire score where higher numbers mean worse sleep; above 5 suggests poor sleep.
Holding and using information in mind for a short time, like a phone number.
A small early study to test whether a larger trial is worth doing.
A behaviour started automatically by a familiar cue, such as a place or time.
Repeating a study to see if the same result appears again.
The speaker's term for being constantly reachable and messaging through devices.
Tools for watching the working brain. Functional MRI (fMRI) tracks blood flow, PET scans use a small radioactive tracer, and EEG records electrical activity through the scalp.

A range of values, worked out from study data, that is likely to hold the true value. A 95% confidence interval comes from a method that would capture the true value 95% of the time if the study were repeated many times. The interval also shows how uncertain the estimate is.
A neurotransmitter tied to reward and motivation. It drives the brain's reward pathway and helps make music pleasurable.
The ability to solve new problems on purpose, by reasoning, without relying on knowledge learned before. It is usually contrasted with crystallized intelligence, which is accumulated knowledge.
A method that pools data from many studies on the same question to get a stronger overall answer.
Awareness of present-moment experience with a kind, non-judging attitude. Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) is an eight-week course built on it.
The checking of a study by other experts in the same field before a journal publishes it.
Information that comes straight from the person, such as how they rate their own pain or sleep, rather than from a lab test or device.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2025, Studio Daniëlle Ooms served a seasonal, plant-based lunch to up to 20 guests at one long table in Eindhoven.
A 2026 review of 50 lab studies found that eating while distracted raised how much people ate later, while the effect during the meal held mainly for passive distractions like TV.
In a small brain-scan study, people rated the same wine as more pleasant when told it cost more, and nobody has tested whether a seasonal story does the same to food.
start_here.how_sure_note: The distraction finding rests on a large review of lab studies with signs of publication bias, and the wine price finding on small scanner studies; the lunch itself was never studied.

could_be_wrong.point: The effect of distraction during the meal was not clear across 50 studies (SMD 0.123, P = 0.051), a publication bias check suggested missing null studies, and every study was done in a lab.

could_be_wrong.point: In the 2017 wine replication the price effect came mostly from a cheap label lowering pleasure, and its brain findings did not survive the strictest statistical correction.
Flavour can change inside a season: early and late picks of one strawberry variety differed in sugar, aroma and liking, so some of the seasonal difference may lie in the fruit rather than the eater.
No study found in a November 2026 search has tested whether seasonal food tastes better when eaten together at one table, or separated the produce from the story told about it.

summary: Ego depletion is the idea that self-control runs on a limited fuel, so one hard task leaves less for the next.
When 23 labs and then 36 labs ran large preregistered tests, the effect was close to zero, and a 12-lab test found only a small one.
So the fuel-tank picture shrank to a small effect or none in the biggest tests, though tiredness and motivation may still matter in other ways.
start_here.how_sure_note: Three large preregistered multilab tests agree the effect is between zero and small; critics still debate whether the tasks were the right ones.

could_be_wrong.point: Defenders of the model said the 2016 test used new, mostly untested tasks; Baumeister and Vohs later called that choice foolish.
could_be_wrong.source: Baumeister & Vohs (2016), as quoted by Englert & Bertrams (2021)

could_be_wrong.point: In the pooled 2016 data, most people did not rate the letter task as depleting, though those who reported more effort did worse afterward.
A 12-lab test with a different task pair found a small but significant effect, d = 0.10, so a small effect is still possible.
could_be_wrong.source: Dang et al. (2021), Social Psychological and Personality Science

could_be_wrong.point: The 36-lab test excluded nearly a third of its participants by preregistered rules, and with everyone included it found a small significant effect; the authors say their findings allow no effect, an unknown effect or a small conditional one.
could_be_wrong.source: Vohs et al. (2021), submitted version, Discussion

could_be_wrong.point: One outcome task in the 36-lab test, guessing odd quantities such as watermelon seeds, may not measure self-control at all.
could_be_wrong.source: Englert & Bertrams (2021), Frontiers in Human Neuroscience

could_be_wrong.point: No one has shown, outside depletion research, which tasks truly demand self-control, so a failed test can always be blamed on the task.
Bias corrections that shrink the 2010 estimate depend on methods with their own limits, and the 2010 authors reply that small-study effects need not mean publication bias.

summary: This post takes one line from RN's Polymath essay, about her father naming the smell of cannabis, and asks how a brain learns a smell.

Smell signals run from the nose to the olfactory bulb and on to the piriform cortex and amygdala without a required stop in the thalamus, and people name odours poorly until they are given words for them.
Smell-cued life memories seem to come from early childhood, but that result rests on few comparisons, and brain scans of such memories are still rare and small.
start_here.how_sure_note: The wiring and the naming findings are well established; the early-childhood result is exploratory and the brain scans are few and small.

could_be_wrong.point: Smell has no required stop in the thalamus, but an indirect route through the thalamus does exist, so the shortcut is not the whole story.
Much of the bulb-to-amygdala wiring cited in the 2013 review was traced in rodents and monkeys, not people.
could_be_wrong.source: Kadohisa (2013), Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience, section on olfactory processing streams

could_be_wrong.point: The early-childhood result for smell memories rests on 8 comparisons and is labelled exploratory, and smell memories showed no clear edge in vividness.
could_be_wrong.source: Bobei, Cîrneci & Podina (2026), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, Table 4 and Limitations

could_be_wrong.point: The studies measure how old, emotional or vivid smell memories feel; none of them checked whether those memories are accurate.
could_be_wrong.source: Bobei, Cîrneci & Podina (2026), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review

could_be_wrong.point: Adding a name to an odour cue shifted older adults' memories later in life and lowered how emotional they felt, so a name may change which memories a smell brings back.
The first brain scan study of smell-cued life memories had five people, and by 2014 only two such studies existed.
could_be_wrong.source: Larsson et al. (2014); Saive, Royet & Plailly (2014)

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, seven design teams pitched health projects at Natlab in Eindhoven, and we checked two of their claims against published studies.
Children in one Danish hospital spent a median 18.8 hours a day lying in bed, but no study we found measures how fast a child on a ward loses strength.
A review of 13 trials found active play lowered children's own anxiety reports, while lower pain showed up only in what parents and staff reported.
start_here.how_sure_note: The bed time and distraction findings come from a careful sensor study and a review of 13 trials, but the 1.5% a day strength figure has no study behind it that we could find.

could_be_wrong.point: No study in this search measured daily strength loss in children on a regular ward, so OverDeTop's 1.5% a day figure is unconfirmed. The nearest data come from intensive care, where children are much sicker and muscle thickness, not strength, was measured.
The 7.9% figure pools studies that differ a lot (I squared about 84%), reflecting different patients and how sick they were.
The bed time data come from one Danish hospital over six months; only children after spine surgery came close to OverDeTop's 95% of the stay in bed (22.6 h a day lying).

Children's own pain scores showed no clear difference with active distraction (SMD -0.02, 95% CI -0.34 to 0.29); the pain benefit appears only in what parents and staff reported, and only 3 trials asked children about anxiety.

A review of 75 papers found no agreed concept of health and recorded critiques of health as the ability to adapt: frail older people or people with mental illness may lack that capacity, and putting health on the individual can breed guilt.
In the Dutch survey only 30% of physicians answered, against 71% of patients, people who liked the idea may have been keener to reply, and it covers one country.

summary: In psychedelic research the room is called the setting, and it has changed from 1950s hospital rooms under fluorescent lights to trial rooms with cushions, plants and music.
Small studies hint that the music experience, curved rooms and a view of trees can matter, each measured in a different place and none in a test that changed only the room.
The evidence is early: small samples, no placebo for the music finding, and trial volunteers who were mostly White.
start_here.how_sure_note: Each finding comes from one small study, most outside psychedelic research, and none changed only the setting of a psychedelic session.

could_be_wrong.point: The music finding comes from 19 patients with no placebo condition, so it is a correlation; the authors say causal inferences are problematic.
The trial was part sponsored by the Beckley Foundation, whose director is a co-author and whose advisor is another co-author, as the paper discloses.

Curved rooms changed beauty ratings but did not change choices to enter or exit, the predicted amygdala response did not appear, and the authors say photos may lack the fidelity to test approach and avoidance.
The window study used records from one hospital and one type of surgery, and the author warns the results cannot be extended to all built views or to other patient groups.
The 88% figure is known only as a 2017 history sums up a 1960 report; the original report was not opened.
Trial volunteers have been mostly White, so ideas of a comfortable room may reflect a narrow group.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, textile designer Svenja Bremen showed silk curtains carrying a notation of flocked and wooden marks meant to be read by touch.
Fingertip skin is packed with touch fibres, and young sighted adults can feel details about 1.2 to 1.7 mm apart, close to the spacing of Braille dots.
In one small study, sighted adults who learned Braille by touch for 9 months began using a visual reading area of the brain for it.
start_here.how_sure_note: The fingertip limits rest on many studies, but the brain findings in sighted Braille learners come from small groups, and nobody has tested reading the curtains themselves.

could_be_wrong.point: No study has tested reading Bremen's curtains, and the listing does not give the size or spacing of the marks or say who the notation is for, so the Braille findings set limits but say nothing direct about this work.
could_be_wrong.source: Dutch Design Week (2026), Tactile Notation listing

could_be_wrong.point: Two neuroscientists argue that brain "reorganisation" is claimed too easily: TMS effects spread beyond the target, and the sighted learners' results may reflect a capacity the visual cortex already had (unmasking) rather than rewiring.
The TMS result comes from 9 women aged 22 to 36, and reading speed after the course ranged from 0 to 17 words a minute.
Nine months after the course, 19 returning learners read only about 3.6 words a minute, and the authors could not rule out that the brain changes reflect imagining the dots visually.
Why blind readers keep finer touch is unsettled: their acuity did not track Braille reading speed, hours or age of learning, and one earlier study found no blind advantage at all.

glossary.plain: A slowly adapting touch nerve fibre in the skin that keeps firing while pressure lasts and reports fine shape and edges.
A rapidly adapting touch nerve fibre that fires when skin contact starts or changes, such as when a finger slides.
The patch of skin that a single touch nerve fibre responds to.
The smallest gap or detail a person can feel by touch, usually measured in millimetres.
The set of up to six raised dots, in two columns of three, that forms one Braille character; standard dots sit 2.28 mm apart.
A region on the underside of the brain's left visual cortex that responds strongly to written words in sighted readers.
A method that sends brief magnetic pulses through the scalp to disrupt a small patch of brain for a moment.
The idea that a brain area tied to one sense, such as vision, can come to respond to another, such as touch.
A textile technique that fixes short fibres onto a surface to make a soft, raised, velvety mark.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Re-charge #3 set one long table in an old factory shed in Eindhoven and served soup to anyone who sat down.
A 2016 survey of 2,000 British adults found that people who ate with others more often were happier and had more friends to rely on, but a survey can show a link and cannot prove cause.
A famous lab study found that comfort food brought thoughts of relationships to mind, yet its loneliness experiment failed a three-country repeat, so the soup itself is the weakest part of the story.
start_here.how_sure_note: The link between shared meals and wellbeing comes from one large survey; the comfort food results come from small student studies, and the loneliness result was not confirmed when repeated.

could_be_wrong.point: The survey is correlational. Dunbar writes that people with more friends, or more outgoing people, may simply eat socially more often, and that experiments are needed to confirm cause.
The survey was run as part of a collaboration with The Big Lunch, a campaign that promotes shared meals, which the paper thanks for making the survey possible.
The comfort food and loneliness experiment was repeated in three samples and the overall effect was not confirmed.
The replication team first planned to repeat the soup-eating experiment and switched to the loneliness one, so the soup and relationship words result has no published repeat (AaN search, Nov 2026).
Comfort food may not travel across cultures: only 25 percent of Singaporean students named chicken noodle soup as a comfort food, and the team's Dutch colleagues knew no common Dutch word for it.
All the original soup studies used US undergraduates, and the authors say the effect may be strongest in that age group.
A 2017 review found that "many uncertainties still surround if, when, and for whom" comfort food helps.

In a 2026 German experiment with 283 people, eating more of a food framed as social happened in people with a high need to belong and "disappeared following prior social inclusion," so food may stand in for company mainly when company is missing.
The one experiment found on strangers eating together is a small preprint, mostly women, that measured body-language signs of tension, not loneliness.
No one measured how visitors to Re-charge #3 felt, so whether this table changed anyone's mood is unknown.

The small circle of close friends and family a person can rely on in a crisis, about five people on average.

summary: In a 2026 Michigan study of 321 Black adults aged 55 to 80, people who reported more lifetime racial discrimination had more small white matter changes on brain scans, and more of those changes went with worse memory scores.
Discrimination itself had no overall link with the memory tests in that study, and a larger Mississippi study of 1,583 Black adults found no link between discrimination and dementia.
Ideas such as allostatic load and weathering explain how long-term stress could wear the body down, but the brain evidence is early, mostly from single time points, and mixed.
start_here.how_sure_note: Brain scan links come from small, mostly cross-sectional studies, while the largest dementia study limited to Black adults found no link.

could_be_wrong.point: The only large dementia study limited to Black adults found no link between discrimination and dementia over a median 13.6 years.
could_be_wrong.source: Dark et al. (2023), Alzheimer's and Dementia

could_be_wrong.point: In the Michigan study, discrimination had no total effect on memory tests, and the authors say the indirect path through white matter should be read with caution; competing paths or unmeasured confounding are possible.
In Chicago, the link between discrimination and thinking scores faded once depressive symptoms were counted.
could_be_wrong.source: Barnes et al. (2012), Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society (read in full for the long form)

could_be_wrong.point: In the Health and Retirement Study, unfair treatment that Black adults put down to race went with higher starting thinking scores, and neither measure predicted faster decline; the authors warn this should not be used to claim discrimination is beneficial.
could_be_wrong.source: Ferraro and Zaborenko (2023), PLOS ONE (read in full for the long form)

could_be_wrong.point: In 764 Black adults in Oakland and Richmond, people with more education reported more lifetime discrimination and also had much better thinking scores, so discrimination counts can partly stand in for opportunity.
could_be_wrong.source: Cintron et al. (2023), Alzheimer's and Dementia (read in full for the long form)

could_be_wrong.point: In Manhattan, six of eight tested links between discrimination and brain measures were null; only race-attributed measures showed links.
could_be_wrong.source: Zahodne et al. (2023), Social Science and Medicine (read in full for the long form)

could_be_wrong.point: How allostatic load is scored changes the answer: in national data only some scoring methods linked it to thinking scores after full adjustment.
could_be_wrong.source: Gasik et al. (2026), Psychoneuroendocrinology (read in full for the long form)

could_be_wrong.point: A review of 19 neuroimaging studies found volume results inconsistent and most studies cross-sectional and small, and it warns that adjusting for income and education can remove part of the harm.

The brain's wiring, bundles of nerve fibres that link brain areas.

summary: Feeling that you understand something and being able to explain it are different tests, and the feeling usually scores higher.
In a 2015 study, graduates overrated how well they could explain topics from their own college major, apparently because they did not notice how much they had forgotten.
Claims can also grow as they are retold: when university press releases overstated health findings, the news often did too, though part of that link did not replicate.
start_here.how_sure_note: The rate, explain and rate again drop has been repeated many times, but the expertise result rests on one paper's online studies, and why teaching helps learning is still open.

could_be_wrong.point: The press release and news link for exaggerated advice did not replicate in a 2014 to 2015 sample (OR 0.7, 95% CI 0.3 to 1.5).
The 2014 press release study was observational, so it cannot show that exaggerated releases cause exaggerated news.
The curse of expertise rests on one paper's online studies, with a college major standing in for expertise; the authors say real experts may behave differently.
Some of the classic drop may come from rating twice: simply re-rating with no explanation lowered ratings a little, and explaining one thing lowered ratings for unrelated things.
Why teaching helps learning is unsettled: the review says the retrieval account has neither passed its tests nor been shown to fail them.
Retrieval practice itself, often called one of the best-documented effects in educational psychology, failed to show up in two online studies.
Some researchers question the theory behind the illusion, arguing that understanding may never be stored as a full theory in the head.
Fast early forgetting fits the meta-forgetfulness account, but no study has yet joined the two directly.

summary: Psychologists split time judgments in two: how fast time feels while it passes, and how long a period seems when you look back.
A review of 117 experiments found that a busy mind makes time feel shorter in the moment but longer in memory, and a small daily-life study linked happier moods to time passing faster.
In a 2007 free-fall study, people remembered their fall as longer but could not see any faster during it, which suggests the stretch happens in memory.
start_here.how_sure_note: The load pattern rests on a large review with a small overall effect; the mood, film and free-fall studies were small or gave no sample size.

could_be_wrong.point: Only 7 people judged the length of their fall, with a one-tailed test, and the comparison was an imagined fall before the jump against their own fall recalled after it. The paper also gives the tower height three ways (31 m fall, 46 m and 50 m).

The paper gives two p values for the same in-flight versus ground comparison of digit reading: its text says p = 0.98, its Fig. 2b caption says p = 0.86. Both say no difference; this page uses the text's value if it cites one.
The load effect across 117 experiments was small overall, most experiments were prospective, and none used durations under 3 s, so it says little about weeks or holidays.
The mood study had 27 people and was correlational; the authors say other studies are needed before the gap between feeling time pass and timing it can be confirmed.
The film and waiting room study behind the holiday paradox is reported with no sample size or statistics, in simplified form, in a book chapter.
The attentional models describe behaviour; their authors say the brain basis of attending to time is unclear and that more research is needed to validate them.
A rival account says wanting something, approach motivation, shortens felt time; unpleasant pictures that also grab attention did not shorten it.
In a survey of 4,364 French adults in the 2020 lockdown, high stress did not explain why time slowed; boredom and sadness did. It was a volunteer online survey with 'before' ratings made from memory.

summary: A 2016 meta-analysis pooled 138 randomized studies in which people were prompted to track their progress toward a goal, or not.
Tracking rose sharply, and goal attainment improved by a small-to-medium amount, more so when progress was written down or shared.
The overall result is solid, but almost all the studies were about health goals, and a bias check suggests the true effect may be smaller.

annotations.note: Pools 138 randomized studies: prompts to monitor progress raised monitoring a lot (d+ = 1.98) and goal attainment by a small-to-medium amount (d+ = 0.40), with larger effects when progress was recorded or shared. Nearly all studies were about health goals, a trim and fill bias check lowered the attainment effect to 0.19, and better-quality studies tended to show smaller effects. Read in full in the authors' accepted manuscript (White Rose, 124 pages).
annotations.funding: The research was supported by a grant from the European Research Council (ERC-2011-StG-280515) to Thomas Webb (author note, accepted manuscript).
annotations.conflicts: not re-checked (the accepted manuscript has no conflicts statement; the APA copy of record was not opened)

could_be_wrong.point: Egger's test found an uneven spread of results, a sign of publication bias; a trim and fill correction lowered the attainment effect from 0.40 to 0.19. The authors judge the bias modest and note this method can underestimate effects when results vary a lot.
could_be_wrong.source: Harkin et al. (2016), Results, Tests for Potential Bias, p. 25

could_be_wrong.point: Only one included study was about a goal unrelated to health, so the result may not carry over to work, study or money goals.
could_be_wrong.source: Harkin et al. (2016), Discussion, The Role of Methodological Factors

could_be_wrong.point: The public monitoring figure (d+ = 0.55) rests on only 3 studies with 214 people, and its confidence interval runs from -0.16 to 1.26, so it is uncertain.
Effects were smaller in better-quality studies, for example when participants and experimenters were blind to condition, which suggests expectations may inflate some results.
could_be_wrong.source: Harkin et al. (2016), Results and Discussion

could_be_wrong.point: The mediation result comes from 21 studies analysed at the study level, and the moderator tests were not corrected for running many tests. Some moderators, such as recording and reporting, may overlap.
Many control groups were assumed to do no monitoring at all because the studies did not measure it, which the authors call possibly suboptimal; this mainly affects the very large monitoring effect.

glossary.plain: A study that combines the results of many earlier studies to estimate an overall effect.
A study in which chance decides who gets the intervention, so differences between groups are more likely caused by the intervention.
Checking how you are doing compared with what you want to achieve, such as counting steps or noting study hours.
How far apart two groups ended up, measured in standard deviations; 0.2 is usually called small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large.
A test of whether an intervention works through a middle step, here whether prompts helped because people monitored more.
A feature of the studies, such as writing progress down, that changes how large the effect is.
The tendency for studies with positive results to be published more often, which can make an effect look larger than it is.
How much the results of the pooled studies differ from one another.

summary: RN Collins's essay remembers a great-aunt whose garden was her medicine cabinet, and this post asks what researchers have recorded about home herbs in the Caribbean.
In one student survey at eight clinics in St. Mary Parish, Jamaica, 43 of 68 adults had used herbs as medicine in the past year, and only 13 of those 43 said their provider knew.
In a 2004 survey of 192 hospital doctors in Trinidad, most thought herbs were beneficial, yet only 29 could name one known herb-drug interaction; neither survey tests whether any remedy works.
start_here.how_sure_note: The counts come straight from two published surveys, but each is a single snapshot of one place, chosen by convenience or quota rather than at random.

could_be_wrong.point: The Jamaica survey reached 68 of 278 people invited (24.5%) at clinics in one parish over two weeks, so the people who agreed may differ from those who did not. The author lists small sample, one parish and recall bias as limits.
