could_be_wrong.conflicts: not re-checked (Nov 20 honest-client re-read: the Wright State CORE Scholar PDF returned HTTP 403)

could_be_wrong.point: In the same survey every herb user ticked aloe vera, bissy and castor nut, a result the report does not explain. It differs from a larger Jamaican survey the report cites, which the author puts down to sample size or location.
could_be_wrong.funding: not re-checked (Nov 20 honest-client re-read: the Wright State CORE Scholar PDF returned HTTP 403)
could_be_wrong.conflicts: not re-checked (Nov 20 honest-client re-read: the Wright State CORE Scholar PDF returned HTTP 403)

could_be_wrong.point: The Trinidad doctors were chosen by quota and convenience, not at random, and the authors warn of interviewer bias and say the sample may not be truly representative; private-practice doctors were left out.

Knowledge was scored with the team's own new open-ended questions, so a low score may partly reflect a hard test; the authors note that open questions tax respondents and answers may be distorted in coding.

The doctor survey is from 2004. A 2019 survey of 288 health workers in western Jamaica found a similar gap (78.4% said they knew little), but it used different questions in a different place, so the numbers cannot be compared directly.

The Trinidad authors describe a progressive loss of plant knowledge between generations, but a comparison of Dominican plant users found people in New York City named slightly more plants than people still in the Dominican Republic.

Surveys record belief and behaviour. A later Trinidad team found most herb users thought their remedies worked and called for randomized trials, noting that most native Caribbean herbs had not been well studied.

A worldwide meta-analysis of 14 studies found that about one in three people (33%) told their doctor about complementary medicine use, and the studies varied so widely that any single disclosure figure, including the Jamaica one, is uncertain.

glossary.plain: A plant or plant part, often from a yard or market, prepared at home to treat or prevent illness.
A change in how a medicine works, or in its side effects, caused by taking an herb at the same time.
A reason, such as a health condition or another medicine, not to use a particular treatment.
A study that asks a group of people questions at one point in time, so it shows patterns but not causes.
People chosen because they were easy to reach, such as patients leaving a clinic, rather than at random.
Choosing a set number of people from each group, such as each hospital, without picking them at random.
The share of people invited to a survey who agreed to take part.
Error that creeps in when people misremember what they did in the past.
A pressed plant sample kept in a herbarium so that anyone can later check which species a name referred to.
The study of how people in a culture know, name and use plants.

summary: Your nose reads smells with a large family of odorant receptors, found by Richard Axel and Linda Buck in 1991 and honoured with the 2004 Nobel Prize.
Each smell-sensing cell carries one receptor type, and each odour switches on a pattern of receptors that works like letters spelling words.
In 2023 a UCSF team imaged one human receptor holding a Swiss cheese molecule; that is one receptor of about 400, and its switch-on model is still speculative.
start_here.how_sure_note: The receptor family and its wiring rules are decades old and Nobel-recognised; the 2023 structure is solid for one receptor, while counts of receptors and smells still vary by source.

summary: In one large school trial in Turkey, students who practiced math with a plain GPT-4 chat scored higher during practice and 17% lower on a later exam without AI.
A tutor set up to give hints instead of answers removed most of that drop, but it did not raise exam scores above the group that never had AI.
Older memory research shows why: pulling an answer from your own memory builds learning, and that link to AI is our inference, since the 2008 study did not test AI.
start_here.how_sure_note: One large, preregistered randomized trial, but at one school, in one subject, over a few weeks; other trials find gains when the tool is built to teach.

annotations.note: A randomized trial in about fifty math classes at one high school in Turkey, fall 2023. A plain GPT-4 chat raised practice grades and lowered scores on the exam without AI; a hint tutor prevented the drop but gave no gain. Limits the authors name: one school, one subject, short-term results, tools still new to students. The article carries a 2025 correction (e2518204122).

annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no competing interest.

annotations.note: College students learned 40 Swahili-English word pairs. A week later, those who kept being tested recalled about 80%, and those who only kept studying recalled 36% and 33%; every group predicted about half. A lab study of word pairs, so it says nothing directly about AI.
annotations.funding: A Collaborative Activity Grant of the James S. McDonnell Foundation to the second author (note 21, author copy read Nov 20, 2026).
annotations.conflicts: no conflict statement in the author copy read Nov 20, 2026

could_be_wrong.point: The trial ran at one school, in one subject, over a few weeks in fall 2023, and measured short-term learning only, as the authors themselves note.
Copying is the authors' inference from error patterns; the logs show students asking for answers, not what they wrote down.
In two preregistered lab experiments with 176 university students learning Python, a ChatGPT window made no clear difference to final test scores overall.
At Middlebury, students allowed ordinary ChatGPT scored 7.2 points higher on an unaided test and 3.9 points higher a week later, so a plain chatbot does not always lower learning.
Across 14 other randomized studies that tested students without AI, results ran from harm to large gains, with an average modest gain of 0.19 standard deviations.
In three online experiments, people tested right after a short session solved fewer problems once AI was removed, but the study cannot say whether the gap lasts.
After adjusting for publication bias, the large learning effect in a now-retracted meta-analysis fell to 0.37 and the evidence became 'anecdotal'.
Many pooled AI studies scored work done with the tool in hand, which measures a person plus a machine, not what the person learned.
The 2008 memory study did not test AI; tying its result to chatbots is an inference.

A common unit that lets researchers compare how big a result is across studies that used different tests.
A study of studies that pools the results of many experiments into one estimate.
The tendency for studies with big positive results to get published more often than studies that found nothing.

summary: Automation bias is leaning on a computer's advice and checking less carefully.
In a 2017 prescribing simulation, 120 medical students missed far fewer errors when alerts were right and far more when alerts were wrong, and false alarms led many to drop safe medicines.
So when people almost never override a system, that agreement may reflect trust in the machine as much as the machine being right.
start_here.how_sure_note: The effects in this one simulation were large and clear, and reviews find the same bias across many studies, but it used students with no real patients, so real-world rates are unknown.

annotations.note: Macquarie University experiment in which 120 medical students in their final two years prescribed for nine made-up patients with correct, incorrect or no alerts. Correct alerts cut missed errors sharply, wrong alerts raised them, and false alarms led many to drop safe medicines; task complexity and interruptions made no difference. Limits: simulated with no consequences, students rather than practising doctors, and the authors say it cannot give real clinical rates.
annotations.funding: This research was supported by a Doctoral Scholarship for David Lyell provided by the HCF Research Foundation.
annotations.conflicts: The authors have no competing interests to declare.

could_be_wrong.point: The authors stress that the task was simulated and the errors had no consequence, so the experiment cannot show how often automation bias happens in real clinics; the errors on offer may also differ from those in practice.
No direct or failed replication of the prescribing experiment was found as of Nov 2026, so its exact sizes rest on one study.
could_be_wrong.source: Long-form research log search (Europe PMC, OpenAlex), checked against Lyell et al. (2017)

could_be_wrong.point: In real hospitals the bigger problem has often been the opposite: across 17 papers, drug safety alerts were overridden in 49 to 96 percent of cases, and the authors note that overriding may often be justified.
could_be_wrong.source: van der Sijs et al. (2006), JAMIA 13(2): 138-147
could_be_wrong.funding: not re-checked (Nov 20 honest-client re-read: Europe PMC full text HTTP 500, NCBI efetch gives no body because the publisher does not allow full-text download)
could_be_wrong.conflicts: not re-checked (Nov 20 honest-client re-read: Europe PMC full text HTTP 500, NCBI efetch gives no body because the publisher does not allow full-text download)

could_be_wrong.point: A systematic review of 40 studies found automation bias in single tasks only when checking the advice took medium or more effort, which differs from the prescribing study's finding that complexity made no difference.
could_be_wrong.funding: not re-checked (Nov 20 honest-client re-read: Europe PMC full text HTTP 500, NCBI efetch gives no body because the publisher does not allow full-text download)
could_be_wrong.conflicts: not re-checked (Nov 20 honest-client re-read: Europe PMC full text HTTP 500, NCBI efetch gives no body because the publisher does not allow full-text download)

could_be_wrong.point: Agreeing with a machine is often right when it is better: in an Australian breast screening study, a single reader leaning toward an AI that outperformed them improved overall results.

A low override rate is open to several readings; one 2026 expert comment says it may reflect good performance as well as automation bias, time pressure or weak authority to disagree. This is opinion, not new data.
could_be_wrong.source: van de Sande, Economou-Zavlanos and van Genderen (2026), npj Digital Medicine 9: 569

listen_watch.speaker: Enrico Coiera and Clair Sullivan, with host Mic Cavazzini
listen_watch.credentials: Coiera is Professor of Medical Informatics and leads the Centre for Health Informatics at Macquarie University; Sullivan is an endocrinologist and director of the Queensland Digital Health Centre, University of Queensland (episode credits)
listen_watch.conflicts: none stated in the episode; Coiera is a co-author of Lyell et al. (2017), the study this post cites, and the podcast is produced by the Royal Australasian College of Physicians

glossary.plain: The habit of leaning on a computer's advice and checking less carefully for oneself.
Software that gives clinicians alerts or suggestions while they make decisions, such as when prescribing.
Choosing to go ahead against an alert's warning, usually after giving a reason.
Missing a real mistake that should have been caught.
Making a change that was not needed because of wrong advice, such as dropping a safe medicine.
A warning that fires when nothing is actually wrong.
A missing warning when something really is wrong.
The simple difference between two percentages, so 46 percent to 79 percent is a rise of 33 percentage points.
Tuning out warnings because so many of them fire, many of which do not matter.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Line Rumhult showed soft connected objects that pair two people and answer the hand through weight, balance, texture and warmth.
Lab studies find that slow stroking feels better than fast, including touch replayed by a device, and that a slow nerve pathway in hairy skin fires most to gentle strokes at skin temperature.
No study has tested these pieces, weight or balance as a channel, or a palm holding an object, so what visitors felt is unknown.
start_here.how_sure_note: The nerve and speed findings come from small lab studies on the forearm, and the tests of touch sent through devices are few, small and mixed.

could_be_wrong.point: C-tactile fibres have rarely, if ever, been recorded in palm skin, yet slow stroking on the palm was also rated more pleasant than fast, and ratings did not separate palm from forearm, so pleasant touch on a held object may not run through C-tactiles.
When the faster, myelinated touch fibres were briefly blocked, the pleasantness of both stroking and pressure nearly vanished, which suggests pleasant touch depends on more than one kind of fibre.
A 2015 review found that the mediated touch field "generally lacks serious validation studies" and that touch through a device from a stranger can cause discomfort.
In a lab test with a fake partner, a touch device gave no benefit for recovery from a sad film, amusement or trust.
Two double-blind replications of the warm cup and heat pack studies, with 128 and 177 people, found effects near zero, so warmth alone is unlikely to make people kinder.

In a meta-analysis of touch interventions, touch from objects or robots helped mental health less than human touch (0.34 against 0.58), results were more variable, and small studies reported larger effects.
Couples apart for two weeks with squeeze bracelets noticed each other more, but felt only slightly closer and no less longing, and the study had no control group.
The same touch can feel welcome or unwelcome depending on expectation and context, so a device cannot fix what a touch means.

glossary.plain: Touch sent between people through a device, such as a sleeve, band or object, instead of skin on skin.
A machine built to carry emotion through touch, for example by vibration, pressure or warmth.
Thin, slow nerve fibres in hairy skin that respond best to gentle, slow stroking.
A fatty coating on many nerve fibres that makes their signals travel faster.
Hairy skin covers most of the body, such as the forearm; glabrous skin is the hairless skin of the palms and soles.
A method in which a fine electrode is placed through the skin into a nerve to record signals from a single fibre.
A small motor, like the part that moves a loudspeaker, used to press on the skin in touch devices.
Repeating a study, often with more people, to see whether the original result holds.
Everyday objects fitted with sensors and connections so they can send and receive data.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Catharina Hospital's care pathway designers were listed to lead a session on planning care routes that link the hospital, GPs and other care groups in the Eindhoven region.
A 2025 Cochrane review of 58 studies found that structured care pathways inside hospitals likely cut complications, 10% against 17%, and shorten stays by about a day.
Effects on deaths, readmissions and costs were uncertain, and no trial has yet tested a whole regional route designed with a method like Metro Mapping.
start_here.how_sure_note: The hospital findings carry moderate certainty in a large review with high risk of bias, while the regional, co-designed routes the session was about are still untested.

could_be_wrong.point: Metro Mapping has no published outcome data yet, and two authors of the methods paper sit on the foundation's board while a third runs a studio that consults on the method.

The one registered evaluation of Metro Mapping, about 500 cancer patients before and after the method, still showed recruiting with no results posted on Nov 20, 2026, and a before-and-after design cannot rule out other changes.
An umbrella review of 50 reviews found that integrated care for long-term illness rarely showed clearly positive effects; about half the reviews found a gain on at least one hospital measure.
A review of 71 sources argues that integrated care is a set of locally shaped practices, so universal answers about whether it works are unlikely.
A meta-analysis of 119 studies of integrated care involving primary care found small gains in access and continuity, with small, non-significant effects on health, deaths and admissions.
The largest randomized test of experience-based co-design found no gain in recovery scores for 287 people with severe mental illness, 84.7 against 86.5.

A Dutch transitional care trial for frail heart patients did not help: readmission or death was 54.2% with the programme and 47.7% with usual care, and the planned handover happened for only 37% of patients.

summary: Lab studies show that stress just before or during recall makes memory a little worse, and that a short ice-water stressor can make some people slower to switch rules.
A 2013 study found that money worries lowered reasoning scores for people with less money, at a mall and in Indian sugarcane farmers before harvest.
Later repeats of scarcity studies were mixed, and a 2010 US law asks federal agencies to write key notices plainly.
start_here.how_sure_note: The memory meta-analysis is large and consistent, while the scarcity findings have failed several large repeats and every study used lab tasks, not real notices.

could_be_wrong.point: A published comment argued the mall result faded when income was treated as a continuous number; the authors replied that pooling three experiments kept the effect. The comment has no open copy, so it is known here only through the reply.
A 2015 commentary noted that lab puzzles differ from daily life and that people under money strain may focus harder on money tasks.

Only 4 of the 18 originally significant scarcity studies replicated in the 2021 audit, while the original authors say the audit's repeat of Mani et al. skipped one of two main measures and had baseline scores near chance.

could_be_wrong.point: A 2025 registered report of 4,280 adults found that scarcity cues did not lower poorer people's attention more than richer people's.
Six preregistered field trials with about one million California households found that friendlier or more personal EITC letters raised clicks but did not raise filing or claiming.
Across 126 nudge-unit trials with 23 million people, letters and reminders raised take-up by 1.4 percentage points on average, far below the 8.7 points in published academic papers.
No published trial as of November 2026 has tested a real court notice or benefits portal built on the essay's five conditions; the step from lab findings to legal design is an inference.

glossary.plain: A short burst of stress from one event, such as a test or a frightening call, that fades once the event is over.
A hormone the body releases under stress that affects energy, alertness and memory over the following minutes to hours.
A study that pools the results of many earlier studies to estimate an overall effect.
Encoding is taking in new information to store it, and retrieval is pulling a stored memory back out.
A lab stressor in which a person holds a hand in ice water for a few minutes.
Sticking with an old rule after the rule has changed, a common measure of flexible thinking on card-sorting tasks.
A reasoning test where people pick the missing piece that completes a visual pattern.
The idea that worry about not having enough money or time takes up mental room needed for other tasks.
Running a study again, often with more people, to see whether the original result holds.
A study whose plan a journal accepts before the data are collected, so the result is published either way.

summary: Lightwall, by Rita Sus and Zach Rattner of Emit Light, was shown at Dutch Design Week 2026: prisms and motorised beam splitters moved light over hand-cut paper, steered by locally run AI as visitors moved.
Lab and museum studies suggest why a work that answers you can feel like your doing, why changes are easy to miss even in a real museum, and why a machine that responds can feel social.
No study has tested Lightwall or any light work like it, so these studies suggest what to look for and say nothing yet about this wall itself.
start_here.how_sure_note: The science comes from small lab studies and one museum study that each tested something other than a responsive artwork.

summary: RELISH, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026, is a set of wearable glass and ceramic pieces for eating that its designer made to change gestures such as holding, dipping and licking.
Small lab and dining studies show that the weight, feel and material of a spoon, fork or cup can shift how people rate the same food, by small amounts.
The shifts go up or down depending on what people expect, no study has repeated the key tests with the same methods, and no one has tested RELISH itself.
start_here.how_sure_note: A handful of small studies, some just past the usual line for chance, with mixed and unreplicated results.

could_be_wrong.point: The yoghurt results came from 35 people who each tried every spoon, and both effects were just past the usual line for chance (p = .046 and .043).

The lab's own 2013 review says Harrar and Spence reported results similar to a heavier-spoon-liked-more study, while the published paper found the lighter plastic spoon favoured; the review also says these effects likely have a number of different explanations.
could_be_wrong.source: Spence, Hobkinson, Gallace and Piqueras-Fiszman (2013), Flavour

could_be_wrong.point: In a 2013 radio interview, Spence described the yoghurt result as about 15 to 16 percent tastier and more expensive with a silver spoon than a plastic or lighter one, which does not match the direction the paper reports for its plastic spoons.
At the hotel lunch, diners chose their own seats, shared tables, and the heavy-cutlery tables also got a different starter layout and dessert plate, so weight was one of several changes.
At a festival, 401 visitors drank from cups with or without a hidden 20 g weight, and weight had no overall effect on liking or taste; it explained 0.24 percent of the variation.
A rough plate made biscuits seem crunchier and saltier when people tried both plates, but the authors' footnote reports no transference when each person saw only one plate (75 people).
could_be_wrong.source: Biggs, Juravle and Spence (2016), Food Quality and Preference, accepted manuscript

summary: In a 2016 lab study, 45 healthy adults faced uncertain odds of a mild electric shock, and their stress ratings, pupil size and skin sweat rose and fell with how uncertain things were.
Public health research links a strong sense of coherence, the feeling that life is understandable and predictable, with better reported health, though these are associations, not proof of cause.
RN's Polymath essay asks what an official notice owes its reader; no study has yet measured what a confusing notice does to the body of the person reading it.
start_here.how_sure_note: The stress finding comes from one small lab study of short-term stress, and the sense of coherence work is correlational; the step from lab to letter is untested.

could_be_wrong.point: The stress study was short-term and small: 45 young, healthy volunteers and brief shocks in one session. The authors write that they do not claim their measures are exhaustive or that chronic stress behaves the same way.

No study yet measures stress in response to a real official notice. A review of 119 administrative burden studies found that most communication trials measure take-up and only theorize that burden is the reason.

Easing paperwork helped only a little. When Denmark suspended benefit-system demands in 2020, stress and lost autonomy fell by small amounts, stigma did not reliably change, and the authors suggest much of the stress comes from money and an uncertain future.

Clearer writing has a thin evidence base. A systematic review of plain-language summaries found no empirical support for most of the criteria in writing guidelines, and most studies used students or highly educated readers.

Better letters do not always change behavior. Six preregistered California experiments with about a million low-income households found no evidence that mailed and texted nudges raised tax-credit claims.
The sense of coherence findings are associations. The 2006 systematic review warns that the sense of coherence does not alone explain overall health.

Uncertainty is not always unpleasant. A review of uncertainty and emotion notes that people seek suspense in novels and games, and that the stakes and a person's tolerance for not knowing shape how it feels.

could_be_wrong.point: The pooled onset data are heterogeneous, with broad confidence intervals and little data from many countries.
Asking adults to remember past problems misses many of them: a birth cohort assessed again and again found about double the lifetime rate that recall surveys report.
Across 24 countries, the most common reason for not seeking care was not seeing a need; among people who did see a need, wanting to handle it alone led, and stigma was named by 7.7%.
In a national Australian survey of teenagers with unmet need, self-reliance was the most named barrier, at 55.1%, and parents and teenagers often disagreed about whether needs were met.
In a survey of 13,984 first-year students in 8 countries, 56.4% said they would handle a problem alone, so stigma may not be the main barrier for every group.
The studies in the 2010 review were mostly small and qualitative, report only perceived barriers, and studied facilitators in just three cases.
Most school help-seeking programmes measured intentions over short follow-ups, and two large school trials found no effect on help-seeking.
A large school mindfulness trial found no lower risk of depression than usual teaching after two years.
Awareness efforts may lead some people to read milder distress as a mental health problem, a hypothesis its authors say still needs testing.
A rapid review found only five studies of AI mental health apps for young people, two of them randomised, so the room's AI environment rests on thin evidence.

summary: CalmReef, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026 by the Kraków studio NIOH NIOH, is a set of soft panels with sound, light, scent and touch, meant to help an overloaded brain rest.
Studies of sensory rooms on psychiatric wards mostly find people feel calmer right after using one, but harder outcomes such as seclusion rates have not clearly changed.
Nature sounds helped stress recovery in one small lab study and not in a larger one, and no study has tested CalmReef itself.
start_here.how_sure_note: The ward evidence is mostly open, non-randomised before-and-after studies, the sound evidence is mixed, and the product has no published test.

could_be_wrong.point: Across 18 studies of sensory rooms on adult wards, distress fell in all 7 that measured it, but effects on seclusion, restraint and assault were mixed, and the review rated the studies at serious risk of bias.
Some people felt worse: the same review reports minorities who had more distress after a sensory room, with boredom, anxiety or flashbacks.
A Cochrane review of Snoezelen rooms in dementia found two trials with 246 people: one programme showed no effects, and the other gave small gains during sessions that faded.
Across 62 Snoezelen studies, mean quality was 1.8 of 5, only 1 of 8 that checked found lasting effects, and the rooms were often no better than other activities.

In a quasi-randomised trial of 60 psychiatric patients, a physical calm room and a virtual reality version did about equally well; the study ended early and had too few people to spot small differences, and one author founded the company that made the app.
A review of 10 studies of multisensory environments in autism found the evidence insufficient, with small samples and no tracking of harms.
Attention restoration from nature has small, uneven support: in a 31-study review, 3 of 13 pooled attention results favoured nature and one favoured the built setting.
In a review of 25 articles on co-design with young people, 5 reported a process evaluation and none evaluated the impact of co-design.

summary: Menthol feels cold because it switches on TRPM8, a cold sensor on nerve cells, at temperatures where that sensor would normally stay mostly quiet.
Two labs found TRPM8 independently in 2002, and mice bred without it lose much of their sense of mild cold; that work shared the 2021 Nobel Prize.
The core finding is strong, but most of the evidence comes from cells and mice, and an eye drop that switches TRPM8 on raises tear flow in people.
start_here.how_sure_note: Two independent discoveries, knockout mice from several labs and detailed protein structures agree; the evidence in people is thinner.

could_be_wrong.point: The two 2002 discovery papers have no legal open copy, so the discovery is described here only through the Nobel committee's account and later reviews.
Labs report different starting points for TRPM8, from about 28°C to 25°C, depending on species, cells and methods, so a single threshold number is not settled.
Mice without TRPM8 were never completely blind to cold: they still avoided 10°C and 5°C plates, and some of their nerve cells still answered cold.
Other molecules take over as cold turns painful: mice lacking the sodium channel NaV1.8 never jumped off a minus 5°C plate.
Human evidence is thin: in 38 healthy men, a TRPM8 gene variant shifted the cold pain threshold, but the ice-water test showed no significant difference.
The link between a TRPM8 variant and higher migraine rates in people of European descent is a hypothesis: the country-level comparison was not statistically significant.
A meta-analysis of six smaller studies, mostly from Asia, found an inconsistent pattern for the same variant and warned that small studies may exaggerate effects.
The TRPM8 eye drop raised tear production, but by three months symptom scores did not differ from vehicle drops in either trial.
The cornea findings on osmolality and blinking come from mice, and how much they explain dry eye in people is unknown.

summary: Navigating Stress, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026, is a physical game in which players build their stress as a landscape of objects and named places.
Lab studies link putting a feeling into words with less amygdala activity, and in one study older adults rated negative pictures as less unpleasant when they named their feelings.
Other studies find naming can get in the way of reframing or fade within a day or two, and no study has tested this game.
start_here.how_sure_note: The brain findings point one way in lab tasks, while studies of how people feel are split, and nothing has tested a game like this.

could_be_wrong.point: Naming emotions before reframing left people feeling worse than reframing alone, and naming alone gave no measurable change.
A replication with 226 people found the same blunting, and any effects were gone one to two days later.
In 35 adults in Japan, labeling before reframing made the reframing less effective.
Labeling eased distress for intense pictures and raised it for mild ones; the authors say it should be used with caution in low-intensity situations.
Labeling one's own emotion on purpose raised brain responses and arousal ratings, which runs counter to the idea that labeling always calms.
In 61 students, choosing an emotion from a list lowered skin conductance while naming it in their own words did not, which matters for a game where players use their own words.
A preprint with Dutch speakers found no lasting labeling effect in ratings or brainwaves about 15 minutes later; it is not yet peer reviewed.
In the four-study series behind the lab task, the drop in distress came from the most upsetting pictures, and the authors call their control condition imperfect.
A meta-analysis of 386 imaging studies found emotion words went with less amygdala activity less often, but none of those studies measured regulation directly.
Pooled trials of digital games for young people found almost no effect on anxiety, and the main games review excluded non-digital games, so a tabletop stress game is untested.
could_be_wrong.source: Townsend et al. (2022); Lau et al. (2016)

summary: The Ripple, a wall of rippled lamps by Studio Koen Steger and Atelier Hendriksen, was shown at Dutch Design Week 2026 with the hope that visitors would slow down.
In one small lab study, 30 minutes of dim blue light slightly lowered slower brainwave bands, and in a 33-person video study still water was rated more restorative than moving water.
Both studies are small, neither tested The Ripple, and the studio's own claim that its 2015 light dome made alpha waves was never measured.
start_here.how_sure_note: The lab effects are small, near the usual cut-off for chance, and not yet repeated; no study has measured anyone in front of The Ripple.

could_be_wrong.point: The blue light effects were under one unit, with p values of .045 and .050, in men only, under steady light; the authors say they require replication.
The still water result comes from 33 students watching screens of one kind of garden, and visual appeal was judged from eye tracking, not a rating.
In a virtual reality study of 64 young adults, a medium scene got the best restoration ratings and brainwaves showed no significant difference between lake, mixed and waterfall scenes.
A review of 26 nature video trials found mostly short-term gains that faded; in one three-week study mood gains were gone two weeks later, and water versus green scenes gave mixed results.
A meta-analysis of 33 brain-recording nature studies rated 29 as weak in method, found large differences between studies and signs that small studies report bigger effects.
A null result: an error-checking brain signal (the ERN) did not differ after 10 minutes of nature or city photos in 60 adults.
Critics argue that soft fascination is vague, has never been cleanly measured, and that most studies tire everyone first and never test rested people.

A 2025 critique calls soft fascination circular and notes that the city comparison scenes are often unpleasant, so feeling better may just mean leaving a bad place; an argument without new data, not yet peer reviewed.
A sleep review reports that in an older Ganzfeld study the EEG showed no drop in alertness, so a dome of even light may keep people closer to waking than to sleep onset.
No brain recording from Hypnagogia and no study of The Ripple has been published; the alpha wave line is the studio's suspicion.

summary: CO2Balance, a hemp board meeting set shown at Dutch Design Week 2026, is called carbon-negative by its makers, and no carbon numbers for it have been published.
Studies estimate that each kilogram of dry hemp took about 1.3 to 1.8 kilograms of CO2 from the air, and that carbon stays stored only while the product lasts.
Making plant boards still emits, and the main counting standards report stored carbon separately, so the label cannot be checked yet.
start_here.how_sure_note: The plant chemistry and the factory-gate studies agree, but none of them tested this furniture, and the makers have not published their own numbers.

could_be_wrong.point: Neither study on the slides tested this furniture or its board: Liu modelled hemp textiles, and Seile car-part composites.
could_be_wrong.source: Liu et al. (2023); Seile et al. (2022)

could_be_wrong.point: Uptake factors differ between studies, from 1.29 to 1.84 kg CO2 per kg, and in one Serbian study the choice alone moved the footprint by 14%.
Counting only to the factory gate can make a component look carbon-negative when its full-life impact is not, the review warns, and results for single components varied by 35 to 200% across methods.
The same fibreboard came out at minus 667.75 under PAS 2050 and plus 816.92 under ISO 14067, so the rulebook can flip the sign.
Temporary storage cools the climate only while the carbon stays stored, and shortcuts that turn tonne-years into permanent credits misstate the benefit.
The other direction: counting with timing can show value the standard 100-year count misses, so a timeless count can also understate storage.
could_be_wrong.source: Van Roijen et al. (2025); Breton et al. (2018)

could_be_wrong.point: A 2026 review of 43 studies found plant-fibre composites usually lower on climate and fossil use but higher on eutrophication, land use and water, with few studies followed to the grave.
No life-cycle assessment, EPD or carbon number for Strumber or CO2Balance was found, and no usability results were published, as of Nov 13, 2026.

summary: Many growers believe a light leak during the dark period turns female cannabis plants hermaphroditic.
Female plants do sometimes grow male flower parts, and hormone blockers and short days can push this on purpose.
The only direct test of night leaks, a 2024 student study of 403 plants, found no meaningful link, and its author says the light was too dim to tell. Verdict: unproven.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Isabel van de Stadt showed handmade kinetic light sculptures, one inspired by the zoetrope, an early moving-image toy.
When two lights blink in turn, people see one light move; scientists call this apparent motion, and brain scans show the visual cortex responding along the path between the lights.
The brain scan study had only 8 people and how the brain builds the motion is still debated, while a 2015 study of 10 people found edges can reveal flicker above 500 Hz.
start_here.how_sure_note: Apparent motion itself is a century-old, reliable effect; the brain findings come from small studies and their mechanism is still argued.

could_be_wrong.point: The 2005 fMRI study had 8 people in total, 5 or 6 per experiment, and the authors leave the mechanism open.
An earlier study with rings found no V1 activity along the path, as the 2005 paper itself reports.
could_be_wrong.source: Muckli et al. (2005), reporting Liu et al. (2004)

could_be_wrong.point: In 9 people, V1 activity followed a curved path set by a faint cue, and the authors write there is no one-to-one correspondence between the percept and the retinotopic activity.
EEG and fMRI timing put the motion area ahead of V1, so the effect cannot be pinned on V1 alone.
In two monkeys, a suppressive wave spread from the second spot back toward the first, which sits badly with simple filling in of the path.
In ferrets, motion feedback and cortical waves lined up in time, but the authors call their model speculative and say the data give no evidence of causal relations.
The 500 Hz flicker result comes from 10 people, two of them authors, and the eye-movement explanation was only partly tested.
Small simulated networks reproduce colour phi effects, which suggests it may be nothing more than ordinary brain dynamics.

safety.note: This post describes flickering and blinking light. In photosensitive epilepsy, seizures can be triggered by flashing or flickering light, most often at 3 to 30 flashes per second, and it affects about 3% of people with epilepsy (Epilepsy Society, page updated Nov 10, 2026: epilepsysociety.org.uk/understanding-epilepsy/photosensitive-epilepsy). The charity notes that covering one eye completely can reduce the effect. Education, not medical advice.

summary: Terpenes are a big family of plant smell molecules, and many kitchen plants make some of the same ones as cannabis.
Beta-caryophyllene is in black pepper, myrcene and humulene are in hops, and linalool is in lavender, according to a 2025 review.
A 2026 study found 125 terpenes in 26 Brazilian seasonings and ranked which ones do most for their smell.
start_here.how_sure_note: The seasoning counts come from one careful lab study; which plants carry which terpene comes mostly from a review, and no study here asked people to compare the smells.

claims.claim: Black pepper and cannabis both make beta-caryophyllene, a spicy, peppery terpene that is high in black pepper and cloves.
Terpenes are a big family of plant smell molecules.
Myrcene, one of cannabis's most abundant terpenes, is also in hops, lemongrass and mangoes.
Linalool is found in lavender.
Humulene turns up in hops, sage and ginseng.
A 2026 study found 125 terpenes in 26 Brazilian seasonings.
claims.study: one lab study, GC x GC-MS of 26 seasonings

claims.claim: Eucalyptol, linalool, pulegone and geraniol did the most for their aroma.
claims.where: Abstract; Results, odor activity values (eucalyptol above 1,800; linalool 151.44; pulegone 144.81; geraniol 143.60)
claims.study: one lab study; odor activity values for 48 compounds

annotations.source: Alfieri et al. 2025
annotations.note: A narrative review of cannabis terpenes and chronic pain. In passing it names plants that carry each terpene (pepper and cloves, hops, lemongrass, mango, lavender, sage, ginseng). Limits: those plant examples are background in a pain review, not measured here, and the review's health claims are not used in this post. CC BY, open in PMC12389225.
annotations.funding: This research received no external funding.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

annotations.source: Oliveira et al. 2026
annotations.note: Chemists at the Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais analysed 26 traditional Brazilian seasonings, identified 125 terpenes in five classes and computed odor activity values for 48. Eucalyptol was far ahead (above 1,800), then beta-ocimene, linalool, pulegone and geraniol. Limits: only 13 terpenes were fully quantified with standards; the rest were estimated. CC BY-NC-ND, quoted and charted only.
annotations.funding: not stated (no funding statement in the full text)
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests.

could_be_wrong.point: Which plants carry which terpene (cloves, lemongrass, mango, lavender, sage, ginseng) rests here on a review about pain, not on measurements; the long form replaced these with primary studies and cut the examples it could not check.

Sharing a molecule is not sharing a smell. No study found here asked people to compare cannabis with black pepper or herbs, and the seasoning study describes beta-caryophyllene's note as woody rather than peppery.
The aroma ranking has a second place the post leaves out: beta-ocimene (OAV 395) came after eucalyptol and ahead of linalool, pulegone and geraniol.

Most of the 125 terpenes were identified by matching spectra, and only 13 were fully measured against standards; the others were estimated with stand-in calibrants. Odor activity values also do not capture how smells mask or boost each other.

Amounts vary widely by plant part and variety. In Indonesian black pepper, beta-caryophyllene was about half of leaf oil but only 13 percent of stem oil, and hop cultivars differed widely in their terpene amounts.
could_be_wrong.source: Nurjanah et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2023 (read in full for the long form; not in set.json)

glossary.plain: A member of a large family of plant molecules built from five-carbon units; many give plants their smell.
A small terpene with 10 carbons, such as linalool, myrcene or eucalyptol.
A terpene with 15 carbons, such as beta-caryophyllene or humulene.
A sesquiterpene found in black pepper, cloves, hops and cannabis.
A monoterpene found in hops and one of the most common terpenes in cannabis.
A flowery-smelling monoterpene found in lavender.
A sesquiterpene found in hops and cannabis, often alongside beta-caryophyllene.
A fresh, camphor-like monoterpene that led the smell ranking in the seasoning study.
A compound's amount divided by the lowest amount people can smell; above 1 means it likely adds to the smell.
The smallest amount of a substance that people can detect by smell.
A lab method that separates a mixture twice and then weighs each molecule to identify it.
The concentrated scented oil distilled from a plant.

summary: Hempcrete, or hemp-lime, is made from shiv, the woody core of the hemp stem, mixed into a lime binder; the outer fibres go to yarn and fabric instead.
Shiv is mostly empty space, about 77% open pores in lab tests, which helps hemp-lime carry little heat, though wetter material insulates less.
Lab tests also show hemp-lime absorbing sound until a render coat is added, but none of these studies measured people living in a hemp-lime home.
start_here.how_sure_note: The numbers come from lab samples, one review and a few small tests; real buildings and the people in them were not measured.

claims.claim: A hemp stem has two parts: the outer fibres are made into yarn and woven fabric, and the woody core, called shiv, goes into hemp-lime.
Shiv is mostly empty space: about 77% of its volume was open pores.
claims.where: Results: mercury intrusion porosimetry, 76.67 plus or minus 2.03%

claims.claim: One review lists hemp-lime at about 0.08 to 0.13 W/m K, and wetter material conducts more heat.
All-plant materials raise the risk of mould in high humidity.
In lab tube tests, a render coat cut hemp-lime's sound absorption by more than half at most frequencies.
claims.study: lab impedance tube tests on six walls

claims.claim: Shown at Dutch Design Week (Oct 17 to 25): FROM FIELD TO REFUGE explored hemp fibre and hurd as materials for acoustic comfort and touch.

claims.claim: At TU/e, Dr. Florent Gauvin studies hemp, miscanthus and cattail in building materials such as hempcrete.

In one study from his group, hemp fibres replaced plastic fibres in 3D printed concrete and did about as well at 0.5% by weight; hemp takes up much water, though in that study it did not much affect mixing or printing.

could_be_wrong.point: The sound tests used an impedance tube, which measures sound hitting the sample head-on over a limited frequency range; the authors say real rooms need other methods.

The review finds only a few studies on the sound, fire resistance, fungal growth and long-term durability of all-plant composites, and names degradation over time as the main problem for biocomposites.
Heat figures depend on moisture and density: wetter hemp-lime conducts more heat, so a wall's real performance depends on how damp it gets.

glossary.plain: A building material made by mixing chopped hemp core with a lime-based binder and water.
The woody inner core of the hemp stem, chopped into small pieces.
The long, strong fibres in the outer part of the hemp stem, used for yarn and fabric.
The material that glues the pieces of a composite together, such as lime or cement.
The share of a material's volume that is empty space.
How easily heat passes through a material; lower numbers insulate better.
The share of sound energy a surface soaks up rather than reflects, from 0 (none) to 1 (all).
A lab tube that sends sound at a small sample to measure how much it absorbs.
A coat of plaster-like material spread over a wall surface.
How much heat passes through a whole wall; lower numbers mean a warmer wall.

safety.note: A plant and building materials topic; no health or drug claims. Hemp here means the stem used in building, not cannabis use.

summary: For a long time, nutmeg trees grew only on the Banda Islands, and in 1621 the Dutch East India Company (VOC) under Jan Pietersz Coen killed, expelled or deported most of the people who lived there.
Two objects tied to that trade are on display at the Rijksmuseum: a VOC painting of Banda Neira and a silver spice box shaped like a ship.

A 2015 Dutch case report describes one woman who became confused, with a dry mouth and a racing heart, after more nutmeg than she meant to use; the authors point to myristicin but say the mechanism is not yet clear.
start_here.how_sure_note: The history rests on the museum's catalogue, the company's own letters and historians, though death counts differ by source; the brain angle rests on one patient, with no drug screen.

claims.claim: For a long time, nutmeg trees grew only on the Banda Islands, about a dozen islands in the southern Moluccas; the VOC built Fort Nassau there in 1607.
claims.source: Rijksmuseum, SK-A-4476 catalogue entry, de Groot (2026)

claims.claim: The threat to the VOC's monopoly on nutmeg and mace led Governor-General Jan Pietersz Coen "to commit an atrocity in 1621-22."
claims.source: Rijksmuseum, SK-A-4476 catalogue entry, de Groot (2026)

claims.claim: On May 8, 1621, Coen "committed a massacre on the Banda Islands"; thousands of Bandanese "died as a result of the violence meted out by the Dutch."
claims.study: historian's essay; could not be re-opened on Nov 11 or Nov 20, 2026 (bot check)

claims.claim: "Most of the inhabitants were massacred, expelled or deported," and the islands were divided into plantations leased to so-called "parkers."
claims.source: Rijksmuseum, SK-A-4476 catalogue entry, de Groot (2026)

claims.claim: A VOC painting of Banda Neira, c. 1662 to 1663, is on display in gallery 2.9 and shows Fort Nassau, Fort Belgica and a gallows field.
A silver spice box from Middelburg, c. 1600, shaped like the ship Mauritius, is on display in gallery 0.7; its lid hides little compartments for spices.
A woman added more nutmeg to a dish than she intended, woke dizzy and confused with a very dry mouth, and in hospital had a heart rate of 120.
The authors point to myristicin, which was a weak MAO inhibitor in rats; the exact mechanism "is not yet clear"; she recovered completely.
claims.study: one case report with a short literature discussion

annotations.source: Rijksmuseum, SK-A-4476 (record page)
annotations.note: The museum's record for the workshop of Johannes Vingboons painting of Banda Neira, ordered by the VOC's Amsterdam chamber before April 30, 1663. It gives the gallery (2.9) and a public domain image. Its short label says all fifteen thousand islanders were killed or driven away, a figure the catalogue entry and historians state more carefully.
annotations.funding: not stated
annotations.conflicts: not stated

annotations.source: Rijksmuseum, SK-A-4476 catalogue entry, de Groot (2026)
annotations.note: The museum's scholarly entry on the painting. It explains that nutmeg grew only on Banda, dates Fort Nassau to 1607 and Fort Belgica to 1611, calls the conquest an atrocity, and counts 78 nutmeg parks in 1694. Limit: a catalogue entry about one painting, not a full history.
annotations.funding: not stated
annotations.conflicts: not stated

annotations.source: Rijksmuseum, BK-NM-4313 (record page)
annotations.note: The record for a silver spice box made in Middelburg around 1600 in the shape of the Mauritius, a ship that sailed to Asia before the VOC was founded. Public domain image; on display in gallery 0.7.
annotations.funding: not stated
annotations.conflicts: not stated

annotations.source: Michiel Baas (2021), The Newsletter 89, IIAS
annotations.note: An essay on the 400th anniversary of the Banda and Ambon events by a Max Planck Institute senior fellow. It dates the massacre to May 8, 1621 and warns against the common claim that all fifteen thousand people were murdered, noting that some escaped to the Kei Islands. Limit: read for the package on Oct 5, 2026; the site has refused every fetch since Nov 11 with a bot check, so it could not be re-read.
annotations.funding: not stated
annotations.conflicts: not stated

annotations.source: Roeters van Lennep et al. 2015
annotations.note: A three-page letter from Erasmus MC internists about one 37-year-old woman who recovered fully after accidental nutmeg poisoning. It reviews the reported symptoms and possible mechanisms. Limits: one patient, her urine was not screened for drugs, and the authors say other substances remain possible.
annotations.funding: not stated (the letter has no funding statement)
annotations.conflicts: none declared (the letter has no conflict of interest statement)

could_be_wrong.point: The case cannot rule out another cause. Her urine was not screened for drugs of abuse, and the authors write that intoxication by other substances is still a possibility.
The step from myristicin to the amphetamine-like compound MMDA is unproven in people. A 2026 poison centre study reports that animal and human urine studies could not confirm it.
Scientists at Germany's Federal Institute for Risk Assessment call myristicin and elemicin toxicologically widely unexplored, with no thorough studies of how people break them down.

Death counts differ by source. Coen's own letter of November 1621 says about 2,500 died of hunger, misery and the sword and no more than about 300 escaped; a historian puts the population at about 15,000 before and about 1,000 after; the museum label says all fifteen thousand were killed or driven away.
could_be_wrong.source: Coen, letter of Nov 16, 1621, in Colenbrander (1919)

could_be_wrong.point: The date of Fort Nassau differs. The museum gives 1607; a 2025 history of the conquest dates the fort to 1609. The number executed on May 8, 1621 also differs between sources: 44 in Coen's letter, 48 in a 1995 history, 24 in one account cited in 2025.

One case says nothing about how common or how serious nutmeg poisoning is. In 10 years, an Illinois poison centre logged 32 cases, none fatal, and all 4 patients who were admitted had also taken other substances.

glossary.plain: The Dutch East India Company, a trading company founded in 1602 that ran forts, fleets and colonies in Asia.
Sole control over selling a product, so no one else may trade in it.
The red, lacy covering around the nutmeg seed, dried and sold as a separate spice.
A Dutch planter who leased a nutmeg plantation, called a perk or park, from the VOC after 1621.
A medical paper about a single patient; it can raise a question but cannot show how often something happens.
A natural compound in nutmeg and, in smaller amounts, in herbs such as parsley and dill.
An enzyme that breaks down chemical messengers such as serotonin.
An amphetamine-like compound that the body may make from myristicin, though this has not been confirmed in people.
A heart rate faster than normal at rest.

posts.how_sure: One lab study of 68 adults with two test smells; no real room or show hall was studied.

summary: In a 2021 lab study, 68 adults breathed a steady rose-like or banana-like smell and rated its strength every minute; it faded fast, then slowly, and half stopped noticing it within about 6 to 7 minutes.
When the smell had faded by one route, sending it in by the other route (through the nose or from the back of the mouth) brought back part of its strength at once.

A 2022 study recorded the smell lining inside the nose of 35 adults: the signal held steady while ratings fell for some smells, which points to the brain doing much of the fading, though the question is not closed.
start_here.how_sure_note: Two small lab studies with a few single test smells; neither measured a real room or show hall, and the nose recordings worked cleanly in only some people.

claims.claim: Hold a steady smell under the nose and its strength fades fast, then slowly; 68 adults rated it every minute.
claims.study: one lab study, 68 adults, two test smells

claims.claim: Half the group stopped noticing a steady test smell within about 6 to 7 minutes, and some still smelled it at 15.
claims.where: Results: median time to full habituation (377.5, 416, 358 and 418 s); 10, 4, 12 and 4 people not at 0 by 15 min

claims.claim: Once it faded, sending the same smell in by the other route, from the mouth, brought back about half its strength at once.
claims.where: Results: cross-habituation (3.9 and 3.8 against 8.0 and 8.3); Fig. 2a

claims.claim: Switched the other way, strength came back only to 2.9 and 1.6 of 10, against 7.6 and 8.1 at the start.
Over ten short puffs, 35 adults rated two of four test smells as growing weaker.
claims.study: one lab study, 35 adults, four test smells

claims.claim: The signal recorded inside their noses did not drop significantly over the ten puffs; the authors read this as fading that happens more in the brain than in the nose.
claims.study: one lab recording study, 35 adults, 69 percent with at least one usable recording

claims.claim: A few people did show a shrinking nose signal, so the question is not closed.

annotations.source: Xiao et al. 2021
annotations.note: Sixty-eight healthy adults aged 23 to 35 breathed a constant flow of a rose-like smell (phenylethanol) or a banana-like smell (n-butyl acetate), by mask or by a thin tube to the back of the nose, and rated strength every minute until it reached zero. Ratings fell fast, then slowly, and switching route brought part of the strength back. Limits: two test smells, young lab volunteers and a mask or tube, not an everyday room.
annotations.funding: Clinical Research and Development Project of Zhongnan Hospital of Wuhan University (lcyf202102), Beijing Municipal Administration of Hospitals (PX2020026) and Beijing Scholars Program (No. 051).
annotations.conflicts: The authors have no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.

annotations.source: Mignot et al. 2022
annotations.note: A Dresden team placed an electrode on the smell lining inside the nose of 35 adults and gave ten one-second puffs of each of four smells. The nose signal did not fall significantly over the puffs, while felt strength fell for two smells, so the authors favour fading in the brain. Limits: usable recordings in only some people, few complete runs of ten, and no link found between signal size and ratings.
annotations.funding: Open Access funding by Projekt DEAL; the paper states the research received no other specific grant from public, commercial or not-for-profit funders.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests for this work.

could_be_wrong.point: Clean nose recordings were hard to get. Only 69 percent of people gave at least one usable recording, and only 11 gave all ten in a row, of whom 5 showed a falling signal; the authors say peripheral adaptation might exist.
The nose signal and people's ratings did not track each other, so the study cannot say where the fading happens, only that it did not show up as a shrinking average signal.

Each study used only a few lab chemicals. A later study of 32 smells found that smells differ in how fast people stop noticing them, and smells that also prickle or warm the nose faded less, so two or four test smells may not stand for all smells.

Attention changes the fade. In 19 adults, a distracting task made a floral smell fade faster at first, while paying attention brought waves of renewed sensitivity; the authors call it a small study that needs repeating.

Fading is not only on the exposed side. In 80 adults, a rose-like smell clipped to one nostril lowered sensitivity on both sides after 2 hours, more on the exposed side, and other smells kept their strength, so adaptation is partly smell-specific.
No study here measured a show hall, a shop or any real room, and none tested how long it takes to recover after stepping outside.

glossary.plain: A drop in how strongly you notice something that keeps going, such as a steady smell.
The changes in the nose or brain that turn down the response to a smell that stays the same.
Smelling through the nostrils, the way you sniff a flower.
Smell that reaches the nose from the back of the mouth and throat, as when you chew food.
Testing whether a smell that has faded by one route also stays faded when it arrives by another route.
The small patch of lining high inside the nose where smell-sensing cells sit.
A recording of the electrical response of the smell lining, taken with a small electrode inside the nose.
Fading that happens in the nose itself (peripheral) or in the brain (central).
The middle value when all the results are put in order.
A lab chemical that smells like rose.
A lab chemical that smells like banana.
The chemical behind the smell of cloves.
Tools for watching the working brain. Functional MRI (fMRI) tracks blood flow, PET scans use a small radioactive tracer, and EEG records electrical activity through the scalp.
A cell that receives and sends messages through the nervous system using small electrical signals and chemical messengers.
The fifth cranial nerve, the main sensory nerve of the face and head. Migraine pain runs through its pain pathways.

safety.note: Education, not medical advice. A sudden loss or change of smell that does not come back is worth checking with a clinician.

summary: MJBizCon is the cannabis industry's big business show, December 1 to 4, 2026, at the Las Vegas Convention Center.
Our count of its official directory on Oct 27 found 428 booth listings from 424 companies; devices, cultivation and packaging were the largest groups, and science groups were tiny.
It is the first MJBizCon since an April 28, 2026 federal order moved FDA-approved marijuana drugs and state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III; all other marijuana stays in Schedule I.
start_here.how_sure_note: The counts are our own dated tally of the official directory, which has grown since; the law comes from the order's own text, though a court challenge to it is still open.

summary: Jet lag is a body clock out of step with local time: after flying west it must run later, after flying east it must run earlier.
A sports expert panel's rule of thumb says the clock catches up about 2 hours a day going west but only 1 hour a day going east.
Light timing decides the direction of the shift, and in 64,847 Oura ring trips, sleep length recovered in about 2 days while sleep timing had not by day 15.
start_here.how_sure_note: The light-timing rules come from decades of lab work, but field tests of light for jet lag are few and mixed, the speeds are a rule of thumb, and the ring data come from one study tied to the ring maker.

summary: Your first night in a new bed usually sleeps worse, so often that sleep labs plan an extra night to absorb it.
Recent studies found the rough first night with lab nights a week apart and on the first recorded night at home, with more waking and less deep sleep.
One small team found that part of the left brain sleeps more lightly on night one, like a night watch, but larger frontal recordings did not tie brain asymmetry to the rough night.
start_here.how_sure_note: A meta-analysis of 53 studies backs the first-night effect, though one large study of young men found little of it; the night-watch explanation rests on small tests from one team.

could_be_wrong.point: The effect is not universal. In 124 healthy young men sleeping in private sound-attenuated rooms, the two nights did not differ in sleep onset, total sleep, waking or efficiency, and stage differences were small.
The night-watch idea has not been repeated by another lab. The only follow-up is the same team's 2019 nap study, and its second experiment had only 6 people with both days.

A larger test did not back the brain asymmetry. In 35 and 30 people, frontal delta asymmetry was not related to how long people took to fall asleep (r about 0); the authors note they used two forehead electrodes, not the network imaging Tamaki used.
The meta-analysis behind 'usually' found the effect milder in young people and no change in deep sleep, and it pooled consecutive-night studies.

posts.how_sure: One records study, 20 doctors; a far bigger study, 231,076 nurse triage calls, found no sign of decision fatigue.

summary: A brain plan for a long trade show day: big choices early, walk between meetings, stop to read, refill water and keep coffee early.
The pieces rest on studies of doctors' choices by hour, willpower tests across 36 labs, exercise and attention, walking while doing a second task, caffeine and sleep, and mild dehydration.
No study tested this plan on a show floor, and several of the findings are small, early or disputed.
start_here.how_sure_note: Walking's small boost to attention is well pooled; the time-of-day choice finding failed a much larger test, and the coffee and water findings are early or debated.

could_be_wrong.point: The doctors' first-hour finding came from one look-back study; a registered test of 231,076 nurse triage calls found no decision fatigue at all.
The fuel model of willpower has collapsed in large tests, so no one knows why choices might drift through a day.
The caffeine trial used 23 young men at home with diet and timing of meals not controlled; women and older adults may react differently.
Light exercise on its own did not give a clear benefit in the pooled studies, and a show-floor walk may be closer to light than moderate.
The strongest dehydration effects come from extreme conditions, such as 36 hours without drinking, in a 12-person trial funded by the Danone Institute China.
The walking studies were small (12 and 26 people) and used short lab walkways, not crowded halls.

posts.how_sure: One lab brain-scan study: MEG in 22 people, fMRI in a second group; an earlier 7-person MEG study agrees.

summary: Seeing faces in sockets, cars and toast is called face pareidolia, and brain scans show the brain's face areas respond to these objects within about a sixth of a second.
In a 2020 study of 22 people, the brain first treated illusory faces as face-like and then, within about 250 milliseconds, as ordinary objects again.
Monkeys also look longer at objects with faces in them, but their face cells barely respond to such objects, and no controlled study has tested pareidolia under psychedelics.
start_here.how_sure_note: Several brain-scan studies agree on a fast face-area response, but the samples are small, studies differ on how long it lasts, and the monkey cell and attention results are mixed.

claims.claim: Seeing faces in things is called face pareidolia, and the brain's face areas take part.
claims.where: Abstract; fMRI results in face-selective regions FFA and OFA
claims.study: one lab study, fMRI and MEG

claims.claim: In 7 adults scanned with MEG, face-like objects drew a face-area response at about 165 ms; ordinary objects did not.
claims.where: Results; 9 recruited, 2 not analysed for motion

claims.claim: In 22 people, the brain first treated illusory faces as face-like, then as ordinary objects within about 250 ms.
claims.where: MEG results, Fig. 5 and Source Data Figure5a
claims.study: one lab study, MEG in 22 people, fMRI in 16

claims.claim: Online raters gave objects with an illusory face 6.27 out of 10 for face-likeness, matched objects 0.70 and human faces 9.96.
5 rhesus monkeys looked longer at objects with illusory faces.
In a later study, monkey face cells barely responded to objects with illusory faces.
claims.study: single-cell recordings in four face patches, 6 monkeys

claims.claim: Told that pure noise hid faces, 20 adults reported a face 34 percent of the time, and the right fusiform face area responded.
Perception is a best guess, and strong expectations can make healthy people see what is not there.
claims.where: Main text: priors and hallucinations in healthy subjects

annotations.source: Wardle et al. 2020
annotations.note: An NIMH and Macquarie team showed 96 photos of illusory faces, matched objects and human faces in fMRI and MEG. Face areas told illusory faces apart from objects, peaking at about 160 ms, but within about 250 ms the brain grouped them with objects. Limits: small scan samples and one photo set.

annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests.

annotations.source: Hadjikhani et al. 2009
annotations.note: MEG in 7 adults at Massachusetts General Hospital: objects seen as faces drew a fusiform response at about 165 ms, like faces, while ordinary objects did not; an earlier 130 ms peak appeared for real faces only. Limits: 9 recruited and 2 lost to motion, so a very small sample.
annotations.funding: NIH NINDS R01NS044824 and Swiss National Science Foundation PPOOB 110741 (Acknowledgments).
annotations.conflicts: not stated

annotations.source: Liu et al. 2014
annotations.note: Twenty young adults in China were told half of a set of pure-noise images held faces or letters; they reported faces 34 percent of the time, and the right fusiform face area responded when they did. Limits: expectation was set by the instructions, and a later study found that only some people show face-area activity in this kind of task.
annotations.funding: National Basic Research Program of China (2011CB707700), National Natural Science Foundation of China, Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities, and NIH (R01HD046526 and R01HD060595).
annotations.conflicts: not stated

annotations.source: Taubert et al. 2017
annotations.note: Five rhesus monkeys looked longer at objects with illusory faces than at matched objects, and fixated the illusory eyes and mouth. Limits: five animals, 45 images, and looking time does not show what the monkeys saw.
annotations.funding: NIMH Intramural Research Program (to L.G.U.).
annotations.conflicts: not stated

annotations.source: Koyano et al. 2025
annotations.note: Recordings from single neurons in four face patches of six monkeys found no general preference for objects with illusory faces over matched objects; a subset of cells did prefer them, and both responses were far below those to real faces. Limits: four face regions only; the authors suggest the attention monkeys give such objects comes from elsewhere in the brain.
annotations.funding: NIMH Intramural Research Program (ZIAMH002838 and ZIAMH002898) to D.A.L. and the Australian Research Council (FT200100843) to J.T.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests.

annotations.source: Corlett et al. 2019
annotations.note: A review arguing that perception is built from incoming signals and prior expectations, and that strong, overly precise priors can produce hallucinations even in healthy people in lab tasks. Limits: a theory review; it does not test face pareidolia or psychedelics.
annotations.funding: Several grants, including NIMH R01MH112887 and R21MH116258, the Wellcome Trust, a Leopoldina fellowship and a NARSAD award (Acknowledgements).
annotations.conflicts: The authors report no relevant biomedical conflicts of interest.

could_be_wrong.point: How long the face response lasts is disputed. Recordings from electrodes inside the brains of 44 epilepsy patients found the response to face-like objects was about a quarter the size of the response to faces but lasted almost as long, not the brief burst seen in the 2020 MEG study.

An MEG study of brain rhythms placed the decisive difference between upright and inverted face-like objects at later processing stages, in a relatively late network, not only in the first fifth of a second.

Seeing faces in noise may depend on the person. In a similar noise task, only 4 of 9 people showed strong face-area activity, and the authors suggest some may have simply answered the way they were expected to.
Illusory faces may not grab attention. Three visual search experiments found that neither real nor illusory faces captured attention, a failure to replicate earlier findings.
Monkeys look at illusory faces, but their face cells barely prefer them over matched objects, so the monkey and human pictures do not fully line up.
No controlled study has measured face pareidolia under psychedelics; the link is a question, not a finding.

A scan that measures the tiny magnetic fields made by brain activity, millisecond by millisecond.

posts.how_sure: Textbook science: place cells and grid cells, found in rats in 1971 and 2005, form a positioning system in the brain.

summary: Place cells and grid cells, found in rats in 1971 and 2005, form a positioning system in the brain, work that won the 2014 Nobel Prize.
In people, a grid-like brain signal shows up when they move through virtual spaces, though two recent studies did not find it when people were moved passively.
People prefer curved shapes on average, but for images of rooms and facades the preference was about zero, and design experts showed none.
start_here.how_sure_note: Place and grid cells are textbook science in rats; the human grid signal is solid in active navigation but missing in passive tests; curve preference for buildings is not supported so far.

claims.claim: The cells that build the brain's map of places won the 2014 Nobel Prize.
In rats, hippocampal place cells fire when the animal is at one spot in a room; other cells take other spots.
claims.where: Press release; place fields shown in Gobbo et al. 2022, Figs. 1 and 2

claims.claim: Entorhinal grid cells fire at points that form a hexagonal grid across the floor, a coordinate system.
claims.where: Press release; firing maps in Ulsaker-Janke et al. 2023, Fig. 1C

claims.claim: 42 men in a virtual arena showed a grid-like signal, with orientations clustered in 34; a steadier signal went with better spatial memory.
The signal was not found in two passive-navigation studies, one preregistered with 110 adults.
In 53 midlife adults scanned at 7T while being passively moved through a virtual room, the grid-like signal was not significant across the group.
Across 106 samples and 11,023 people, people preferred curved contours to angular ones on average (Hedges' g = 0.39).
With interiors and facades the preference shrank to about zero (g = -0.04), and design experts showed none (g = -0.034).
claims.where: Results: stimulus type and expertise moderators

claims.claim: A review of 56 papers links memorable places to easier wayfinding and asks for replicable ways to measure them.

annotations.source: Nobel Assembly 2014
annotations.note: The Nobel Assembly's announcement of the 2014 prize to John O'Keefe and May-Britt and Edvard Moser for discovering cells that make up a positioning system in the brain: place cells in 1971 and grid cells in 2005.
annotations.funding: not stated
annotations.conflicts: not stated

annotations.source: Doeller et al. 2010
annotations.note: Forty-two men explored a virtual arena in an fMRI scanner; the entorhinal cortex showed a six-fold signal that depended on running direction, with orientations clustered in 34, and a more coherent signal went with better spatial memory. Limits: men only, virtual movement, and fMRI sees only an indirect signal of many cells, not grid cells themselves.
annotations.funding: UK Medical Research Council and the European Union (SpaceBrain grant).
annotations.conflicts: not stated

annotations.source: Chuquichambi et al. 2022
annotations.note: A preregistered meta-analysis of 61 studies, 106 samples and 11,023 people found a medium average preference for curved contours (g = 0.39), larger with brief viewing, near zero for interiors and facades, and absent in design experts. Limits: few studies with experts (18 effect sizes) and mostly images rather than real spaces.
annotations.funding: Spanish Ministerio de Ciencia e Innovacion, Agencia Estatal de Investigacion and European Regional Development Fund project PSI2016-77327-P, and an FPU fellowship (FPU18/00365).
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare that there are no competing interests.

annotations.note: A systematic review of 56 papers on imageability, how easy a place is to picture and remember, using Kevin Lynch's five elements. High-imageability places tend to help wayfinding, but methods vary widely and brain-imaging studies and studies of older adults are scarce.
annotations.funding: NIH grant 1DP1AG069870-01 (to G.E.M.).
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work.

annotations.funding: Wellcome Trust Advanced Investigator Grant 207481/Z/17/Z.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no competing interest.

annotations.source: Ulsaker-Janke et al. 2023
annotations.note: Grid cells in rats raised without flat, straight-edged surroundings still formed hexagonal firing patterns; used here for its firing maps.
annotations.funding: European Research Council Advanced Grant 268598, Research Council of Norway (223262 and 295721), K.G. Jebsen Foundation, Kavli Foundation and other prizes to M.-B.M. and E.I.M.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no competing interest.

annotations.note: Midlife adults at genetic or family risk of Alzheimer's disease watched themselves being passively moved through a virtual room during 7T fMRI; the grid-like signal was not significant across the 53 scanned, though people with stronger signals lost less path-integration accuracy. Limits: a subset of a specific risk cohort.
annotations.funding: Merck Investigator Studies Program (MISP-57175), Alzheimer's Society, NIHR, Alzheimer's Association, Wellcome, UK MRC and NINDS, among others.
annotations.conflicts: The authors have no conflicts of interest.

annotations.source: Kransberg et al. 2026
annotations.note: A preregistered fMRI study of 110 adults moved passively through virtual space found no group-level grid-like signal in the entorhinal cortex; the authors note that active-navigation studies have repeated it.
annotations.funding: European Research Council (771375) and Research Council of Norway (301395) to K.B.W.
annotations.conflicts: The authors have no conflicts of interest to disclose.

could_be_wrong.point: The human grid-like signal did not appear in a preregistered study of 110 adults moved passively through virtual space, so it may depend on active, self-directed movement.
In midlife adults at risk of Alzheimer's disease, the grid-like signal was not significant across the 53 people scanned.
fMRI does not record grid cells; it picks up a six-fold pattern in blood flow that is read as a sign of grid-like coding, in 42 men only in the 2010 study.

The curve preference does not carry over to buildings so far: for interiors and facades it was about zero, and experts in architecture, design and the arts showed none, though only 18 expert effect sizes exist.
Most curve studies used images, and the effect was largest with brief looks (0.75) and smaller with unlimited viewing (0.32), which is closer to living in a space.
Imageability research uses many different methods, and the review calls for standard, replicable measures before strong claims are made about brain health.
