glossary.plain: A nerve cell in the hippocampus that fires when an animal is at one particular spot.
A nerve cell in the entorhinal cortex that fires at many spots forming a hexagonal grid across the floor.
A curved structure deep in the brain that is key for memory and for knowing where you are.
A brain area next to the hippocampus that feeds it information about space and movement.
A six-fold pattern in fMRI that changes with movement direction, read as a sign of grid-cell-like coding.
Moving yourself through a space, versus being moved along a path you do not control.
A study whose plan and analysis were published before the data were collected.
A study that pools results from many studies to estimate an overall effect.
A measure of effect size; 0 means no difference, and about 0.4 is a medium effect.
How easy a place is to picture and remember, from its paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks.
Finding your way from one place to another.

An almond-shaped structure in the temporal lobe, part of the limbic system, that is important for emotional memory, such as learning to fear something. THC reduced its response to threatening faces in one study.
A region of the cortex that works with the insula in reading signals from inside the body and in emotional responses such as fear.
How big a difference or link is, not just whether it exists. It is one of the main things that decide whether a result matters in practice.
A potent classic psychedelic that acts mainly on 5-HT2A receptors.
A cell that receives and sends messages through the nervous system using small electrical signals and chemical messengers.
A review that uses clear, planned methods to find, select and combine the results of all the studies on a clearly stated question. A meta-analysis is often part of one.

posts.how_sure: Small brain-scan studies (10 people in 2001, 49 in 2024); many studies agree on the reward link.

summary: When music gives you chills, brain regions tied to reward become more active; this link has been found again and again since a 2001 brain scan study.
In one careful trial of 27 adults, a drug that raised dopamine increased musical pleasure and a drug that blocked it lowered pleasure.
Smaller, newer studies suggest chills and tears are different peaks, that the brain's state just before a song predicts chills, and that music makes imagined scenes more vivid.
start_here.how_sure_note: Many studies agree on the reward link, but each study here is small (10 to 100 people) and the newer findings have not been repeated.

could_be_wrong.point: The first chills scan had only ten people, all trained musicians listening to their own favourite pieces, so the music differed from person to person and was already well known to each listener.
Dopamine may be a step rather than the source of the pleasure. The trial's own authors suggest the opioid system might be what finally produces it.
Chills and tears were measured in two separate groups, so differences between the people may explain part of the result; the songs also had lyrics and were familiar.
A button press captures only part of what music feels like, and the authors say they cannot yet tell what drives the brain state before a song.
The imagery study used only Western music and mostly Western listeners, so it may not hold for other traditions.

glossary.plain: Goosebumps or a shiver at a peak moment in music, sometimes called frisson.
Brain areas, such as the ventral striatum and nucleus accumbens, that respond to food, money and other things we want.
A chemical messenger that helps the brain learn what is rewarding and how much to want it.
A brain scan that follows a mildly radioactive tracer to show blood flow or chemical activity.
A brain scan that tracks changes in blood oxygen as areas become more or less active.
How closely activity in two brain areas rises and falls together.
Tiny changes in how well the skin carries electricity, which rise with arousal and sweat.
A study in which each person gets every treatment in turn, and neither they nor the researchers know which one they got.
A dummy pill with no active drug, used for comparison.
Seeing pictures in the mind's eye without looking at them.

An almond-shaped structure in the temporal lobe, part of the limbic system, that is important for emotional memory, such as learning to fear something. THC reduced its response to threatening faces in one study.
The part of the cortex that processes sound. Cannabis without CBD dampened its response to music in one study.
Tools for watching the working brain. Functional MRI (fMRI) tracks blood flow, PET scans use a small radioactive tracer, and EEG records electrical activity through the scalp.
Shivers or goosebumps during intensely moving music. They come with changes in heart rate, breathing and activity in the brain's reward areas.

A mental health condition with ongoing sadness, loss of energy and loss of pleasure that makes daily life hard. It can also bring feelings of worthlessness, changes in sleep or eating, and thoughts of death.

A brain structure in the limbic system that is essential for learning and for forming new memories of facts and events. People with damage to the hippocampus have great difficulty forming new memories of this kind.
A deep fold of the cortex that helps process signals from inside the body.
An anesthetic medicine that, at some doses, causes dissociative effects (feeling detached from the body or surroundings). It blocks the NMDA receptor, a receptor for the messenger glutamate.
A potent classic psychedelic that acts mainly on 5-HT2A receptors.
A lab-made drug, also called Molly or ecstasy, with stimulant and mind-altering effects. It increases serotonin, dopamine and norepinephrine by boosting their release and blocking their reuptake.
A reward area deep in the brain that is part of the dopamine reward pathway.
A class of pain-relieving drugs, made from the opium poppy or in a lab, that block pain signals by binding to opioid receptors. They can be highly addictive.
The front part of the cortex, involved in mood, thinking and perception. The strongest psychedelic effects are linked to activity here.
The main psychedelic compound in "magic" mushrooms. The body turns it into psilocin, the active form. It is being studied for depression and for distress in people with cancer.
A molecule, usually a protein, on or inside a cell that a specific chemical messenger binds to, which sets off an effect in the cell. It is often pictured as a lock that only certain keys fit.
A review that uses clear, planned methods to find, select and combine the results of all the studies on a clearly stated question. A meta-analysis is often part of one.
A relay station deep in the brain that passes information from the senses on to other brain areas.
A reward hub deep in the brain that responds to music and other rewards.

summary: Awe is the feeling of meeting something vast that makes you update your picture of the world, and a review links it to goosebump tingles, a calmer heart rhythm and lower inflammation markers.

In a scanner, 32 adults watching mountains and waterfalls showed less rise in self-focused brain regions than with funny or plain clips, and older adults on weekly awe walks felt more joy and filled less of their own photos.
The body and kindness findings are shaky: a study of 210 students found no filmed link between awe and goosebumps, and six 2026 replication attempts changed only 3 of 33 outcomes.
start_here.how_sure_note: Most findings come from small single studies, the review calls the evidence promising and preliminary, and newer replications found fewer effects.

could_be_wrong.point: The scanner study had no separate scan to locate the default mode network, so the authors warn against reading the result as a direct drop in that network.
Only 16 people took part in the VR goosebump study, which the authors say reduces statistical power.
In two larger samples, filmed goosebumps were rare and not linked to awe, even though students often said they felt them; the authors suggest reports of goosebumps may not match the skin.

In the awe walk trial, anxiety, depression and life satisfaction did not change, more feeling of kindness did not lead to more reported helping, and distress may have fallen partly by regression to the mean.
Direct replications with larger samples did not repeat most famous awe effects, and no kindness measure changed, though feeling small did repeat.
The review itself flags conflicting findings on whether awe calms the body's stress system and calls the evidence for health benefits promising and preliminary.

summary: Apps borrow from how the brain learns from reward: an endless scroll pays off now and then, and one study of over a million posts found people post faster when likes come faster.

How much it matters is small on average: across 355,358 teenagers, technology use explained at most 0.4 percent of differences in wellbeing, and whether heavy phone use is an addiction is still debated.
Small changes can help: in one trial, a ten-part nudge cut daily screen time by 57 minutes, against 11 minutes for tracking alone.

could_be_wrong.point: The design analysis is theoretical: the authors say designer intent is speculative and the data needed to test it are held by the app companies.
The million-post analysis is correlational, and the authors say other explanations cannot be ruled out.
The 0.4 percent figure comes from one-time surveys with noisy self-reported use, which can shrink or hide effects, and it does not say whether screens affect wellbeing.
Screening studies label anywhere from about 0 to 35 percent of people as addicted, and one study 48 percent, which suggests the screening tools disagree.
Participants chose their own strategies and the groups started with different screen time, so it is hard to tell which parts of the nudge worked.

summary: Fractals repeat at many scales, and a number, the fractal dimension D, measures how rough a pattern is; clouds sit near D 1.3.
On average, people in these studies liked fractals of middle roughness best, but person by person only about half peaked in the middle; about a fifth liked the smoothest and a fifth the roughest.

Claims that fractals lower stress come from small studies mostly by one research network, some of whose members design commercial fractal products, and whether Pollock's paintings are fractal is still debated.
start_here.how_sure_note: The average preference for middle roughness has repeated within one research network; individual differences are large, and the stress and Pollock claims are early or disputed.

claims.claim: Across 443 people from around the world, preference for nature-like fractals peaked near D 1.2.
Clouds sit near D 1.3, coastlines span 1.05 to 1.52, and trees reach 1.9.
Natural scenes share middle-range statistics, and human vision is most sensitive in that range; in 184 online adults, middle-D synthetic images won 46 percent of choices.
Only about half of 310 students peaked in the middle; about 20 percent liked the smoothest best and 20 percent the roughest.
In 78 adults, liking rose as fractal patterns got rougher, while they were rated less relaxing.
A second study from the same network found appeal and relaxation fell as perceived complexity rose.
Whether Pollock's paintings are fractal is still debated: they are fractal over too small a range, and freehand sketches give the same signature.
Fractal criteria cannot tell real Pollocks from other drip paintings.

could_be_wrong.point: The average hides big differences: only about half of 310 students preferred middle roughness, and the rest liked smooth, rough or showed no clear pattern.
Where the peak falls depends on who is asked: in 443 people, the overall peak was at D 1.2, men peaked at D 1.2 and women at D 1.6.
Average preference was not always in the middle: for flowers and forests, people preferred low D.
Most of this work comes from one research network, and a 2021 paper from it discloses three co-authors employed by a fractal design company and a flooring collaboration.
Liking and calm can pull apart: in 78 students, rougher patterns were liked more but rated less relaxing.
Pollock's paintings may not be fractal in a meaningful sense: they scale over too small a range, and freehand sketches meet the same criteria.
No peer-reviewed study was found that measures the fractal dimension of Persian rugs, so the link to the 2026 rug artwork is a question, not a finding.

summary: Literate adults have a visual word form area, a patch of left visual cortex for letter strings, and it copes with letters drawn in unusual ways, even words made only of dots.
Its limit is spacing: letters closer than about half their distance from your gaze jumble together, an effect called crowding, and it sets reading speed.
Wes Wilson's 1960s posters stretched and packed free-hand letters to fill the space; our reading, not yet tested, is that packed letters crowd each other, so the posters read slowly but surely.
start_here.how_sure_note: Crowding and the word form area are well studied, but the dot-word result comes from a few people and no study has tested the posters themselves.

could_be_wrong.point: No study has tested whether Wilson's posters are crowded or slow to read; the link between the posters and crowding is our own synthesis.
The dot-word result rests on 4 adults in the follow-up experiment, so it is early.
The half-the-distance rule is a rule of thumb: a 2023 study of 50 observers found a smaller standardized factor (0.24) than Bouma's rescored 0.35, so the exact spacing varies between people.
Crowding is weaker between dissimilar objects, so ornate, varied letter shapes may crowd less than the rule suggests.

summary: In virtual reality tests, people remembered the order of two objects better when both sat in the same room than when a doorway lay between them.
The researchers' model says memories attach to a mental backdrop that drifts over time and shifts faster when you cross a boundary.
A week-long diary study of 152 adults found that forgetting to do something was the most common everyday memory slip; no study tested Mal Yu's Shift Hook, a keyhole-shaped key hook shown at DDW 2026.
start_here.how_sure_note: The doorway result held across three lab experiments with about 40 people each, and the diary study is larger, but both rest on lab or self-report settings and neither tested a key hook.

claims.where: Methods; Results (838 of 1319 failures, 64 percent); Fig. 1

claims.claim: Shift Hook is a keyhole-inspired wall hook for keys, about the threshold between entrance and exit.
None of these studies tested the hook.

annotations.source: Horner et al. 2016
annotations.note: Across three virtual reality experiments, people judged the order of two objects more accurately when the objects had been seen in the same room than in adjoining rooms, and a simple drifting context model captured the result. Limits: desktop virtual rooms rather than real ones, about 40 young adults per experiment, and the doorway effect was shown for the order of objects only.
annotations.funding: Funded by the Medical Research Council UK and the Wellcome Trust UK.
annotations.conflicts: none declared (the paper has no conflict statement)

annotations.source: Niedźwieńska et al. 2020
annotations.note: Young, middle-aged and older adults logged every memory failure for 7 days. Of 1319 failures, 838 (64 percent) were prospective, forgetting to do something, and young adults reported more of these than older adults. Limits: self-report diaries depend on noticing a slip and carrying the diary.
annotations.funding: The authors received no specific funding for this work.
annotations.conflicts: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.

could_be_wrong.point: The effect was shown only for the order of objects. Recognition of the objects was high, and memory for which room an object was in sat at chance level, so the study could not show a doorway effect on those.
The rooms were virtual, seen on a screen. The model's drift rates were chosen by the authors, who say future studies are needed to measure the real-world rates.
Diary studies count only the slips people notice and manage to write down; the authors note that the hardest part is remembering to carry the diary.
The diary study counted forgetting in daily life but did not test any aid, so it says nothing about whether a fixed key spot prevents lost keys.

summary: In one small 2013 study, yoghurt eaten from lighter plastic spoons was rated denser than the same yoghurt from heavier ones, and the authors say novelty may explain it.
Earlier work found the reverse for bowls: yoghurt in heavier bowls was rated denser and more expensive, and a 2019 review maps weight as one of many hand-feel cues.
In a 2025 study of 242 students, the same meals were rated higher with steel, ceramic and glass than with plastic or wood and cardboard, and wooden cutlery added a woody flavour.

annotations.note: A review of how touch cues from packaging, cutlery and tableware, such as weight, texture and temperature, change how food is perceived and chosen. Limits: a narrative review that summarises studies rather than pooling them, and it calls for more work on why these effects happen.

The regular set got higher ratings and a more positive emotional profile, and wooden cutlery added a woody flavour. Limits: students aged 18 to 30 in one country, and each group tasted one meal.
annotations.funding: This research received no external funding.

could_be_wrong.point: The spoon authors themselves say many of their effects might come from the novelty of an unusual spoon making people stop and taste carefully, rather than from weight itself.
The spoon size mattered too: only the lightest teaspoon differed from most other spoons, so size and weight expectations may have mixed together.

In a later restaurant study, heavier cutlery went with more liking and a higher price people would pay for a main course, the opposite direction from the light spoon result. The diners chose their own seats, which the authors list as a limitation.
The review says the reasons behind touch and taste links remain unknown and calls for more research, including brain measures.
The tableware study tested young students in one country, with each group tasting only one meal, so the results may not hold for other people or foods.

summary: SoundSelf, the 2026 Psychedelics Design Products and Services winner, describes itself as voice-activated biofeedback; we found no published clinical trial of the current system.
Classic heart rate variability biofeedback pairs live heart-rate feedback with slow breathing near six breaths a minute, and across 14 trials it eased depressive symptoms by a moderate amount.
None of those trials could hide the treatment from participants, and a placebo-controlled breathing trial of 400 adults found slow breathing did no better than a matched placebo.
start_here.how_sure_note: Pooled trials point to benefit, but none was blinded, many were at risk of bias, and a well-controlled breathing trial found no difference; nothing has tested SoundSelf itself.

could_be_wrong.point: The depression benefit could vanish in a new setting: the prediction interval runs from -0.19 to 0.96, and no trial blinded participants.
When slow breathing was tested against a matched placebo in 400 adults, both groups improved equally, which suggests expectation can explain much of the benefit.
The large stress and anxiety effect comes from a review in which only one study was at low risk of bias and every outcome was self-reported.
A meta-analysis of 223 slow-breathing studies rated 215 at high risk of bias, so even the heart-rate effects are less certain than they look.
For blood pressure, device-guided breathing lowered office readings slightly across 8 trials, but 5 were linked to the device maker and no effect remained without them.
No clinical trial of the current SoundSelf system was found in Europe PMC, Crossref or ClinicalTrials.gov as of Nov 13, 2026.

summary: On stage at Psychedelics Design 2026, a speaker said 8 weeks of a diet and lifestyle program took 3.23 years off biological age; the number comes from one pilot trial of 38 analysed men.

The 3.23 years is the gap between two groups on one DNA clock read from saliva; after a 2024 correction, the program group's clock fell 2.04 years and the controls' rose 1.10, which was not significant.
The supplement maker funded the trial, two authors profit from the program, and a 2026 Yale reanalysis of the public data with 12 clocks did not confirm the result.
start_here.how_sure_note: One small pilot trial with one clock, corrected once, funded by an interested company, and not confirmed when other researchers reanalysed its data.

claims.claim: The program combined diet, two supplements, exercise, sleep and breathing exercises for 8 weeks after a week of instruction.
Biological age here is one epigenetic clock, the Horvath clock of 353 DNA methylation sites, read from saliva.
The 3.23 years is the difference between the two groups' average clock changes.
After the 2024 correction, the program group's clock age fell 2.04 years and the controls' rose 1.10, which was not significant; the two add to 3.14.
Of the 18 men in the program, 8 scored younger, 9 were unchanged and 1 scored older.
Mean triglycerides in the program group fell from 112 to 89 mg/dL.

Limits, as the authors say: small sample, one clock, many program parts at once, and no proof that clock changes alter disease risk.

It says the comparison between groups is unchanged but does not explain why the corrected figures add to 3.14 rather than 3.23.

For this trial, none of the 11 added clocks changed significantly in the reported direction, and the original effect reached only p = 0.09. They recommend reporting several clocks and their average.

Higgins-Chen has received consulting fees from TruDiagnostic and FOXO Biosciences; R. Sehgal from TruDiagnostic, LongevityTech.fund and Cambrian BioPharma; the other authors declare none.

could_be_wrong.point: The authors themselves say the small sample limits statistical power and that no single part of the program can be credited.
The corrected within-group changes add to 3.14 years, but the correction keeps the 3.23-year gap without explaining the difference.
When the public data were rescored with 11 more clocks, none changed significantly in the reported direction, and the original clock's effect reached only p = 0.09.
Retesting the same person can shift clock age by about 0.9 to 2.4 years from technical noise alone, a range close to the trial's effect.
could_be_wrong.source: Borrus et al. 2026 (citing Higgins-Chen et al. 2022)

could_be_wrong.point: The trial's registry entry lists a quality-of-life questionnaire as the primary outcome and the methylation array as an additional outcome, and the paper found no difference between groups on emotional health.
In the large two-year CALERIE caloric restriction trial, only one of three clocks (DunedinPACE) slowed, and the effects were small, which suggests results depend on the clock chosen.

summary: In 1952 Alan Turing proposed that stripes and spots can grow out of random noise, when tiny differences in a uniform field are amplified; at DDW 2026 Ralf Jacobs stitched that idea into an embroidered banner.
A 2022 review says the idea got a boost from fish skin and digit patterns, while fruit fly stripes turned out to use a different, step-by-step genetic mechanism.
The review also argues that brain wiring may be where Turing's ideas matter most, which is still a proposal.
start_here.how_sure_note: Turing-type patterning is well supported for some animal patterns and ruled out for others, and the brain idea is one author's proposal.

claims.claim: Stripes and spots can grow out of random noise; at DDW 2026, an artist stitched the maths behind that idea.
Ralf Jacobs embroidered Alan Turing's own mathematics, starting with noise, with the Queer Needlework Circle.
Turing published The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis in 1952, the same year he was convicted for being gay.
His idea: pattern arises by amplifying differences concealed in the random disorder of molecules and cells.
Turing-type models got a boost from fish skin and digit patterns; fruit fly stripes turned out to use another mechanism.
claims.where: Abstract; sections on stripes, spots and digits; Fig. 2 legend

claims.claim: In 1951 Turing wrote to J. Z. Young about the brain; Lacalli argues brain wiring may be where his ideas matter most. It is still a proposal.
Equality is the unstable state: DayDayGay on Ralf Jacobs' embroidered work at Cocktales 10, Plug-In-Paviljoen, Strijp-S, 24 October 2026.

annotations.source: Lacalli 2022
annotations.note: A review of Turing's 1952 theory of pattern formation, from plant shoots to animal skins, centred on order from fluctuations: patterns built by amplifying small random differences. It weighs where the theory fits and where it failed, and ends with a case for applying it to brain development. Limits: a single-author review, and the brain section is a proposal, not a test.
annotations.funding: Funds to support this work were received from the Lionel G. Harrison Research Trust.
annotations.conflicts: The author declares that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.

could_be_wrong.point: The review notes disappointments for theorists: patterns that seemed to match Turing's predictions were later shown to arise by other mechanisms.
Fruit fly segment stripes, once a hoped-for example, proved not to depend on a Turing-type mechanism; they come from a detailed set of genes acting in steps.

Even where Turing's logic fits, the details often differ from his original model: other self-enhancing processes replace chemical reactions, and fish patterns come from cells interacting rather than diffusing chemicals.
The idea that Turing's theory matters most for brain wiring is presented as a case that can be made, not a tested result.

summary: Casinos are often said to hide clocks so visitors lose track of time; we searched and found no study that tests this.
Studies of regular slot players link absorbed dark flow play to enjoyment and problem-gambling scores, and regular gamblers chose smaller, sooner rewards more often in a slot venue than in a cafe.
Gamers did not, on average, underestimate how long they had played, and the one tested clock reminder, a pop-up in online blackjack, made no difference.
start_here.how_sure_note: The clock claim is untested; the related studies are small, tested gamblers or gamers rather than casino visitors, and several come from one lab.

claims.claim: Casinos are often said to hide clocks so visitors lose track of time; we searched for a study that tests this and found none.

Three studies from one lab agree.

claims.claim: 30 regular gamblers chose smaller, sooner rewards more often in a slot-machine venue than in a cafe; no non-gamblers tested.

claims.claim: Gamers stopped after 12, 35 or 58 minutes did not, on average, underestimate how long they had played; 116 people.

summary: A name has no synonym: forget the word for scissors and you can describe it, but forget a person's name and nothing else will do.
In 5,907 US adults over 70, scores on naming objects barely moved from 2004 to 2012, while naming the President and Vice President fell from 1.75 to 1.49 out of 2.
Linking a face to a name is arbitrary, which makes it demanding, and the front of the temporal lobes plays a part in recalling names.
start_here.how_sure_note: The survey is large and the gap between names and objects is long known, but it used only two items of each kind and the names changed after the 2008 election.

claims.claim: A name has no synonym; blank on it, and no other word can stand in.

Matching a face to a name is arbitrary, which makes it demanding, and the front of the temporal lobes plays a part in recalling names.

could_be_wrong.point: The survey used only two object and two name items, and the people to name changed after the 2008 election, which the authors link to the 2010 dip; older and less educated people may also follow the news less.
Not every study finds that older adults lose names more than other words; some found results inconsistent with this claim, possibly because familiarity and testing differed between age groups.
The brain stimulation result comes from 14 people in one session, on slow trials only; it is early lab work, not a treatment or advice.
Much of the brain evidence on naming people comes from small samples of patients and volunteers, which the review notes.

summary: In 1,112 Israeli parole rulings, favourable decisions fell from about 65 percent to near zero within each session, then jumped back after a food break.
Why is still argued: granting took longer, and a simulated judge who never tires but holds long cases until after the break makes a similar drop.
The lab idea of willpower running out has also weakened: a 36-lab test found an effect of d = 0.06 that was not significant, and a large nurse study found no decision fatigue.
start_here.how_sure_note: The drop is in the data, but why it happened is still debated, and the willpower idea behind it failed a large replication.

summary: In a lab task, 22 adults kept nine spoken digits in order while sentences they were told to ignore played; the clearer the ignored speech, the fewer digits came back in order.
Older adults scored lower overall but paid the same cost, and whether a sentence ended predictably made no difference.
In a survey of 1,078 office workers, most named lost concentration as the main effect of colleagues' chatter; no study here measured a trade show hall.
start_here.how_sure_note: The memory cost of background speech is an old, often repeated finding, but the clarity result here rests on one study of 22 people and the office numbers are self-report.

claims.claim: Speech you are trying to ignore still taxes memory; the clearer the ignored speech, the more it cost.
claims.study: one lab study, 22 adults, 120 trials each

claims.claim: Younger adults recalled 66 percent of digits in order with blurred background speech and 58 percent with clear speech; older adults 52 and 45 percent.
claims.where: Results, proportions correct at 2, 8 and 32 channels; Fig. 2
claims.study: one lab study, 12 younger and 10 older adults

claims.claim: Older adults recalled fewer digits overall (48 against 61 percent), but clear speech cost both groups about the same; predictable sentence endings made no difference.
claims.where: Results (age comparison; Bayes factor for predictability)

claims.claim: 69 and 66 percent of 1,078 office workers named lost concentration as the main effect of colleagues' chatter.
claims.study: one online survey, 1,078 office workers in Italy

claims.claim: Headphones were the main way of coping for 22 percent in shared and 32 percent in open-plan offices.
In open-plan offices, 72 percent said they would lower their voices if a light signalled that the room was too loud.
Offices of more than 20 people had 8.7 times the annoyance odds of offices of 6 to 20, with a range of 1.1 to 68.
claims.study: regression on survey data; about 1 percent of respondents worked in large open-plan offices

claims.claim: Five studies, 13,277 employees: open-plan offices went with modestly higher odds of sick leave, a finding about office type, not noise alone.
claims.study: systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 mostly cross-sectional studies

claims.claim: US workplace rules start a hearing conservation program at an 85 decibel average over 8 hours.

annotations.source: Wöstmann and Obleser 2016
annotations.note: Twelve younger and ten older adults held nine spoken digits in order while ignoring three sentences, blurred to 2, 8 or 32 channels of detail. More detail meant worse recall at both ages; whether sentence endings were predictable did not matter. Limits: 22 people, lab digits, and unconnected sentences; the authors say longer connected speech is an open question. CC BY, open in PMC5078496.

Limits stated by the authors: the questionnaire was not validated, the design is cross-sectional, and more annoyed people may have been more likely to answer. CC BY, open in PMC6351961.

could_be_wrong.point: One small study. The clarity result rests on 22 people; the authors used Bayes factors partly to deal with the small sample, and they note that only single, unconnected sentences were tested.
The office survey is self-report with an unvalidated questionnaire, it is cross-sectional, and people more annoyed by chatter may have been more likely to fill it in.
The 8.7 odds ratio for large offices has a range from 1.1 to 68, because only about 1 percent of respondents worked in large open-plan offices, so the true size is very uncertain.
The sick leave link is small, its ranges include no effect, and it is about office type, not noise; the review found only five studies and one longitudinal one.

People differ a lot. Two experiments failed to replicate the one earlier finding that predicted who is most disrupted, and the authors conclude that a measure predicting a person's disruption remains elusive.
could_be_wrong.source: Elliott et al. 2020 (read in full for the long form; not in set.json)

could_be_wrong.point: Meaning is debated. A review of the field says meaning matters little in serial recall and that backward speech disrupts almost as much as forward speech, while a 2025 study found meaningful speech cut accuracy a little more than scrambled syllables.
could_be_wrong.source: Ellermeier and Zimmer 2014 (read in full for the long form; not in set.json)

glossary.plain: The drop in short-term memory when speech you are told to ignore plays in the background.
The small mental workspace that holds information, like a phone number, for a few seconds while you use it.
Repeating a list back in the exact order you heard it.
A way of blurring speech by keeping its rhythm but removing detail; fewer channels make it harder to understand.
One frequency band kept in noise-vocoded speech; 2 channels sound like rough noise, 32 sound close to clear speech.
How easy it is to guess the last word of a sentence from the words before it.
A workspace where many people share one room without walls between desks.
How much more likely an outcome is in one group than in a comparison group; 1 means no difference.
The span of values the true result most likely falls in; a wide span means an uncertain result.
A survey taken at one point in time, which can show links but not causes.
A study that pools the results of several studies to get one overall estimate.
A sound level scale adjusted to match how human ears hear different pitches.
The average sound level over a work shift, usually 8 hours.
The noise testing, hearing tests, training and ear protection US employers must provide from an 85 dBA average.
Certification that a testing lab meets a set standard for competence and quality. ISO/IEC 17025 is the international lab standard that New York and many other states require of cannabis testing labs.
A brain-imaging method that records the tiny magnetic fields made by the brain's electrical activity, moment by moment.
Information that comes straight from the person, such as how they rate their own pain or sleep, rather than from a lab test or device.

summary: A 2024 review of 113 studies in young adults found that one bout of exercise gives a small boost to thinking speed, but walking on its own showed no clear effect.
Pooling 50 studies, one aerobic session made people a little faster at ignoring distractors, and exercise lifts mood more steadily than it lifts focus.
Adding a second task to walking has a cost: in small studies, a hand task slowed 12 young adults by 15 percent, and harder memory tasks worsened both walking and answers.
start_here.how_sure_note: The exercise effects come from large meta-analyses but are small and vary a lot; the dual-task costs come from small single studies.

Reaction time to the tone task rose from 282 ms alone to 344 ms while walking.

summary: An early-afternoon dip in alertness, roughly 2 to 4 pm, is common.
In one lab, 17 students who usually nap skipped their nap; bright bluish light cut their sleepiness and helped working memory, though a nap helped more on some measures.
In a second lab, bluish and reddish office light shifted brain waves toward alertness in 20 men, but sleepiness and scores did not beat normal office light.
start_here.how_sure_note: Two small lab studies with different lights point in different directions, and reviews of daytime light find small, uneven effects.

claims.claim: An early-afternoon dip in alertness is common, roughly 2 to 4 pm; one lab kept 17 students who usually nap awake after lunch.
claims.study: one lab crossover study, 17 habitual nappers (11 women)

claims.claim: Without their nap, they rated sleepiness 5.5 of 9; under bright bluish light 3.5; after a nap 2.4.
On a working memory task, accuracy was 63 percent without the nap, 78 under bright bluish light and 76 after a nap.
Lapses of attention were 5.3 percent without the nap and 1.7 after one; bright light, at 2.8, was not a significant change.
In 20 men, bluish and reddish office light shifted brain waves toward alertness; sleepiness and test scores did not improve compared with normal office light.
claims.where: Results: EEG lower alpha, KSS, task accuracy
claims.study: one lab study, 20 men, four light conditions

claims.claim: Without the nap, negative mood rose to 1.75 of 5; under bright light it was 1.18.

annotations.source: Zhou et al. 2021
annotations.note: Seventeen Chinese students who nap daily had three afternoons in random order: nap, no nap under ordinary light, and no nap under bright bluish light. Bright light cut sleepiness and negative mood and helped working memory, but not lapses of attention or response inhibition. Limits stated by the authors: lunch, sleep and light history not controlled, and brightness and color changed together. CC BY, open in PMC8215386.
annotations.funding: Guangzhou Philosophy and Social Sciences Planning Project (2019GZQN19), Science and Technology Program of Guangzhou (2019050001), Program for Chang Jiang Scholars and Innovative Research Teams in Universities (IRT_17R40), Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Optical Information Materials and Technology (2017B030301007); the article record also lists the National Key Research and Development Program of China (2016YFB0401202).
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.

annotations.source: Askaripoor et al. 2019
annotations.note: Twenty young men worked in a mock office from about 1:50 pm under dim, normal white, blue-enriched white and reddish white light. Bluish and reddish light lowered alpha brain waves against normal light; all white lights beat dim light on sleepiness and mood, but not each other, and task accuracy did not change. Limits stated: lunch not measured, young men only. CC BY-NC-ND, facts only.
annotations.funding: The authors thank the vice-chancellor for Research and Technology, Hamadan University of Medical Sciences, for financial support.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare that they have no competing interest.

could_be_wrong.point: Tiny samples: 17 and 20 people, each in one lab. The Zhou study tested only habitual nappers who skipped their nap, so its results may not apply to people who do not nap.

In the Zhou study the bright light was ten times brighter and bluer at once, so the authors cannot say whether brightness or color did the work, and lunch, sleep and earlier light were not controlled.

The two studies used very different lights: Zhou's bright light gave about 12 times the melanopic light of its control (998 against 83), while Askaripoor's bluish light gave about twice its control (388 against 195). That gap may explain why they disagree.

In Askaripoor, all white lights did cut sleepiness and some response times compared with dim light; what failed was beating normal office light. Lunch composition was not measured, and only young men took part.

Reviews are cautious. A Cochrane review of workplace lighting found only five studies and rated the evidence that high color temperature light helps alertness as very low quality, with two studies sponsored by industry.
could_be_wrong.source: Pachito et al. 2018 (read in full for the long form; not in set.json)

could_be_wrong.point: A 500 lux study room in Munich found no change in task scores or felt alertness with more melanopic light, in the morning or at 5 pm; the authors disclosed that a lighting company supplied materials and participant payments.
could_be_wrong.source: Zauner et al. 2020 (read in full for the long form; not in set.json)

summary: Going without any drink for 13 hours cost people about 1 percent of body weight, and 37 hours about 2.7 percent, in a study a 2011 review reports.
In one small study, 12 young men went 36 hours without drinking: thirst and fatigue rose and some test scores dipped, then improved an hour after water.
A 2011 review found little evidence that everyday dehydration harms thinking in healthy young adults; the steadiest results come from children given a drink of water.
start_here.how_sure_note: Studies in adults disagree, are small and are hard to blind, and the one primary study here had 12 men, no control group and a practice effect.

claims.claim: With no drink at all for 13 hours, people lost about 1 percent of body weight; after 37 hours, 2.7 percent.
claims.where: Section on defining dehydration (reporting Shirreffs et al. 2004, reference 32)
claims.study: review reporting one fluid restriction study

claims.claim: 12 young men went 36 hours without drinking, with meals; urine concentration rose from 803 to 1,123, then fell to 387 after water.
claims.study: one self-controlled trial, 12 men, no separate control group

claims.claim: Their digit memory score dipped from 14.3 to 13.3, then rose to 15.4 an hour after water.
Self-rated vigour fell from 11.9 to 8.8 after 36 hours; fatigue eased after water, from 4.3 to 2.1.
One task rose at every session, dry or not: 67.5, 70.8, then 75.4; each man did the tests in the same order.
In children, 79 percent of class time was on task after a drink of water and 53 percent without, as reported.
claims.where: Section 5.6.5 and Table 1 (Benton and Davis, 22 children aged 9)
claims.study: review reporting one classroom study, 22 children

annotations.source: Benton 2011
annotations.note: A review of dehydration, mood and thinking. It concludes that in young adults there is little consistent evidence that everyday dehydration disrupts cognition, that many adult studies are confounded by heat and exercise, and that results in children are the most consistent. Limits: a 2011 narrative review; the children's figures come partly from the author's own study. CC BY, open in PMC3257694.
annotations.funding: not stated (no funding statement in the full text)
annotations.conflicts: not stated (no conflict statement in the full text); the children's study it reports with the 78.8 and 53.0 percent figures is the author's own (Benton and Davis).

annotations.source: Zhang et al. 2019
annotations.note: Twelve male students in Cangzhou, China, were tested at baseline, after 36 hours without drinks (meals allowed) and an hour after water. Thirst, urine concentration and fatigue rose; vigour fell; most scores improved after water. Limits: 12 men, no control group, the same test order each time, and sweat and conditions not recorded. CC BY, open in PMC6603652.
annotations.funding: Danone Institute China (DIC2015-10). Danone sells bottled water.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

could_be_wrong.point: No control group and a fixed test order. Digit-symbol scores rose at every session, even while the men were dry, which points to practice, so part of the 'recovery' after water may be learning.

The dip in total digit span after 36 hours (14.3 to 13.3) was not marked as significant in Table 4; only the rise after water was. On a color-word test the men were slightly faster while dehydrated (30.7 to 30.2 seconds).
The study was funded by the Danone Institute China; Danone sells bottled water. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

After 13 hours with no fluid, blood concentration was still within the normal range, and the review finds little consistent evidence of harm to thinking in young adults under normal living conditions.

People know when they have had water, so most studies cannot be blinded. One study that disguised dehydration with a pill and opaque bottles notes that earlier studies were not blinded, and a later review calls blinding particularly difficult.

could_be_wrong.point: A 2019 review of the field calls the evidence linking mild dehydration to thinking largely associative and inconsistent.

summary: In a 2020 study, 74 university students answered a short text four times a day for four days about how tired they felt and how sociable they had been in the last hour.
Acting sociable went with better mood at the time and with feeling more tired at the next check-in, 2 to 3 hours later, but not with tiredness in the same hour.
The link held after the researcher accounted for time of day, earlier tiredness and work or study, but the study is correlational and small, with mostly women.
start_here.how_sure_note: One small correlational study with a single question for sociability; it repeats an earlier, smaller study by the same research group, and a 2025 sensor study found a similar delayed tiredness.

claims.claim: Acting sociable went with feeling more tired 2 to 3 hours later, not in the moment.
74 students, 1,046 check-ins.
Students got a text four times a day for four days, at 11, 2, 5 and 8, and answered 1,046 of 1,184.
Tiredness rose toward evening but sociability did not.

The link held when each day's last or first check-in was dropped (0.16 and 0.18).
The estimate was 0.19, with a 95 percent range of 0.10 to 0.26.
The link did not vary detectably between people.
Participants were 58 women and 16 men, mean age 26.8.
People higher in trait emotional stability felt less tired overall (estimate -0.29).

Sociable behaviour in the previous hour predicted more tiredness at the next text, 2 to 3 hours later, and better mood at the time. Limits, as the author states: a small sample, many more women than men, one 'sociable' item, and too few people to test whether trait extraversion changes the link. Read in full through the Europe PMC open copy (PMC7260435, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0).

annotations.note: A one-week randomized trial in 147 adults: acting bold and outgoing raised positive feelings on average and did not change tiredness on average. The most extraverted felt less tired in the moment and the most introverted more tired. Limits, as the authors state: the tiredness measures were new, and those results are tentative. Read in full as the accepted manuscript on OSF (CC BY 4.0).

More people nearby went with more vigor at once and more fatigue later, with the peak effect on negative mood about 3 hours on. Limits: effects were small, Bluetooth passes through walls, and personality was not measured. Read in full in the Europe PMC copy (PMC12179627, CC BY).

could_be_wrong.point: The author writes that the sample was too small to test whether trait extraversion changes the link, so finding no difference between people is not a test built for that question.
Sociability was one self-rated item, 'sociable', which the author calls a very narrow measure; the result may not apply to other sides of outgoing behaviour, such as being dominant.

In a one-week trial of 147 adults, acting outgoing did not change tiredness on average, but the most introverted people felt more tired in the moment and the most extraverted less; the authors call the tiredness results tentative.
In the earlier 12-day study by the same group, the number of people met did predict later tiredness and explained 36 percent of the link, unlike the 2020 result for meeting people.

A 2025 study that counted nearby Bluetooth devices found the same pattern, more energy at once and more tiredness later, but the effects were small, Bluetooth can pass through walls, and personality was not measured.
No study measured a trade show floor. The post's advice to plan a break before the afternoon is its own reading and has not been tested.

glossary.plain: A study method that asks people short questions several times a day as they go about their lives.
One answered questionnaire, here sent by text message at a fixed time of day.
How talkative and outgoing a person says they acted in the last hour, rated on one item.
A personality trait describing how outgoing, talkative and energetic a person tends to be.
Someone low in extraversion, who tends to be quieter and more reserved.
A link between something at one time point and an outcome at the next time point, here 2 to 3 hours later.
Measured at the same time, here within the same hour.
The number a statistical model gives for how much one thing changes with another, on the study's 1 to 5 scale.
The span of values the true effect most plausibly lies in, given the data.
Shows that two things go together, not that one causes the other.
A personality trait describing how calm and even-tempered a person tends to be.
Acting organised, careful and dependable.
A state of balance among the body's systems, such as temperature, blood pressure and blood sugar, that keeps it working.
A method that pools data from many studies on the same question to get a stronger overall answer.

A way of comparing how likely something is in one group with how likely it is in another. An odds ratio of 1 means no difference; above 1 means higher odds in the first group. It is often used in backward-looking (case-control) studies and shows a link, not a cause.
Information that comes straight from the person, such as how they rate their own pain or sleep, rather than from a lab test or device.

safety.note: Education, not medical advice. Tiredness that does not lift with rest, or that comes with low mood, is worth raising with a doctor; in the US, call or text 988 in a crisis.

summary: ARKANA (Nova Arkana), an edible oracle by Joanna Wallace Cuervo, won the Experimental award at Psychedelics Design 2026, and food art like hers is seen before it is tasted.
A long record of studies shows that a drink's colour can change which flavour people name: a cherry drink dyed green was called lime by 26% of tasters.
In one 2020 study, a headset changed only how far light and dark spread across a cake, and 13 students rated the same cake less moist and less delicious; sweetness did not change.
start_here.how_sure_note: Colour's pull on naming a flavour has been shown many times; the contrast study is two small experiments of 13 students with small effects that have not been repeated.

claims.where: Winners Gallery 2026, Experimental entry and winner card

A cherry drink dyed green was called lime by 26% of tasters; dyed orange, nearly 20% said orange; dyed red, none named either fruit.

It finds that colour most reliably changes which flavour people name, while effects on how strong a taste seems are mixed. Limits: a narrative review by one author, and many of the studies it reports were small lab tests in which colour was often the only cue.

could_be_wrong.point: The contrast study was small. Each experiment had 13 students, and the authors report a statistical power of 0.56, so a real effect of the size they planned for could be missed more than 4 times in 10.
The ratings differed only between the most extreme settings, 0.5 and 3.0, and the effects were small, so it is not clear that everyday changes in lighting would shift taste at all.
Results on whether colour changes how strong a taste seems are mixed, and several studies found nothing; the review calls those effects not altogether clear.
In the lab, colour is often the only cue people have to go on, which may make its effect look larger than it would be at a real meal with smell, labels and context.

A 2023 systematic review of 52 papers found that visual cues change taste and flavour intensity only under certain conditions, with mixed or null results in a number of studies, and most studies were not pre-registered or planned with power calculations (read in full as the accepted manuscript; the package's long form log records the read).

Outside the lab, plate colour did not change sweetness: at a Lyon restaurant, 253 diners rated desserts on white or black plates, and sweetness depended only on the dessert, though liking and appeal did shift.

summary: Being judged, with little control over how it goes, switches on two stress systems: heart rate rises within minutes, and the stress hormone cortisol peaks about 20 to 30 minutes after the start.
At real solo recitals, 39 music students' cortisol rose before they played and stayed up for at least 30 minutes after.

In 298 piano students in China, more stage anxiety went with lower expert ratings of their playing, partly through lower confidence and weaker attention control; it was one snapshot, so it shows a link, not a cause.
start_here.how_sure_note: The lab stress response is well studied across many experiments; the link between stage anxiety and rated playing comes from one cross-sectional study in one province.

claims.claim: In 298 student pianists, more stage anxiety went with lower expert ratings of their playing.
One snapshot: a link, not a cause.
Classic lab trigger: usually 5 minutes to prepare, a 5-minute mock job interview, 5 minutes of surprise arithmetic, judges giving no positive feedback.
claims.where: Description of the TSST and of its CAVE virtual versions
claims.study: review of the Trier Social Stress Test and its virtual reality versions

claims.claim: Being judged with little control raises heart rate within minutes and cortisol over about 20 to 30, in person and in VR.
claims.where: Sections on stress mechanisms and on physiological responses in TSST-VR
claims.study: review of the Trier Social Stress Test and its virtual reality versions

claims.claim: Part of the link ran through confidence: more anxious players felt less able, and that went with weaker attention control.
Almost half the anxiety link passed through confidence and attention; the rest was direct.
The pianists were 18 to 26, all in one Chinese province, playing one piece each.
The authors note some arousal can help performers.
Stage anxiety alone accounted for about 23 percent of the spread in rated performance.
At solo recitals, 39 music students' cortisol rose before they played and stayed up for at least 30 minutes after.
claims.study: one field study, 39 students, two recitals each

claims.claim: Five judges' averages were within 0.03 of each other on a 10-point scale.

annotations.source: Sun and Zhou 2026
annotations.note: A survey of 298 piano majors in Yunnan, China, with recorded playing of one set piece rated by five senior experts who did not see the questionnaires. More stage anxiety went with lower ratings, partly through lower self-efficacy and attention control. Limits: one time point, one province, one piece, and self-report scales.
annotations.funding: The authors declared that no financial support was received for this work.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declared no commercial or financial relationships that could be a potential conflict of interest.

annotations.source: von Dawans et al. 2026
annotations.note: A review of the Trier Social Stress Test, a mock job interview and surprise arithmetic before unsmiling judges, and its virtual reality versions. The in-person test reliably raises heart rate and cortisol; VR versions raise felt stress and heart rate but often less cortisol. Read in full through Europe PMC (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, facts only).
annotations.funding: not stated
annotations.conflicts: The authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships.

annotations.source: Turan et al. 2022
annotations.note: Saliva from 39 University of Alabama at Birmingham music students on a neutral day and around two solo recitals. Cortisol rose with the recital and stayed above the neutral-day level for at least 30 minutes after; alpha-amylase was higher before playing. Limits: a small sample (24 women, 15 men), and the recitals were in-class performances whose quality did not set the grade. Read in full through Europe PMC (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, facts only).
annotations.funding: A University of Alabama at Birmingham Faculty Development Grant to Bulent Turan.
annotations.conflicts: The authors declared no conflicts of interest.

could_be_wrong.point: The piano study measured everything at one time, so it cannot say whether anxiety lowers playing, weaker playing raises anxiety, or something else drives both; the authors say this themselves.
All the pianists came from one province in China and each played one piece, so the result may not hold for other musicians, other countries or real concerts.
Virtual reality versions of the stress test raise felt stress and heart rate reliably but often raise cortisol less, with more people showing no cortisol rise, than the in-person test.
The '5 minutes to prepare' step is common but not fixed: across 35 studies, preparation lasted 3, 5 or 10 minutes, which makes results harder to compare.

The popular idea that some arousal helps performance, the inverted U, is often told as the Yerkes-Dodson law, but the 1908 work found a straight-line link for easy tasks and a curve only for hard ones.
None of these studies tested a way to reduce stage fright. A meta-analysis of 35 trials of stress reappraisal found small gains that shrank after correcting for missing studies.

How spread out the scores are; 'accounts for 23 percent of the variance' means it lines up with about a quarter of that spread.
The idea that performance is best at middle levels of arousal and worse when arousal is too low or too high.
A hormone and neurotransmitter released in stress that speeds the heart and readies the body for action.
Conditions in which worry, fear and dread are strong and lasting enough to disrupt daily life. They include generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder and PTSD.

glossary.term: Autonomic nervous system: sympathetic and parasympathetic
glossary.plain: The automatic control system for heart rate, breathing and digestion. The sympathetic side speeds things up for action (fight or flight); the parasympathetic side slows the heart and supports rest and digestion. The vagus nerve is the main parasympathetic nerve.
How big a difference or link is, not just whether it exists. It is one of the main things that decide whether a result matters in practice.
A substance made by a gland that travels in the blood and changes how certain cells or organs work. Cortisol and melatonin are hormones.
A method that pools data from many studies on the same question to get a stronger overall answer.
A review that uses clear, planned methods to find, select and combine the results of all the studies on a clearly stated question. A meta-analysis is often part of one.
Computer-made surroundings that feel like a real place. A group VR study produced ego-dissolving, connected states that scored like published psychedelic studies on its measures.

safety.note: Education, not medical advice. If anxiety about performing or speaking disrupts daily life, a doctor or psychologist can help; in the US, call or text 988 in a crisis.

summary: A master clock in the brain keeps daily rhythms, and light reaching the eye is its main time cue: morning light moves it earlier, evening and night light push it later.

In 2022, light scientists agreed three indoor targets for healthy adults aged 18 to 55: at least 250 lux melanopic EDI at the eye by day, at most 10 from 3 hours before bed, and at most 1 during sleep.
In one early field study, 89 UK adults wore light sensors for a week, and longer, steadier daytime light went with earlier sleep timing.
start_here.how_sure_note: The clock and its light input are settled science and the targets are an expert consensus built on lab data; the field results are early and observational.

annotations.note: The first expert consensus on indoor light for the body clock, sleep and alertness, from a 2019 workshop. It sets targets in melanopic EDI measured at the eye for healthy adults 18 to 55. Limits: built mostly on lab studies in healthy adults with regular daytime schedules; the authors say special considerations may apply to children, older people and shift workers.

annotations.source: Akgun et al. 2026
annotations.note: 89 healthy Manchester adults wore wrist light sensors and sleep trackers for a week. Most fell short of the daytime target on many days, and longer, more regular daytime light went with earlier sleep. Limits, as the authors state: light measured at the wrist, not the eye, sensors too weak to read below 1 lux, small effects, and no control for activity or meal timing.
annotations.funding: Includes a BBSRC DTP CASE studentship and investigator-initiated grant funding from Signify/Philips Lighting, Wellcome Trust awards, TUBITAK and the Izmir Institute of Technology.

could_be_wrong.point: The targets come from lab studies of healthy adults aged 18 to 55 with regular daytime schedules; the authors say special considerations may apply to children, older people, shift workers and people whose light sensitivity is far from average.
Light was measured at the wrist, not the eye. The authors say wrist sensors can miss light from phones and screens in the evening, so the evening results should be read with caution.
In a lab test, two lights that looked the same but differed in melanopic light changed melatonin by about 14 percent but did not change sleep, sleepiness or alertness.
People differ widely: in 55 adults, the evening light needed to halve melatonin varied more than 50-fold, so one number will not fit everyone.
Several consensus authors and the field study's authors report funding or ties from lighting companies, including Signify; the papers disclose this, but readers should know it.

glossary.plain: A body cycle that repeats about every 24 hours, such as sleep and wake.
A small group of nerve cells in the hypothalamus that acts as the body's master clock.
A small region at the base of the brain that controls hormones, temperature and daily rhythms.
A signal from outside, such as light, that sets the body clock.
A light-sensing pigment in some eye cells that responds most to blue-green light and signals the body clock.
Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cell: an eye cell that contains melanopsin and sends light signals to the clock.
A unit of how much light falls on a surface.
Melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance: a light measure in lux weighted for how strongly it drives melanopsin.
A hormone the body makes in darkness that helps signal night; bright evening light holds it back.
Moving the body clock earlier (advance) or later (delay).
A unit for the wavelength of light; 480 nm is blue-green.
A study that measures what people already do, so it shows links, not causes.

A mental health condition with ongoing sadness, loss of energy and loss of pleasure that makes daily life hard. It can also bring feelings of worthlessness, changes in sleep or eating, and thoughts of death.
A substance made by a gland that travels in the blood and changes how certain cells or organs work. Cortisol and melatonin are hormones.

safety.note: Education, not medical advice. Ongoing sleep problems, or low mood in the darker months, are worth raising with a doctor; in the US, call or text 988 in a crisis.

summary: This round-up follows a trade show trip in six findings, from the flight in to the evening after a day of talking.

After travel, sleep length came back in about 2 days but sleep timing had not by day 15; ignored speech still cost memory; an after-lunch dip hit people who usually nap; a steady smell faded from notice within minutes.
Acting sociable went with feeling tired 2 to 3 hours later. No study here measured a trade show, and several are small.
start_here.how_sure_note: Each finding comes from one study, ranging from a 64,847-trip wearable dataset to lab studies of 17 to 74 people; the first-night result was not seen in two larger studies.

claims.claim: After 64,847 trips, sleep length recovered in about 2 days. Sleep timing had not by day 15, worst going east.
claims.study: one observational wearable study, 57,240 sleep-ring users

claims.claim: Night one, new bed: 27 people woke more than on night two.
claims.study: one sleep-lab study, 27 people, two nights of high-density EEG

claims.claim: Larger studies of 124 and 240 adults found no first-night difference.
claims.study: one sleep-lab study, 124 healthy young men, two nights

claims.claim: In 240 adults monitored at home with wrist actigraphy, there was no first-night difference; total sleep was about 3 minutes apart.
claims.study: one actigraphy study, 240 adults, five nights

claims.claim: Speech you ignore still costs memory: younger adults recalled 66 percent of digits with muffled talk, 58 with clear.
claims.study: one lab study, 22 listeners (12 younger, 10 older)

claims.claim: Older listeners showed the same pattern: 52, 47 and 45 percent.
After lunch, 17 habitual nappers kept awake rated sleepiness 5.5 of 9; under bright light, 3.5; after a nap, 2.4.
Working memory accuracy was 63 percent without the nap, 78 under bright light and 76 after a nap.
Lapses of attention were 5.3 percent without the nap and 1.7 after one; bright light, 2.8, was not a significant change.
A steady smell rated 7.5 at the first breath fell to 4.6 a minute later; half stopped noticing it within 6 to 7 minutes.
Acting sociable went with feeling tired 2 to 3 hours later, not at the time.
Tiredness rose from 2.34 at 11 am to 2.74 at 8 pm on a 1 to 5 scale.
Across 11,481 NBA games, home teams carrying two hours of eastward jet lag lost by almost 3 points on average; westward jet lag showed no such cost.

could_be_wrong.point: No study in this round-up measured a trade show. Each finding comes from a lab, a sleep ring or a phone survey, and the post's advice is its own untested reading.

The first-night result came from one small lab study whose effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons, and two larger studies, of 124 and 240 adults, found no first-night difference in waking or sleep efficiency.
The travel data are sleep-ring estimates from people who own the ring, cover outbound trips only, and belong to the ring maker, which employs or advises two authors.
In the after-lunch study, bright light lowered sleepiness, but its drop in attention lapses was not significant; only the nap made a clear difference, in 17 people.

How fast a smell fades depends on the method: a study with a different test found ratings fell in about two minutes, and attention can bring the smell back. That study was supported by Unilever, where one author works.
The NBA jet lag study assumed teams flew straight to their next game, because league schedules do not show travel, so the jet lag each team carried is an estimate.

summary: In the US, 'child resistant' is a federal test: pairs of children aged 42 to 51 months get 5 minutes to open a package, see one demonstration, then try for 5 more minutes.
To pass, at least 85 percent of the children must fail before the demonstration and 80 percent after, and at least 90 percent of 100 adults aged 50 to 70 must open and close it properly.
So some children are expected to get in: in Canadian emergency data, 904 children and youth were hurt by detergent packets from 2011 to 2023, most aged 4 or under and almost all at home.
start_here.how_sure_note: The test rules are quoted from the federal regulation; the injury figures come from one large surveillance system that does not cover every hospital.

could_be_wrong.point: Passing the test does not mean no child can open the package: up to 15 percent of children may open it before the demonstration and up to 20 percent after, and unit packaging needs only 80 percent.
The test runs in a familiar nursery or kindergarten setting with a calm tester and a 10-minute limit; children at home may have more time, watch adults, or find a package left open.
Child resistance only works if the package is closed: in a 2012 Atlanta trial with 110 children aged 3 and 4, 82 percent emptied incompletely closed bottles within 2 minutes.

In calls to five US poison centers in 2017, more than half of the prescription pills young children swallowed had already been taken out of the original packaging by an adult, so no child-resistant closure stood in the way.
The Canadian figures come from a sentinel hospital network, not all emergency departments, so they show patterns, not national rates; rural, Indigenous and fatal cases are under-represented.
The fall in poisonings after 2015 lines up with a voluntary standard, but the study cannot show the standard caused it, and some makers changed packets from 2013.

summary: At Psychedelics Design 2026, Joyce Braverman, MD, cited James Clear: one per cent better every day makes you 37 per cent better in a year.
Worked out, 1.01 multiplied by itself 365 times is about 37.8, so about 38 times the starting value, not 37 per cent; one per cent worse a day leaves about 0.03.
Missing compounding is common enough to have a name, exponential growth bias, and in one experiment 90 per cent of students guessed too low until the same growth was put as a doubling time.
start_here.how_sure_note: The arithmetic is certain and the bias is long documented, though the experiment here was one online study of students; nobody has measured a person improving one per cent a day.

could_be_wrong.point: The bias was measured in one online experiment with non-STEM students in Switzerland answering hypothetical questions, so the sizes may differ in other groups and real decisions.
Real habits do not compound. Studies of automaticity show a fast rise at first that slows to a plateau, the opposite shape to one per cent more each day.
How long a habit takes varies widely between people and depends on how a study defines a formed habit, so 59 to 66 days is a rough middle, not a rule.
Practice data fit a curve in which each stretch of practice removes a share of the remaining gap, so gains shrink over time rather than grow (read in full in the package's long form research).

annotations.note: University of Delaware lettuce trial: six light schedules under one LED spectrum for 28 days, run twice. Brighter steady light grew more mass with lower light use efficiency, and the 250, 250, 350 schedule matched bright steady light with 23 to 31 percent higher efficiency. Height rose consistently; weight, leaf area and fruit results varied, and chlorophyll usually fell. Limits: the studies used different setups and cultivars, and many did not report background conditions such as light and temperature.

could_be_wrong.point: The stepped-schedule result comes from one cultivar in one lab, and the two runs differed by 5 to 6 degrees in nutrient solution temperature; the authors say treating runs as blocks may not capture every interaction between root-zone temperature and light.
could_be_wrong.source: Kang, Ding and Meng (2026), Experimental limitations

could_be_wrong.point: The lettuce study counted light delivered, not electricity used or money spent, so a saving in light is not yet a measured saving in energy or cost. No replication had been published as of Nov 20, 2026.
could_be_wrong.source: Kang, Ding and Meng (2026), Methods and limitations

could_be_wrong.point: The tomato review says many studies did not report background conditions such as light and temperature, which makes it hard to tell why far-red results differ.
could_be_wrong.source: Fischer, Vänninen and Himanen (2026), Future perspectives

could_be_wrong.point: Far-red responses depend on cultivar. In lettuce, the same far red raised dry weight by 39 percent in 'Cherokee', 19 percent in 'Little Gem' and not at all in 'Green SaladBowl'.

Far red works differently at different brightness: more far red increased lettuce leaf expansion under strong light and reduced it under weak light, and the tomato review calls this interaction underexplored.
could_be_wrong.source: Kusuma and Bugbee (2023), Frontiers in Plant Science 14: 1185622

could_be_wrong.point: Whether far red should count as photosynthetic light is still debated: one group argues photons up to 750 nanometres should count, while the tomato review says the photosynthetic role of far red remains unclear.
could_be_wrong.source: Zhen, van Iersel and Bugbee (2021), Frontiers in Plant Science 12: 693445

could_be_wrong.point: The review's counts differ slightly between text and figure: the text gives 36 height and 43 dry-weight observations, while Fig. 2 gives n = 35 and n = 41.
could_be_wrong.source: Fischer, Vänninen and Himanen (2026), Results and Fig. 2 legend

Photosynthetic photon flux density, the number of light particles between 400 and 700 nanometres landing on a square metre each second.
The total amount of plant-usable light a plant receives over a whole day.
How many grams of plant grow for each unit of light delivered.
Light just past the red end of the rainbow, from about 700 to 800 nanometres, which people barely see but plants sense strongly.
The number of hours of light a plant gets each day.
A light-sensing pigment in plants that red light switches on and far-red light or darkness switches off.
A plant's response to more far red, such as stretching its stems and lifting its leaves, as if neighbours were shading it.
The green pigment in leaves that captures light for photosynthesis.
A review that counts and summarises the results of many studies on the same question.

summary: The Sphinx Gate, a walk-through rite of passage between two 44-foot sphinxes, won the Architectural & Space award at Psychedelics Design 2026.
Vast scenes, videos and memories reliably make people feel awe and a smaller sense of self.
But in six larger repeat studies, brief awe barely changed kindness, belief or life satisfaction, and no one has studied the Sphinx Gate itself.
start_here.how_sure_note: Stirring awe in a study works almost every time, but its after-effects held up poorly in larger repeats, and other reviews still find positive averages, so the question is contested.

could_be_wrong.point: The repeat studies could have missed real effects: the first three used a fixed order of questions, two drew online workers, and the authors suggest brief lab awe may be too subtle to change much.
could_be_wrong.source: Graziosi et al. (2026), Limitations and General Discussion

could_be_wrong.point: One direct repeat did not raise awe at all (2.76 against 2.48), so its null results on time and life satisfaction do not test the original claim.
The paper's text and figure disagree on Study 5: the Results text swaps the pride and neutral labels, while Fig. 5 and the planned contrasts agree with each other.
could_be_wrong.source: Graziosi et al. (2026), Study 5 and Fig. 5

could_be_wrong.point: Effects on time are mixed: in Amsterdam, awe videos did not reliably change time judgments in two small studies, while a Utah team found vaster images lengthened judged time.
could_be_wrong.source: van Elk and Rotteveel (2020), Attention, Perception, and Psychophysics

could_be_wrong.point: Awe can stretch or shrink time depending on what people are timing: longer when timing the images themselves, shorter when timing something else during them.
could_be_wrong.source: Droit-Volet, Dambrun and Monier (2024), Acta Psychologica

could_be_wrong.point: Longer, repeated awe may matter more than a single clip: in an eight-week awe-walk trial with 52 older adults, daily prosocial emotions rose and daily distress fell, though anxiety, depression, life satisfaction and helping did not change.
A small trial of four weekly online awe sessions in 68 adults with long COVID found less stress and depression and more well-being, but it used a waitlist control and short follow-up.

summary: How options are laid out, such as what is ticked by default or what comes first, can shift what people choose; researchers call this choice architecture.
A 2022 meta-analysis of 212 publications found an average effect of d = 0.43, with structure changes such as defaults working best and food choices moving most.
After correcting for missing null studies, other teams found an average near zero, so how big the effect really is remains under debate.
start_here.how_sure_note: The pooled data are large and public, but the corrected averages range from about zero to 0.31 depending on the method, and effects vary widely between studies.

could_be_wrong.point: After a correction for publication bias, the combined estimate fell to 0.04, and the authors conclude that no evidence remains that nudges work as a general tool; they add that wide variation means some nudges might still work.

Three other corrections gave -0.01, 0.07 and 0.08, and even under severe bias the estimated effects of single studies spread about 1.00 either side of the average, so a typical nudge is hard to predict.
The original authors accept that the true average is likely smaller than 0.43 and that the conditions behind the variation are mostly untested.

The meta-analysis first included four results from a since-retracted paper plus coding errors; the published correction fixed them and the headline stayed at 0.43. The paper also kept non-retracted studies from a lab criticized for misconduct, and reports that its results hold without them.

Across all 126 trials run by two US nudge units, with over 23 million people, nudges raised take-up by 1.4 percentage points, against 8.7 in published academic studies; publication bias and small samples could explain the gap.
Defaults look stronger: 58 default studies averaged d = 0.68, though most found an effect, several found none and two found the opposite.
The menu position study found items at the edges up to twice as popular, but in the real café only the soft drinks category showed a reliable shift on its own.
The decoy effect, a classic layout trick, did not appear in any of 19 studies that used options people could taste or see.

glossary.plain: The way options are presented, such as their order, layout or which one is preselected, without changing the options or their prices.
A change in choice architecture meant to steer behaviour in a predictable way without banning options or changing costs much.
The option a person gets if they do nothing, like a box that is already ticked.
A study that pools the results of many earlier studies to estimate an average effect.
A standard measure of how big a difference is, where 0.2 is usually called small and 0.5 medium.
The tendency for studies that find an effect to be published more often than studies that find nothing.
A check of how much a result changes under different assumptions, such as how severe publication bias is.
How much results differ from one study to the next, beyond what chance alone would cause.
A statistical method that tries to estimate what the average would be if the missing studies had been published.
