summary: The Kalahari truffle, Kalaharituber pfeilii, is an underground fungus that Kalahari peoples have long eaten, and in Khoisan lore it is the egg of the lightning bird because it appears after storms.
It fruits only after enough rain, partners with the roots of several Kalahari plants, ranks high for food energy and is also eaten by hyenas, meerkats, bat-eared foxes and baboons.
The food use is well recorded; the lore reaches the papers through one travel guide, and the truffle's main plant partner is still unknown.
start_here.how_sure_note: Two reviews agree on the food use and the rain, but the plant partners each rest on a single study and the lore and nutrition figures come second-hand.

could_be_wrong.point: The lightning-bird story is in print, but the 2008 review's only source for it is a 2007 travel guide, and no older ethnography of it was found.
The 2019 review repeats the lore with a citation that gives no older primary source, so both reviews rest on a thin record.
The main plant partner is unknown; the authors of the tsamma work later wrote that the melon is presumably not the original, and certainly not the sole, partner.
No rain threshold has been measured for the Kalahari truffle; the 180 mm figure comes from other desert truffles in Kuwait.
The energy ranking rests on one analysis of 24 vegetables, reported second-hand, and no source read gives a starch figure for this species.
Animal dispersal of the spores is little recorded, and no study has tracked how far animals carry them.
The reviews give different fruiting seasons: about April to July in the 2008 review, January to June in the 2019 review, which ties dates to local rain.
could_be_wrong.source: Trappe et al. 2008; Thomas et al. 2019

could_be_wrong.point: A genome study suggests the Kalahari truffle might fertilize itself, since it alone carries both mating-type genes, but the authors say this still needs testing.

summary: In two small Australian experiments, the same café latte was rated more intense from a white mug than from clear glass, and less sweet from a white-sleeved glass than from clear or blue ones.
Shown plain colour patches online, 452 people in China, India, Malaysia and the USA tended to pair pink with sweet, black with bitter, white with salty and green with sour.
The colour and taste matches are fairly solid, the mug effects are early, and why colours carry tastes is still debated, with learning from the world around us one leading idea.
start_here.how_sure_note: The mug results come from two small studies that each found a change on a different rating, while the colour and taste matches rest on one larger online study.

Limits: a narrative review that weighs accounts without settling between them.

could_be_wrong.point: The mug tests were small: 18 people split across three mugs and 36 split across three glasses, each person tasting from only one, and the experimenter knew the hypothesis.
Each test found a change on a different rating, intensity in the first and sweetness in the second, and bitterness, the barista's original claim, did not differ in either.
Why white mattered is unsettled: the authors suggest colour contrast and also discuss sensation transference and priming.
The jar, cup and plate findings are earlier studies that this post reports only as Van Doorn and colleagues describe them.
The colour and taste matches came from choosing a taste word for a colour patch online, with no food tasted, and the patterns for green and white differed by country.
The review treats the explanation as open: learning from the environment is one appealing account, and emotional mediation may also play a part.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, twofold Design Studio showed unwanted plates, cups and glasses part-coated in urushi, the sap of the lacquer tree, as a way to give them a second life.
Lab studies show the sap sets through an enzyme in damp air, and that strong UV light dulls and cracks the hardened film.
The chemistry is well supported, but the drying times and the UV damage come from single lab tests, and the studio's claims about microbes are its own.
start_here.how_sure_note: The enzyme account of how lacquer sets is well established; the exact times and gloss losses come from one lab study each, under set lab conditions.

summary: Eco-Amnesia, by nojoke studio at Vitalis Berckelhof during Dutch Design Week 2025, turned seniors' memories of nature into drawings, cards and story boxes.

A German study that weighed insect catches in 63 reserves found flying insect biomass fell about 76% from 1989 to 2016, and a review across 30 countries found older people usually hold a richer picture of normal nature.
The insect loss is well measured for those reserves but its cause is open, and the memory studies compare age groups at one time, so they cannot show baselines falling.
start_here.how_sure_note: The insect decline is a large, careful 27-year dataset from one region; the shifting baseline review is broad but rests on cross-sectional surveys.

could_be_wrong.point: Every study in the review compared age groups at one moment, so it cannot show whether baselines are actually falling over time.
Older people may recall change where there was little or none (a memory illusion effect), and most studies lacked historical records to check.

About 80% of the reviewed studies surveyed farmers, fishers and other primary industry workers, and only five were about biodiversity loss, so the result may differ for city residents and for insects.
The windshield sentence is the exhibition's memory; windshields are not how scientists count insects.

summary: In a small German trial, 24 people with severe lupus, systemic sclerosis or myositis got one infusion of their own immune cells, engineered to remove B cells.
22 of 24 met their disease's goal at 24 weeks, and all stayed off their usual immune drugs over that time, though 10 needed short steroid courses for a side effect.

There was no control group and follow-up is months to a few years, so this is early evidence; relapses have been reported elsewhere, and only bigger, longer trials can show how lasting and safe it is.
start_here.how_sure_note: One single-arm trial of 24 people plus an 11-person lupus series from the same centre; no randomized trial of this treatment yet.

could_be_wrong.point: CASTLE had no control group, so part of the improvement could come from other causes; the authors call the missing control arm a limitation.
14 of 24 took prednisolone as a bridge before the infusion and 4 had lupus flares treated before it; the authors say this may have influenced results, though they think it unlikely.
could_be_wrong.source: Müller et al. (2026), Results and Discussion

could_be_wrong.point: One serious adverse event did not resolve: lasting grade 3 kidney impairment after a lupus flare, and kidney damage markers appear in two lupus patients during follow-up.
could_be_wrong.source: Müller et al. (2026), Results; Extended Data Fig. 10

could_be_wrong.point: Relapse can happen: a woman with anti-synthetase syndrome relapsed 9 months after CD19 CAR-T, a second infusion failed, and T cells against the CAR were found, and a different CAR-T target restored remission.
could_be_wrong.source: Müller et al. (2025), Nature Medicine 31(6) (full text read for the long form)

could_be_wrong.point: In a myasthenia gravis series, one patient's rheumatoid arthritis came back about a year after CD19 CAR-T while his myasthenia stayed in remission.
could_be_wrong.source: Hegelmaier et al. (2026), Cell Reports Medicine (full text read for the long form)

could_be_wrong.point: Stopping inflammation may not undo damage: in one man with autoimmune encephalitis, the cerebellum still shrank by 19% over about two years after a drug-free remission.
could_be_wrong.source: Mougiakakos et al. (2026), Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology (full text read for the long form)

could_be_wrong.point: The only placebo-controlled CAR-T trial in autoimmune disease found so far tested a different, mRNA-based product in myasthenia gravis, and its primary endpoint was changed before unblinding.
could_be_wrong.source: Vu et al. (2026), Nature Medicine (full text read for the long form)

could_be_wrong.point: Long-term risks are open: the FDA requires a boxed warning for T cell cancers after approved CD19- and BCMA-directed CAR-T products for cancer, and a trial guide advises following patients for 15 years or more.
could_be_wrong.source: US FDA (2024); Caricchio et al. (2025), ACR Open Rheumatology (both read in full for the long form)

glossary.plain: A person's own T cell, engineered in a lab to carry a receptor that finds and kills cells with a chosen marker.
An immune cell that can mature into cells that make antibodies, including the autoantibodies that attack the body in lupus.
A marker on the surface of B cells from early stages up to plasmablasts, used here as the CAR-T cells' target.
A mature antibody-making cell; long-lived plasma cells usually lack CD19, so CD19 CAR-T cells largely spare them.
A new B cell that has not yet met its target, the kind that returned after treatment.
Treatment given before the infusion that lowers existing immune cells to make room for the CAR-T cells.
Fever and inflammation caused by a burst of immune signals when CAR-T cells activate, graded 1 (mild) to 4.
Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, a nerve and brain side effect of CAR-T cells.
An agreed definition of lupus remission based on low disease activity scores and low steroid use.
A trial that tests one treatment in several different diseases at the same time.

summary: Three Berlin Science Week panellists study how hormones such as estradiol and cortisol relate to the brain, memory and stress.

Their papers find a hippocampus measure that tracked estradiol in one woman, slightly older-looking brains in current hormone therapy users, less cortisol after a hug in women, and worse navigation on a cortisol tablet in men.
Each is one study, often small or cross-sectional, and larger trials of hormone therapy found no lasting harm or benefit to thinking, so none of this says what hormones do to any one person.
start_here.how_sure_note: Single lab studies, one single-person scan series and one cross-sectional database study; randomized trials point the other way on hormone therapy and thinking.

summary: Only about 1 percent of what you see is sharp, so you take in a packed shelf one fixation at a time.
In one German supermarket pilot, 19 shoppers wore eye trackers, and 81 of 88 unplanned buys had been looked at directly at least once before they were taken.
Looking and choosing go together in many studies, but the pile-up of gaze just before a choice may follow the decision rather than cause it.
start_here.how_sure_note: The narrow window of sharp vision is basic physiology; the shelf findings rest on one small store pilot and lab tasks, and whether looking causes choosing is still argued.

could_be_wrong.point: The store study is a pilot: one supermarket, 19 shoppers and 88 purchases, observational, with results the authors call highly preliminary.
The gaze cascade appears in models even when attention is random and unrelated to the choice, so it is weak evidence that looking causes choosing.
A 2026 reanalysis of several food-choice datasets found no support for two key predictions of the idea that gaze multiplies value, and a post-decision attention model explained the last-look bias.
Making pictures vanish depending on where people looked did not let researchers control their choices; eyes moved to the empty spot of the chosen item about 400 ms before people answered.
could_be_wrong.source: Morii and Sakagami (2015), Frontiers in Psychology

could_be_wrong.point: A follow-up study of food images reported firm evidence against the idea that longer viewing builds preference; viewing time and preference followed an inverted U.
could_be_wrong.source: Wolf et al. (2019), Frontiers in Psychology

could_be_wrong.point: Across 18 articles that steered attention on purpose, the looked-at option was chosen 53.32 percent of the time against 50 percent by chance: a real push, but a small one, and partly due to how attention was steered.

could_be_wrong.point: Wearable eye trackers lose accuracy when people move; in one test, errors reached 5.8 degrees, though most stayed under 3.

summary: Headache after a concussion is common and often looks like migraine, with light and sound sensitivity, nausea and moderate to severe pain.
The link may also run the other way: a review of athlete studies found some evidence, strongest in the better-designed studies, that people who already had migraine recover worse.
Brain injury can set off spreading depolarization, the wave behind migraine aura, in about half of severe cases; whether it follows a mild concussion is not settled.
start_here.how_sure_note: The migraine-like pattern is shown again and again; the reverse link rests on studies with mixed quality, and the aura wave after mild concussion has not been recorded in people.

could_be_wrong.point: In a Norwegian study with two comparison groups, people with mild brain injury had more new headache at 3 months, but by 12 months the uninjured groups reported more headache too, so the injury could not be shown to cause lasting headache.
could_be_wrong.source: Nordhaug et al. (2019), Journal of Neurotrauma

could_be_wrong.point: A 28-day diary study of 64 Danish adults found 13% had only tension-type-like headache, and the authors wrote that their findings dismiss the notion that lasting post-traumatic headache is simply trauma-triggered migraine.
could_be_wrong.source: Ashina et al. (2020a), Journal of Headache and Pain

could_be_wrong.point: A genetic study of 433,010 veterans found strong genetic overlap between migraine and brain injury, but Mendelian randomization found no causal link in either direction.
Most studies in the athlete review found no link between earlier migraine and worse recovery, and migraine history was usually one self-report question.
The 26% clinic figure is preliminary data that the 2026 review cites from another study; it was not collected for that review.
Spreading depolarization after a closed head injury has been recorded in mice, and the authors note that human studies after milder injury are lacking.
A migraine drug that blocks CGRP, fremanezumab, did no better than placebo in 87 adults with post-traumatic headache, which questions whether it works the same way as migraine.
could_be_wrong.source: Teva Branded Pharmaceutical Products R&D (2020), ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03347188 results

glossary.plain: A mild traumatic brain injury caused by a blow or jolt that briefly disturbs how the brain works.
A headache that begins within 7 days of a head injury, by the international diagnostic criteria.
A brain disorder with attacks of moderate to severe headache, often with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound.
Short-lived visual or other sensory changes, such as zigzag lines, that come before or with some migraine attacks.
A slow wave of near-complete electrical silencing that moves across the brain's surface; its milder form, spreading depression, is linked to migraine aura.
A study that searches for every relevant study on a question by a set method and sums up what they found.
A rating of how likely a study's design is to tilt its results away from the truth.
The pattern of features a condition shows in a person, such as which symptoms come with a headache.
A method that uses inherited gene differences to test whether one condition causes another.

lines: Call 911 (or your local emergency number) for red-flag signs after a head injury, such as a headache that gets worse and does not go away, repeated vomiting, seizures, slurred speech, weakness or numbness, unusual drowsiness or confusion, or one pupil larger than the other.
988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (US): call or text 988
Poison Help (US): 1-800-222-1222
safety.note: Education, not medical advice. Anyone with headache after a head injury should talk with a doctor about their own case. No dosing information.

summary: The slime mould Physarum polycephalum is one cell with no neurons, yet in two labs it learned to hesitate less at a bitter bridge it met day after day, the simplest kind of learning, called habituation.
One lab found that cutting or turning the cell's trained tube network made it act as if it had forgotten, but the idea that tubes hold memory is disputed.
Fish skin slime comes from mucous cells, which were smaller in stressed lumpfish in one small study; whether any of this counts as intelligence is still argued.
start_here.how_sure_note: Habituation in the slime mould is shown in two labs; tube memory rests on one lab and is disputed, and the fish result is one small study of one species.

summary: Pisa is 6 hours ahead of Cape Coral, Florida, in winter and in summer, so the flight is a 6 hour jump east.
The body clock stays on Florida time at first, and moving it earlier is harder than moving it later because its own cycle runs a little over 24 hours.
A 2019 guide projects full adjustment by about day 6 for a 6 hour eastward trip, but those day counts come from lab curves and models, not trials of travellers.
start_here.how_sure_note: Time zone and sun data are official and the east versus west difference rests on lab research, while the day counts are model estimates with few field tests.

could_be_wrong.point: The day counts are projections from lab phase response curves and models; the authors say only a few field studies of light plans exist and their results are equivocal.
The 24.2 hour cycle is an average. In 157 adults the measured average was 24.15 hours and only about 21 percent had a cycle under 24 hours, so the east-is-harder rule may not fit everyone.
A systematic overview of jet lag treatments, searched to January 2014, found no studies that tested lifestyle or environmental changes.

Sports data are mixed: in the 2019 to 2020 NBA season teams lost more after westward travel with no significant eastward effect, and in back-to-back games eastward travel was linked to better odds of winning.
could_be_wrong.source: McHill and Chinoy 2020; Charest et al. 2021

could_be_wrong.point: Wearable data from 64,847 trips showed sleep timing had not fully returned 15 days after long trips, longer than the guides suggest; two of the four authors work for or advise the ring maker, as the paper discloses.
No published guide covers an 11 hour eastward shift, and no study has tracked Florida to Italy travellers in particular; the closest field study followed 28 travellers from North America to Rome.

summary: Alex Valentina won the Art and Photography award at Psychedelics Design 2026 for work about natural forms seen up close, which he said can feel a little uncomfortable.
In one online survey of 284 students, everyone found skin disease pictures uncomfortable, while only people who scored high on a trypophobia questionnaire found clusters of holes about as bad.
Most researchers now favour a disgust reflex aimed at signs of disease as the cause, but that idea is still being tested, and simple image statistics did not explain the effect.
start_here.how_sure_note: The survey result held in both rounds and under two ways of grouping people, but it comes from students at one university, and the cause is still debated.

could_be_wrong.point: The central survey used psychology students at one university, and its 23.6% above the cut-off is higher than the 7 to 17% in earlier work, so the exact share may not travel.
Priming people with words about skin problems raised discomfort with clusters in a first run of 903 people, but a second run of 541 did not repeat it.
Rural villagers in southwest China reacted less to clusters than city students, the opposite of what a simple disease account expects, though the villagers were much older.
In 14 high scorers, clusters raised heart rate and blood flow at the back of the head, which leans toward fear, so the authors think fear and disgust may both be present.
could_be_wrong.source: Le, Cole and Wilkins (2020), Journal of Affective Disorders

glossary.plain: A strong discomfort, mostly disgust, at the sight of dense clusters of small holes or bumps.
A 17-item self-report scale scored from 17 to 85, with scores above 31 counted as trypophobic.
A classic set of photographs of everyday textures such as bark, cloth, stone and brick, used in vision research.
Dividing people into a higher and a lower group at the middle score.
How fine or coarse the detail in an image is, from broad shapes to tiny edges.
Two parts of an image's make-up: phase holds where edges and shapes sit, amplitude holds how much contrast there is at each scale of detail.
A number from minus 1 to 1 showing how closely two groups put the same items in the same order.
Fast, automatic reactions, led by disgust, that keep people away from possible sources of infection.
A slow brain-wave over the top of the head that grows when a picture holds our attention because it matters to us.

summary: KojiGotchi, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026, is a pink wearable egg that its makers say grows rice koji, the mould behind miso, soy sauce and sake, on the wearer's body heat.
The makers' own trials grew one worn batch in 60 hours after a back-pocket test grew almost nothing; no independent study of the device exists yet.
Lab studies show koji growth and smell change with time, water and temperature, and koji makers keep the mould warmer than the makers' stated range, so the body-heat claim is plausible but untested.
start_here.how_sure_note: The koji science is well studied, but the device rests on the makers' own few unreviewed trials.

could_be_wrong.point: Koji makers give an optimum of 35 to 38 °C, above the makers' stated 25 to 35 °C, so the device may grow koji slowly.
could_be_wrong.source: Kusumoto et al. (2021), Journal of Fungi

could_be_wrong.point: A closed armpit averaged 36.5 °C in 141 healthy young adults, warmer than the makers' "about 32 °C" for skin; the egg hangs against the chest, and its chamber temperature over a full day is unpublished.
could_be_wrong.source: Marui et al. (2017), Journal of Physiological Anthropology

could_be_wrong.point: The makers' first back-pocket trial was largely unsuccessful, their trials are not peer reviewed, and the incubator comparison is described in words, not numbers.

Uncooled koji can pass 50 °C and stop growing, and heat-tolerant Bacillus bacteria rise fast above 35 °C, so a warm, unstirred batch can go wrong; the makers also saw contamination where rice overheated.
could_be_wrong.source: Yamashita (2021), Journal of Fungi (the author works for a koji starter maker)

could_be_wrong.point: Some koji strains still carry the whole aflatoxin gene cluster, even though no properly identified Aspergillus oryzae strain has been shown to make aflatoxin.
Cyclopiazonic acid and beta-nitropropionic acid are real toxins reported from authentic Aspergillus oryzae strains, which is why industrial users screen for them.
could_be_wrong.source: Frisvad et al. (2018), Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology

could_be_wrong.point: Which wild mould koji came from is still argued: a 23-species comparison points to two other species, though with one genome per species.
The miso comparison used one sample of each of four misos, so it describes these products rather than all miso.
could_be_wrong.source: Kothe et al. (2026), Frontiers in Microbiology

summary: Hempcrete, a mix of hemp core, lime and water, can store some carbon, but life-cycle studies range from a net store to a net source depending on how it is made and used.
The lime takes carbon back from the air only slowly, and measurements found far less of it than many carbon accounts assume.
Lab tests show it soaks up and releases moisture well, but indoor humidity has been measured in only one lived-in house, never compared with homes built another way.
start_here.how_sure_note: Moderate for carbon storage under good conditions, since every whole-wall total is modelled; early for humidity in real homes.

could_be_wrong.point: In measured blocks, the lime below 6 cm barely carbonated after 240 days, far less than the full carbonation many carbon accounts assume.
A review of the measurements found the assumption of full carbonation seems overestimated.
In one life-cycle study a 20 cm wall was a net source and the balance only broke even at 22 cm, and repeated renewals of the coating could tip it positive.
A life-cycle study left out indirect land use and end of life, noting that no hempcrete structure has yet been dismantled.
Hempcrete walls scored worse than a reference wall on ecosystem damage, mainly from the land used to grow hemp.
Indoor humidity has been measured in only one lived-in hempcrete house, with no comparison house.
Lime-hemp renders cured in a factory all showed new microbial growth, so the material does not ensure protection from bio-decay.
In a test wall, vapour stayed high inside for 15 days and could condense if the temperature dropped.
Plastering lowers a hempcrete wall's moisture buffering compared with bare lab samples.
In a European fire test series, all hemp-lime formulations were prone to smouldering.

glossary.plain: A building material made of chopped hemp core, a lime binder and water, packed around a timber frame as insulation.
The woody inner core of the hemp stem, chopped into small pieces.
The glue in hempcrete, made from limestone, that slowly hardens by taking carbon dioxide from the air.
The slow reaction in which lime takes carbon dioxide from the air and turns back into a stone-like carbonate.
A method that adds up a product's environmental effects from growing or mining the raw materials to disposal.
A way of counting all greenhouse gases as the amount of carbon dioxide that would warm the planet the same.
A material's ability to soak up water vapour from humid air and release it when the air dries.
How easily heat passes through a material; lower numbers insulate better.
Material packed between the parts of a frame that carries no weight of its own.

law_policy.citation: International Code Council, 2024 International Residential Code, Appendix BL: Hemp-lime (hempcrete) construction
law_policy.status: Appendix BL is part of the 2024 model code for houses and limits hempcrete to nonstructural infill; its base text says hemp-lime walls do not have a fire-resistance rating. A trade magazine reported that a change adding three one-hour fire-rated walls passed 11 to 0 at ICC hearings in Cleveland in October 2025 for the 2027 code; the final 2027 text could not be checked because the ICC site blocks our client. Text read as reproduced in a Washington State adoption proposal.

summary: The shaggy inkcap really does digest its own cap into black ink as it matures, and white rot fungi such as turkey tail really do break down lignin, the tough material in wood.
Using fungi to clean up old pollution in open ground is much less proven: in a Swedish field trial, oyster mushrooms grew well on aged DDT soil and the DDT did not measurably fall.
For plastic, reviewers say weight loss or a film of microbes is weak evidence, and they ask for proof that the plastic's carbon was used up.
start_here.how_sure_note: The fungal biology rests on several studies and a review and is well established; the cleanup evidence rests on one small field trial and reviews of mostly lab work.

could_be_wrong.point: The Swedish null result is small and short: three replicates, one site and six weeks in the field. The authors say it should not be taken as evidence that fungal cleanup is ineffective under other conditions.

The Swedish test used a tired waste product. The spent substrate's lignin-enzyme activity was about ten times lower than before the mushroom crop, and in the pots it fell below what the assay could detect.

Managed piles may do better than open ground. Casey's team describes pilot trials on 10 and 7 tonnes of soil that reported 94 percent breakdown of PCBs and 98 percent of PAHs; the post could not read those two papers in full.

Feeding the soil often did as much as adding fungus. In a review of oil cleanup, no-fungus controls removed 80 percent against 86 percent with oyster mushroom in one soil, and 69 against 68 percent in sub-arctic soil boxes. The review was written within the EU LIFE MySOIL project, and three authors work for remediation companies.

White rot fungi may be the wrong candidates. A Duke University team wrote that the group has been found unreliable when used at scale in the field, and isolated 132 native fungi, mostly ascomycetes, from a creosote site.

Lost weight can hide how little plastic is eaten. A Sri Lankan wood-decay fungus cut a polyethylene film's weight by 46.8 percent in 88 days, while only 3.1 percent of its carbon came off as carbon dioxide.
Fungal water filters are untested outside the lab: a systematic review found 156 mycofiltration experiments from 1990 to 2023, every one in a laboratory, with no standard methods.
The inkcap studies each used one strain, and the exact trigger for the cap's self-digestion is still unknown.

glossary.plain: Self-digestion, in which a living thing's own enzymes break down its tissue, as when an inkcap's cap turns to ink.
The stiff, waterproofing polymer that binds the fibres in wood and makes it hard to digest.
A kind of wood decay in which fungi remove lignin and leave pale, stringy cellulose behind.
A single thread of a fungus; a mass of hyphae is called mycelium.
Using fungi to break down or take up pollution in soil or water.
The straw, sawdust or other material left over after a crop of farmed mushrooms, still full of fungal threads.
A pollutant that has sat in soil for years and become tightly bound to it, which makes it harder for microbes and enzymes to reach.
Complete breakdown of a material into carbon dioxide, water and living cells, the proof reviewers ask for before saying a plastic was eaten.
A thin, sticky layer of microbes growing on a surface.

summary: On the December 2026 solstice, US Naval Observatory tables give Pisa 8 hours 55 minutes of daylight and Honolulu 10 hours 50 minutes, a gap that comes from latitude alone.
Daylight is the main time signal for the brain's master clock, the suprachiasmatic nuclei, which the retina reaches along its own nerve tract.
The day lengths are measurements and the light pathway is well established; whether short winter days lower mood is a mixed and contested question.

could_be_wrong.point: The winter mood story is mixed. A systematic review of 41 studies called the field fragmented: 13 found more depression in winter and the rest found no seasonal pattern or a peak in another season.
The same review reports a survey of 34,294 people across the United States that found no seasonal difference in depression.

In 5,282 Dutch adults, winter was not the low point for mood, seasonal differences were small, they appeared only in people high in neuroticism, and 503 people who answered twice showed no reliable change.

A pre-registered year-long study of 418 adults in Germany, Switzerland and Austria found no seasonal pattern in fatigue severity, daytime sleepiness, insomnia or sleep quality. The lead author reports talk and workshop fees from several companies, listed in the paper.
In Swedish office workers, time spent in bright daylight did not track mood from day to day.
Winter melatonin changes look modest: a study of 334 adults in Spain found only a non-significant trend toward higher winter levels.

summary: Tractor Beam, a speculative fiction publication, won Visual Design and Branding at Psychedelics Design 2026, and its founders said the design was inspired by the earth's layers.
In one lab study, black stripes felt more uncomfortable and made the pupil tighten more as they got finer or covered more of the screen, and discomfort built up over repeated viewings.
The findings come from one lab and young adults viewing black stripes, and why some people are more bothered than others is still unclear.

could_be_wrong.point: The study assumed that people who rated more discomfort are more visually sensitive, without checking this against validated clinical measures.
Boredom, drowsiness and fatigue also shrink the pupil in long sessions; the authors argue these cannot fully explain the rising discomfort, but they likely contribute.
With no chin rest, people who sat close reported more discomfort and tightening, so focusing effort may have played a part; the paradox analysis rests on 42 of 70 people.
In 166 adults, and in groups of 22 high and 27 low pattern sensitivity, visual gamma oscillations showed no link to discomfort, against the leading over-excitation theory.
In 160 adults, resting GABA and glutamate in the visual cortex did not track pattern glare as the over-excitation theory predicts.
In 26 students, the peak of discomfort across stripe widths was 'not as clear cut' as often described.
An image statistics study found the effect of spectral slope on unpleasantness weak and opposite to earlier work.
A review by 32 authors notes that tests of visual discomfort are subjective and poorly standardised.

A 2024 study filmed real insects at lamps and found they keep their backs turned to the brightest light, which in nature is the sky, so near a lamp they circle, stall or flip over.

could_be_wrong.point: The study did not test how far away a lamp starts to affect insects; the authors suggest lights may trap passing insects more than draw them in from afar.
Classing each video as orbit, stall or flip was, in the authors' word, somewhat subjective, and tracking worked best on large insects while most insects at the light were under a centimetre long.
Not every insect fits: oleander hawkmoths in the lab ignored the bulbs and vinegar flies were unaffected, and the team cannot yet say why insects ignore a low moon.

In a harmonic radar test in Germany, only 2 of 50 released moths ended their flight at a streetlight 85 metres away, though the lights still bent the paths of many; the lamps were older sodium lamps and LEDs were not tested.
Counting insects at lamps records only where an animal ended up, so it misses bent paths and barriers, and the radar result still needs repeating with blue-rich LEDs.
Urban moth populations in a common-garden test flew to light about 30% less than rural ones, so the reflex is not fixed and may be evolving under city lights.

summary: A small 2011 study reported more gray matter in the hippocampus and other regions after an eight-week mindfulness course.
Two larger randomized studies, with 218 and 585 people, found no such gain, including in the exact regions the 2011 study named.
So short mindfulness courses have not been shown to change brain structure; effects on brain function, and of much longer practice, are still open questions.
start_here.how_sure_note: The early gains came from small, non-randomized samples, and the two large randomized trials agree on no structural change from short courses.

could_be_wrong.point: The 2011 groups were not randomized and the sample was small; the authors say replication is necessary.
The 2022 null tested healthy volunteers and an eight-week course; the authors suggest longer training, or one focused practice, might be needed to change structure.
A nine-month training study of 332 adults reported cortical thickening after a breathing and body-scan module, mostly compared with other training modules.
A meta-analysis of 25 studies found only the right anterior insula consistent, with signs that small studies overstate effects.
Fifteen researchers warned that head motion, breathing and pre-existing differences can mimic training effects, and called for large preregistered trials.
A 2023 meta-analysis reporting brain changes was retracted in July 2025 because four null papers, about 40% of participants, were left out; the authors disagree with the retraction.
A 2026 scoping review of nine studies found most reported gains but judged the evidence insufficient for firm conclusions about cause or consistency.
In a population study of 3,742 people, those who meditated had a smaller right amygdala and more stress symptoms, which may mean people with certain brains or moods choose meditation.

summary: Hadza foragers in Tanzania walk many kilometres a day, yet a 2012 study found they burn about the same daily energy for their body size as Western adults.
The team measured energy with doubly labelled water over 11 days in 30 adults and found activity level higher in men and only slightly higher in women.
It is one study of one community; later pooled data agree on the Hadza, while other studies argue that energy use keeps rising with activity in some groups.
start_here.how_sure_note: The method is well validated and a 2025 pooled study repeated the Hadza result, but the sample is small, resting energy was estimated, and how firm the limit is remains disputed.

annotations.note: Doubly labelled water in 30 Hadza adults over 11 days: after adjusting for lean mass and age, daily energy did not differ from Western adults, though activity level was higher. Resting energy was estimated rather than measured, the sample is one community in one season, and the authors ask for measurements in other hunter-gatherers.
annotations.funding: Funding was received from the National Science Foundation, Washington University, and the University of Arizona; the funders had no role in the study (re-read Nov 20, 2026).
annotations.conflicts: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.

could_be_wrong.point: Hadza resting energy was estimated from equations, so the activity level figures for the Hadza rest on an estimate, and the study covered one community in one season.
In 584 adults aged 50 to 74 in Pittsburgh, daily energy rose in a straight line with activity, with a flat curve only in people losing weight.
In 75 very active adults, daily energy kept rising in a straight line with training volume and resting energy did not drop.
Twelve Tuvan herders in deep winter cold burned well above the energy predicted for their size, counter evidence to a firm ceiling.
A critical review argues the constrained model's statistics and data are weak and notes that no randomised trial has been built to test it directly.
In pooled data from 1,754 adults, about 28% of activity energy was offset on average, so the limit looks partial, and the analysis was mainly cross-sectional.
In a trial secondary analysis of 29 exercisers, the 14 who compensated showed no slowdown in sleeping or resting energy, so where the missing energy goes is still unknown.
A 2025 letter challenged doubly labelled water itself; the study team replied defending it, and the debate is open.

glossary.plain: Water tagged with rare forms of hydrogen and oxygen; how fast they leave the body in urine shows how much energy was burned.
All the energy the body uses in a day, usually counted in kilocalories.
The energy the body uses at complete rest just to stay alive.
Daily energy divided by resting energy, a rough index of how active someone is.
Body weight minus fat: muscle, organs, bone and water.
The idea that the body keeps daily energy use within a fairly narrow range by spending less elsewhere when activity rises.
The share of extra activity energy that does not show up in the daily total.
Communities that live mainly on wild foods they hunt and gather.
A study that compares different people at one point in time instead of following them.
